#8291. Welcome to the Outdoor Life Shop: Your New Destination for the Best Hunting, Fishing, and Camping Gear

Published Nov 12, 2026 1:14 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Since our very first issue published in 1898, Outdoor Life has covered outdoor gear with independence and rigor. From Jack O’Connor’s old gun columns to today’s in-depth video reviews, field testing gear and reporting the results has always been part of our publication’s DNA.

Which is why I am excited to now introduce our new online gear shop, which represents the culmination of more than a century of gear coverage. This new online retail site will carry a wide variety of quality outdoor products, and purchases made from the site will help to power the Outdoor Life you know and love into the future. There are a few key points that longtime OL readers should know.

If you’ve followed Outdoor Life closely, you know that we’re not scared to piss off folks on occasion. This often includes manufacturers who have overhyped their products. That’s because we believe that reader trust is OL’s single most important asset. If we report the truth, good or bad, we have faith that you will keep coming back. This has been the promise that the OL editors made at the very beginning, and it’s the contract we uphold today.

In all of our gear reviews and buying guides, we will continue to celebrate the top-performing products (whether they are carried in the Outdoor Life shop or not). Likewise, if a product falls short, we’ll continue to call out those flaws.

Unlike some other media outlets in our space, we have no editorial obligation to a single brand. We shoot, hunt with, and wear whatever is new and noteworthy, because that makes the most interesting content. This will continue, regardless of which brands are carried in the shop. Simply scan a few of our recent gear reviews (like our rifle scope test or binocular test) and you will find this to be true.

Over time, the shop will begin to host content from the hundreds of gear reviews we’ve written through the years. Beyond basic specs and product descriptions, the Outdoor Life shop will include details about how the products actually performed during testing. Our “editor’s picks” will highlight the top performing items in a category. Video reviews will show how products work (or don’t work) in the field.

Our aim will be to educate the reader, or potential customer, about the gear they are considering buying, whether they end up buying it from us or someone else.

The OL team is proud that we already spend a ton of time and effort producing the most in-depth gun and gear reviews in the outdoor space. We have been able to fund these efforts by linking to online retailers who sell the gear that we cover. If one of our readers purchases a product from these online retailers, we made a small commission. Added up over the course of the year, these commissions become a meaningful source of revenue that powers our editorial team to create more content.

At its best, it’s a system of meritocracy. Those who create the best content grow the biggest audiences and, in turn, make the most money — to make more content.

But that system has been corrupted with the popularization of Artificial Intelligence. Now, more and more folks are simply asking ChatGPT or Claude, “what’s the best wader for duck hunting?” These chatbots scrape online articles to produce an answer for the user, who then makes their purchase. That hunter will rarely see the original source material. In other words they will never come to our reviews and field tests at Outdoor Life.

And the chatbots don’t much care if they are lifting content from OutdoorLife.com or someone’s basement blog, or even a manufacturer’s own website. In time, this will lead to the degradation (I believe the modern term is “enshittification”) of  gear reviews, and, well, first-hand expert information in general.

Our way to combat this is to own the online shop ourselves. We believe that so long as we have the best and most thorough information, and the best available products, the reader will end up with us.

In the weeks and months to come, we will be adding many more brands and gear categories to the shop. We’ll be offering deals on select products that have performed admirably in our field testing. And we’ll be turning out a lot more stories and videos.

If you’re looking to purchase some new gear, I do hope you check out the OL shop. But the truth is, there are many reasons to love the outdoors and our passion for quality gear is only a sliver of Outdoor Life.  So, after all these years, thank you for reading, following, and watching.

Alex Robinson is Outdoor Life’s editor-in-chief. He oversees an ace team of writers, photographers, and editors who are scattered across the continent and cover everything from backcountry sheep hunting to trail running.

#8290. Scarpa Golden Gate LT Review: Moderate Stack Is So Back

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Trail shoes with a moderate stack are becoming harder to find. New trail models either have inches of soft, bouncy foam underfoot (sometimes with a carbon plate), or they are minimalist models that let your feet feel every pebble. Fortunately, a few that balance protection and ground feel still exist. I’ve just discovered one: the Scarpa Golden Gate LT.

Scarpa is an Italian mountain brand based in the Dolomites. Specializing in mountain climbing footwear, elite mountaineers historically wore the brand’s lightweight mountain shoes to cross rugged terrain. Scarpa’s trail running shoes reflect that heritage; they’re known for their rugged protection and firm, surefooted ride. But many trail runners who don’t live in places like the Alps or the White Mountains don’t need an indestructible mountain running boot. Enter Scarpa’s new trail shoe line-up.

The Golden Gate LT is Scarpa’s lightweight “door-to-trail” shoe meant for a broader trail running audience who want a single functional trainer on runs that bridge varied terrain, from asphalt to gravel to rocky singletrack. I put the shoe’s prowess to the test across Los Angeles’s urban streets, steep horse trails, and sandy beaches.

Weight: 10.5oz (men’s 9, women’s 10) Stack Height: 30 – 24 mm Heel-to-Toe Drop: 6 mm

+ Handles road-to-trail transitions smoothly + Stable base + Excellent traction – Fit too narrow for wide feet – Slightly sluggish on quick turnover

The Golden Gate LT may be a departure from Scarpa’s roots in many ways, but not in style: I received a hot orange-white colorway that immediately reminded me of the Orange Crush soda can and blends right in with Scarpa’s line up of mountain running shoes and ski boots. Though the flashy look isn’t entirely my style, I’m just glad it’s not a monster truck of a trail shoe.

Most of my test runs were on the hilly, paved roads of my neighborhood. Cruising through the familiar streets, I was happy to find that while cushioned, my landings weren’t squishy at all. Instead, I noticed a small bounciness in the midsole — like I was running on a shallow trampoline. That’s likely because Scarpa blended 20% PEBAX into the EVA compound midsole to provide extra responsiveness for what I call the “road” side of the hybrid shoe’s performance.

Taking the shoes uphill, the rebound was still there but didn’t do the heavy lifting for me. That changed, however, when I picked up the pace. With some downhill momentum, my stride lengthened, and any feeling of a firm trail shoe was completely gone. At quicker paces, the bounce takes over and helps maintain speed, feeling like an uptempo road shoe. Normally I don’t like shoes with much cushioning, but the upper’s gentle TPU-reinforced support wrapped my feet so nicely that I felt confident running faster and farther.

Later, I took them out for a long run mostly on trails, connected by some roads, to see how they held up on different surfaces. On the trails, the midsole bounce was less noticeable, which I appreciated, as bouncing over unstable surfaces doesn’t make sense to me.

Compared to other trail models I’ve worn, the lugs are far more flexible, providing amazing traction across sand, dirt, and rocks. The flexibility of the outsole kept my stride smooth and stable on uneven trails and helped the shoe maintain its beginning-of-the-run feeling late into a 14-mile long run. Overall, the outsole’s efficiency felt more alive on the trails than on paved surfaces.

If you’re crazy, like me, and sprint down steep trails, you’ll appreciate the moderate, 24 mm stack under the forefoot, making toe-offs effortless, helping short, quick strides remain stable, and ensuring that tight cornering is no problem. The 30 mm heel stack, however, which contributed to the smooth cushioning on the road, could sometimes feel a bit sluggish on steep trail descents. I prefer 4 mm-drop shoes to keep my steps quick and agile and maximize the thrill of heading downhill with my hair on fire. But if you’re more sensible and take it easy on descents, then the 6 mm drop shouldn’t be a problem at all.

Back on the roads toward the end of my long run, I felt the same road-shoe ride I get on my neighborhood runs. Though my legs were more tired after battling the dusty, hilly terrain, the flexibility of the upper and the outsole encouraged me to keep my pace until the end of the run.

Durability seems mixed so far: After testing the shoe for a month of road and trail runs, the outsole has progressively felt more flexible under my feet and can take on rocks and tough objects on the trails. The edges of the lugs have retained their sharp definition from when it was new, while the upper and overall cushioning still feel just as comfortable. The midsole bounce, however, is much gentler than when it was new (for better or worse), and the bright Orange Crush splash has since faded.

Quality moderate-stack trail shoes are becoming harder to find. If your favorite model lost its way in the “space-age arms race of trail super shoes,” as our editor Cade Michael aptly put it, and you don’t like feeling every rock beneath your feet through a thin minimalist sole, this one’s for you.

Runners with narrow or medium-narrow feet who prefer a tight fit should appreciate this shoe. The heel and midfoot’s gentle padding hug my narrow feet quite tightly, and the toe box has some room for toe splay, though it’s not wide — it’s right in the middle. This close-fitting shape is useful for tight cornering and platform stability, but if you have wide feet and need breathing space for your toes, the M2C H1, an Altra, or a Topo trail shoe might be a better fit.

So, is this the lower-stacked hybrid shoe that we’ve been waiting for? With its dual personality, the Golden Gate LT certainly handles roads and trails like it’s built for both. You can also totally wear this exclusively as a trail shoe for runs of any length. Though difficult trails with demanding terrain may not be its greatest strength, this shoe provides a comfortable, energetic ride on all other terrain, achieving exactly what it’s designed for.

#8288. Video: The Ultimate Squirrel Rifle

Published Nov 12, 2026 3:00 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Some people dream of assembling a long-range rifle capable of ringing one-MOA targets at 1,000 yards. Others dream of an ultralight mountain rifle that’s easy to carry for miles and can make a single precision shot. I dream of an ultra-quiet, accurate, and handy rifle for dropping squirrels out of trees. Here’s how I turned a CZ 457 into my dream gun and how it performed in my testing this fall.

The base rifle for this build is a CZ 457 American. I kept the American’s stock because I love a wood stock on a hunting rifle, and its ergonomics work great for squirrel hunting. There are a ton of ultralight chassis you can go with, but wood and squirrel hunting just go together. I did have to sand down the inside of the stock to create room for the new barrel, but that’s easy to do with a palm sander, a dowel wrapped in sandpaper, or every garage gunsmith’s favorite tool: a Dremel.

Lilja makes CZ 457 pre-fit barrels that are fantastic for competition shooting, but I wanted something lighter. That’s why I went with a 16-inch Proof Research pre-fit barrel. One of the great things about the CZ 457 is that the barrel changes are a piece of cake. You simply loosen two set screws to remove the barrel and the new one slides right into the action.

The entire Nightforce NX6 line is fantastic, and the 2-12x F1 variant is perfect for a versatile rimfire. It can take a 50-yard head shot on a squirrel or snap shoot one up close. It also makes this rifle excellent for shooting long range. Dialing in to 300 yards and ringing steel is quite easy with this setup. The scope is fairly light and short, so I don’t think I’m giving up much in terms of weight compared to a traditional 3-9x, but I’m gaining a lot of capability and versatility.

This suppressor is quiet, light, relatively affordable, and easy to clean — everything I look for in a .22 can. There are plenty of other great options like the Dead Air RXD22Ti and the CAT BEN 22 Ti. A .22 silencer is a must-have accessory because it makes shooting a rimfire significantly more fun.

I added an Area 419 CZ 457 Scope Base and bolt handle to my 457 action. The rail makes it much easier to mount scopes and adds some elevation, so I can plink with this rifle out to 300 yards. The bolt handle makes running the bolt easier than the stock round one. One final upgrade I’d like to make is the Timney CZ 457 Trigger.

For accuracy testing, I shot SK Rifle Match, Lapua Center X, and CCI Select. I shot five, five-shot groups with each. All three averaged around a 1/2-inch group at 50 yards. I was most impressed by how well this barrel shot CCI Select, which is relatively inexpensive compared to other ammo I shot.

The new barrel is definitely accurate, and it also made this rifle significantly easier to maneuver in the woods. With the rifle slung over my shoulder it was unobtrusive as I weaved my way through thick cover. When I saw a squirrel, the rifle came to my shoulder quickly and was easy to get stable.

The result of this build is a rifle that’s fun to shoot on the range and a joy to carry in the woods. To me, it perfectly blends a nostalgic wood-stock rifle with modern features. Is it a bit extreme for a squirrel gun? You betcha. But I love this rifle all the same.

No problem, there are insulated and waterproof jackets that could survive a January lobster boat ride on the Atlantic. Ice storm? There are boots with steel studs and excellent traction. You know you’re not a fair-weather skier, so here are 10 picks to help you outlast every other diehard out there. Then pick where to put it all to work: start with SKI’s resort guide and our list of the best ski resorts in the East, live now.

If you like high edge angles and a low-volume fit, the Kaliber Pro 120 LV GW BOA is for you. Designed for groomers and hardpack snow, this ski boot prioritizes precision, control and a secure fit. The BOA Fit System allows for a close wrap around the leg and foot, while softer plastic makes the boot easy to get on and off. The back of the shell features stiffer plastic for more stability and power. The low-volume 98mm last means a high-performance fit, but Liquid Fit material helps the liner mold better to your foot.

If you’re looking to hone your carving chops, the Elan Ace SC2 S will help you progress. With a turn-happy 74-millimeter waist and a confidence-boosting wood and fiberglass construction, the ski is designed to turn easily. Thanks to tip rocker, the Ace SC2 rolls into a turn, while the full Power Cap sidewall provides enough edge grip to handle hard conditions. The best news of all: The Ace SC2 S comes with a pair of Elan bindings for a turnkey skiing experience at an affordable price.

Serious East Coast skiers will find an ally in the Nordica Dobermann Multipista 80 DC. With a 16-meter turn radius, these carving skis eat up corduroy and hardpack snow for breakfast with short-swing turns, but when afternoon push piles show up, the tails know how to heel and release. Nordica’s Energy 2 Ti Pulse Core construction means that a full wood core is sandwiched between two sheets of titanal, with an elastomer layer that smooths out the ride and absorbs vibrations. Though not as burly as the Enforcer line, the Dobermann Multipista 80 DC holds an edge like a race ski and powers through choppy conditions like a frontside ski.

There’s a case to be made that Norway and New England share some similar ski days, so rest assured, the Norwegian-based Norrona knows how to keep skiers protected. Whether cold and clear or wet and stormy, this insulated ski jacket is designed to keep skiers warm and dry. The Gore-Tex 2-layer laminate and fully sealed seams are like a fortress from the elements. PrimaLoft Silver Eco insulation has a high warmth-to-weight ratio, trapping heat in key areas, but keeping the jacket streamlined enough to make it backpack-friendly. More storm-taming features include a helmet-compatible hood, a powder skirt and thumbhole cuffs.

A timeless technical fleece, the Evolved Air ½ Zip moves from skiing to après. Bluesign-approved recycled polyester adds warmth and breathability while wicking moisture. The half-zip adds deep venting from the collar to the chest when needed, or high neck protection when temps plummet. A vertical zippered chest pocket offers secure storage for the items you need stashed for the day. Color options include classic black or washed navy.

Once you try the Emilie High Waist Capri Pant, you’ll be hooked. This down-insulated capri pant has 450 fill down on front and back panels to keep you warm on cold chairlift seats and windy ridgelines. The capri style goes below the knees, keeping your precious ligaments warm without getting in the way of your boot top. It’s streamlined enough to fit under shell pants, and thanks to the elastic side panels, can move along with you. They’re so cozy, you might end up wearing them all winter long.

This ski and binding combo delivers rigidity and control on even the crispiest of resort runs. The edge-to-edge steel layer lends itself to hard turns and the double steel layer construction gives you optimal power transmission and grip. The full Sidewall Sandwich keeps you confident in your edge control while the Power Woodcore dampens vibration and keeps you stable under speed. Plus, the black metal vapor coating and laser engraving gives each ski a durable, one-of-a-kind finish.

Capilene’s talent for wicking moisture helps make the Capilene Thermal Weight Boot-Length bottom a great choice for a long day skiing. The Polartec Power Grid fabric saves the day with a stretchy combo of recycled polyester and spandex for warmth without inhibiting movement. There’s even a plant-based treatment to control odor—your ski buddies will thank you. Diehard skiers will appreciate the boot-length cut since every expert knows that baselayer bunching can ruin a day on the slopes.

“Prevail” is an apt name for Outdoor Research’s heated Gore-Tex glove because having warm hands and fingers allows you to prevail even during an ice storm. On its own, this  gauntlet-style ski glove is designed for warmth and dryness, thanks to EnduraLoft insulation and a Gore-Tex waterproof and windproof insert. A goat leather palm gives the glove good grip for holding ski poles, but the battery-powered heat inside the glove is the game changer. The rechargeable lithium batteries can last for 8 hours on low, 5 hours on medium or 2.5 hours on high.

Ice Coast Diehards are serious about their traction—whether it’s their car tires or winter boots. Icebug is the queen of grip thanks to BUGrip technology, which incorporates carbide-tip steel studs onto the outsoles of the boots. Much like studded snow tires, the steel tips bite into ice and snowy surfaces to help reduce slips. The Ivalo 4 BUGrip has fleece insulation and over-the-ankle coverage for snowy excursions, plus a front zipper for easy entry and exit.

Trying to put on cold boots can be an excruciating experience when the plastic stiffens. Enter the Kulkea Thermal Kart Heated Ski Boot Bag. The Advanced Warming System wraps your shells in warmth, powered by a car or wall outlet, so you can warm your boots on the drive to the resort or in the lodge. The 40-liter bag has zippered front stash pockets for accessories and a helmet sling to complete the kit. The sleek backpack-style bag is carry-on-friendly for your ski trip out West.

#8283. No Cameras, No Bait. Old-School Tactics Pay Off for Ohio Bowhunter with 190-Class Buck

Published Nov 12, 2026 5:46 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

It was Dave Talbott’s first year hunting a small farm in southeast Ohio. The property, which is owned by a family friend, has rolling hills and steep hardwoods and is scattered with hayfields.

“I never walked the farm until the week just before bow season opened,” says Talbott, who lives in Logan. “I found good deer sign, with lots of buck rubs on trees.”

Talbott didn’t set any trail cameras or bait. Instead, when the season opened, he just walked the woods, scouting and hunting different locations. He used a lightweight tree saddle and climbing sticks to check areas quickly and quietly.

“I sat in six different trees over 12 hunts, moving according to wind and weather conditions,” says the 26-year-old, who works in heavy construction.

On the morning of Nov. 7, he hunted a pinch point where he knew a few does were bedded.

“But I didn’t like the place and started walking the farm again when I climbed down that morning.”

It was the first cold day of autumn, cloudy and with temperatures around 40 degrees. Talbott located a couple of fresh scrapes, and climbed into a nearby tree around 1:30 p.m. to hunt that afternoon. He didn’t see much until about 4:30. That’s when he spotted a big deer headed his way along the field edge.

“I knew he was big, and a shooter, and it all happened very fast.”

When the buck stepped behind some brush 15 yards from Talbott, he drew. The deer stepped into an opening, and Talbott released his arrow.

Talbott saw the deer run about 30 yards and, pouring blood, enter the timber toward a distant hayfield. Then it disappeared over a hill.

“I was shaking uncontrollably when I called my wife, dad, and best friend [Brady Garren] and told them what had happened,” Talbott says. “Dad and Brady got there after sunset to help me look.”

Carrying flashlights, the three men followed a blood trail for about 150 yards. But the trail petered out. Then they heard thrashing in a nearby ravine. Thinking it might be Talbott’s buck, they backed out and called in Triple BC Deer Drone Recovery for assistance.

“They got there with a drone a couple hours later,” says Talbott. “They flew the drone to where we last found blood and in just a minute the buck was found in the ravine, but its head was up.”

They waited an hour and flew the drone again but saw just a slight movement from the buck. An hour later when they flew the drone a third and final time, they saw the buck was dead.

By then, around 11:30 p.m., more friends had arrived and seven people went into the ravine to help haul out Talbott’s huge buck.

“I knew he was a great buck, but I had no idea he was that big until I walked up to him,” Talbott says. “I was beyond ecstatic.”

It was after midnight by the time they field dressed the buck and dragged it 600 yards to the truck. They loaded it and drove to a friend’s cooler.

The next day Talbott’s wife, Alison, took photos before they caped the buck and processed the meat. The buck has 16 points and is an estimated 5.5 years old.

Read Next: Counter Drone Technology Has Come to Deer Hunting and Landowners Are Starting to Fight Back

“My taxidermist says it should score about 190 inches,” says Talbott. “The whole thing is so unreal I can’t explain how I feel. I spent a lot of time there hunting and learning the farm, how to use the wind and where the deer were bedding and scraping … It’s just an incredible experience.”

Bob McNally has been an outdoor writer since shortly after the earth’s crust cooled. He has written 12 outdoor books, more than 5,000 outdoor magazine stories (including many for Outdoor Life) and more newspaper outdoor columns and features than there are hairs on a grizzly bear.

#8281. The 11 Best Mid-Priced Hunting Rifles of 2026

Published Nov 12, 2026 6:15 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

The latest for gun hunters and competitive shooters.

Long before I was a writer at Outdoor Life, I was an OL reader, and mid-priced hunting rifles were my bread and butter. I grew up with modest means, so when it came to buying a hunting rifle, I sought out the best information I could in order to spend my money wisely. I know you appreciate value and an honest evaluation, especially when it comes to hunting rifles.

A hunting rifle is a significant purchase for most people and narrowing the field can be difficult. Hunting rifles can range from around $350 to north of $7,000, which is quite a staggering spread. All hunters want to find that sweet spot between price and quality. We strive to give you valid information on rifles of every price point from budget hunting rifles to premium custom builds.

This is a comparison of mid-priced rifles, retailing from $700 to $1,500, which captures many of the most popular hunting rifles on the market. That’s because so many hunters are willing to spend a little more for a nicer rifle, but don’t want to throw down on a $2,000 gun. This price block has traditionally included mainstream flagship rifles like the Winchester Model 70 and Remington Model 700, Savage Model 110, and others. It is in this range of mid-priced hunting rifles that the average hunter will likely spend their money.

Mid-priced hunting rifles are typically nice, but without many frills or flourishes. They are general production, standard rifles that are made of good, economical materials with basic stocks and run-of-the-mill triggers. Some at the top end of this price range historically have features like better coatings or threaded muzzles — though with the popularity of suppressors for hunting, threaded muzzles are becoming a new standard.

You’ll see better-quality parts and workmanship on mid-priced hunting rifles than their bargain basement counterparts. Bargain rifles use cost-cutting parts and construction methods to keep prices down. The rifles that cost a few hundred dollars more will usually have nicer stocks, finishes, fit, and more consistent accuracy. The mid-priced hunting rifle is the bread-and-butter standard to which both lower and higher-priced rifles are compared.

The Outdoor Life staff has always strived to present you with the most relevant and practical data for rifle accuracy. At one time, we believed that three-shot groups told us what we needed to know. Then, after seeing too much variability, it became five-shot groups, and averages of large numbers of five-shot groups.

Within the last couple years, we have realized that even that doesn’t give us the best information for evaluating or comparing rifles — or knowing what we can expect from them in the field. Based on the statistical and range-tested information that the guys in the lab at Hornady presented in their podcast series beginning with Your Groups are Too Small, we took a fresh look at our accuracy protocol and found it lacking.

We will still present you with five-shot group accuracy data, but we’ve also developed an easy method to take those five-shot groups and compile them into a 20-shot composite, which is a much better representation of how the rifle actually shoots and can be expected to shoot. You can read about how to do that, and some of the benefits, here.

We tested some of the rifles in this story using our old protocol, but as we get to re-test some, and test more current versions of others, we will keep this story populated with the best data that we have for each mid-priced hunting rifle. All rifles were tested with multiple types of quality ammunition. All recorded groups were fired from either bench or prone positions, with front and rear support.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (27 Groups total): 1.96 inches

20-shot Group Size (Stainless Laminate Model in 6.5 CM tested with Barnes Harvest 140-grain): 1.42 inches

The Tikka T3X family has a cult-like following, especially here in Alaska. These rifles are affordable, accurate, and dependable. They aren’t ultralight, but aren’t too heavy either. The Finnish rifles have a proven track record and are never a bad option for someone looking for a mid-priced hunting rifle.

The T3X Lite is a sleek and simple rifle. It’s like a budget rifle, only nicer in just about every way. It features a closed-top action and simple two-lug stainless-steel bolt. It has a short bolt throw for a two-lug action, and it’s exceptionally crisp and smooth for its class. The bolt features a metal rear shroud, and the bolt handle is dovetailed into the bolt body.

The T3X platform is also available in threaded models and has great aftermarket support for things like scope rings, stocks, and other accessories. You can get into a base model affordably and use that, or upgrade to your liking.

The rifle is plain but shows good craftsmanship and attention to detail. Even the small textured portion of the bolt release button matches the texture pattern of the stock—a nice touch. Overall, the T3X Lite is a very sleek and clean rifle, with no sloppy machine work or tool marks. It’s very well-balanced for an all-around hunting rifle, and lots of models are available in the $700 to $1,500 price range. The only complaint I could come up with is that the blued sample I have has a finish that is very susceptible to surface rust, so I’d opt for a stainless or Cerakoted model.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (16 groups): .79 in.

Average 20-shot Group Size (4 types of ammo): 1.36 in.

The Browning X-Bolt is a highly popular flagship model rifle, and for good reason. They’re generally accurate, dependable, and come in a variety of configurations. Many of their configurations push them beyond the category of mid-priced hunting rifles, but the X-Bolt 2 Composite can be found at retailers for under $1,200.

The X-Bolt is a three-lug push-feed action that’s fed from a rotary magazine with a rounded bottom, which sits flush with the profile of the stock. It uses an M-16-style extractor and single plunger ejector. It has a two-position safety on the tang that locks the bolt closed when engaged, but the bolt has an override button to allow the shooter to open the bolt or unload while the rifle is on “safe.” The cheek piece is comfortable, and the pistol grip aids with consistent hand placement and trigger pull.

This rifle is similar in weight to more expensive models like the Speed and Mountain Pro, and lighter than some of their heavier target models. It’s got a black stock and basic blued finish. More expensive models — some of which can squeeze under the $1,500 mark — feature camo patterns and Cerakote finishes.

The Browning X-Bolt has been one of the most consistent factory hunting rifles that we’ve regularly tested over the years. While they do vary a lot in price, a base model X-Bolt 2 like this is one of the best values for rifles in this category.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (37 groups): .952 inches

20-Shot Group Size (Hornady 143-grain Precision Hunter): 1.13 inches

Known for their affordable rifles, 9mm carbines, and Glock clone handguns like the PSA Dagger, Palmetto State Armory has a hell of a good rifle in the PSA Sabre 10. I got one of these to test, chambered in 6.5 Creedmoor, and was floored by its accuracy. The PSA Sabre 10 is designed to replicate the M110 service rifle, but at a much lower price point. It’s not very flashy, but includes key quality components like a Magpul PRS Lite adjustable stock, a Radian Raptor charging handle, stainless-steel barrel, and adjustable gas block. The bolt also uses double springs on the extractor and dual plunger ejectors for reliable extraction and ejection.

It took me a while to get the ideal bolt speed down — which I manipulated by adjusting the gas system. Eventually, I added a heavier buffer too. I did find that I needed to fine-tune the system any time I switched ammo or added a suppressor. For anyone wanting an affordable, quality AR to hunt with, these requirements are a small price to pay. I shot a lot of different ammo through the Sabre 10, and loads using Hornady’s 143-grain ELD-X were best. This rifle is more accurate than most of the bolt-action hunting rifles on this list. It would be an excellent choice for hunting hogs at night using a thermal scope.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (50 yards)(30 groups): 1.8 inches

Smith & Wesson got everyone’s attention when they introduced the model 1854 in 2024. We eagerly got a sample chambered in .44 Rem. Mag., which also accepts .44 Special, and were thoroughly impressed with the execution on this rifle. Smith & Wesson not only introduced a new platform for the brand, they made one of the nicest production lever guns we have seen. This was following Ruger’s acquisition of Marlin and the Smith can go toe-to-toe with the finest Marlins made.

The initial models of the 1854 were blued and all-weather versions of the same gun, chambered in .44. The stainless version we tested was a smooth-running, reliable workhorse that would excel at shorter distances common to a lot of deer hunters. It also incorporates key modern features such as M-Lok slots on the side of the fore-end, a threaded muzzle, and Picatinny rail for mounting an optic.

You can check out our in-depth review of the 1854 here. Since its debut, the 1854 roster has expanded to include .30/30, .45/70, .360 Buckhammer, and .45 Colt models, including the blacked-out tactical-styled Stealth Hunter model. These are well-built rifles that will last generations, and they’re a great value.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (12 groups): .63 inches

Average 20-Shot Group Size (3 types of ammo): 1.07 inches

Christensen Arms is known for their flagship rifles featuring carbon-fiber barrels and stocks, but in 2025, they introduced the Evoke. This is a simplified, more affordable rifle with a steel barrel and synthetic stock that incorporates modern ergonomics and grip geometry. This step towards simplicity gave us a rifle that comes in under a thousand bucks and has proven to be a reliably accurate hunting rifle.

We tested and reviewed our first Evoke in 6.5 Creedmoor in 2025, but I’ve also been shooting one chambered in the high-pressure 7mm Backcountry. Editor-in-Chief Alex Robinson has been shooting another 6.5 Creedmoor and used it to kill a whopper bull elk with Federal’s new 6.5 Plus Peak Ammo. The Evoke has earned its place as one our favorite hunting rifles under a thousand bucks.

On this rifle, you’ll see price-appropriate features like a somewhat noisy synthetic stock, but the gun has good coatings and is well protected from harsh weather. Despite its scratchy material, the stock does have great modern ergonomics that make it easier to shoot consistently and features a Picatinny rail on the fore-end for mounting a bipod.

This is one of the best new hunting rifles for the price, and it’s even available in magnum cartridges like the .375 H&H.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (50 yards): 1.36 inches

Most people think of imported lever guns as little more than a novelty, but don’t make that mistake with Rossi. Their R95 is high quality and all business. The laminated .45/70 model that I tested has a smoother action than many of the older Marlins I have shot, though it does lag a bit behind the newer Ruger Marlins. I tested mine with a variety of loads including factory ammo from Black Hills ammo and Federal, as well as hand loads with bullets from Lehigh Defense and Speer, ranging from 300 grains to 405 grains. It cycled everything wonderfully, no doubt aided by its improved M16-style extractor. This rifle comes with a tall front bead sight and a rear peep, with a long length of Picatinny rail for mounting a red dot or LPVO. It handled heavy-recoiling rounds well, but before I did anything, I would remove all components and add thread locker — I did have some optic base screws loosen during testing.

Read More: Rossi R95 Laminate .45/70 Review

This is a modern-featured lever gun that’s ready for a suppressor, but also maintains a nostalgic look. For the price, it’s a really good value, though the receiver flats are a bit over polished, and if I squeeze the fore-end, it has some flex. I plan on either bedding it or swapping it out for an aftermarket set. If you want to get into a lever gun in the mid-priced hunting rifle market, this is a tough one to beat.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (21 groups): 2.26 inches

The Winchester Model 70 Featherweight is one of the longest-running mid-priced hunting rifles that’s still in production. The featherweight was first released in 1952, and the signature “Featherweight” stock was introduced in 1982. The rifle has seen some changes, but the current production model has a pre-64-style controlled-feed action that Model 70 fans love.

The Featherweight was a lightweight rifle for its time and introduced in the brand new .308 W.C.F. cartridge of 1952 (what we now know as the .308 Win.). That’s what I tested the current production model in, and with the post-1982 Schnabel fore-end and signature checkering, it’s an authentic Featherweight.

Read More: Is the Winchester Model 70 Featherweight As Good As It Used to Be?

The controlled-feed action features a two-lug bolt and Mauser-style claw extractor, as well as a coned breech for feeding reliability. It also uses a blade ejector rather than a spring-loaded plunger. The blade ejector ejects cases with a force proportional to how hard the bolt is pulled to the rear. Need to reload in a hurry? Grip it and rip it. On the bench though, you can slowly pull the bolt to the rear and hand-pluck your spent case from the bolt face. Because the claw extractor grabs and controls the cartridge as soon as it’s stripped from the magazine, you don’t have to close the bolt to withdraw the cartridge from the chamber like you do with most push-feed rifles.

The wood stock is warm and comfortable and features good wood-to-metal fit with only a couple uneven spots on my sample. Unlike older models, the stock features bedding around the recoil lug and at the tang to help reinforce the wood and provide a more stable connection. My only complaint with the stock is that it’s slightly thicker and blockier than older model Featherweights, particularly in the grip and around the magazine floorplate.

The metal on the rifle features a nice satin blued finish, and the muzzle has a recessed target crown that’s well-protected. An older Model 70 Featherweight I have possesses only a slightly contoured crown, and the muzzle shows some wear from riding around on the floorboards of a pickup.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (22 Groups): 2.2 inches

The Howa 1500 is another long-running hunting rifle that has models in the 600-1,200 price range. The Model 1500 has been in production since 1979, and it’s been a staple, affordable rifle for many hunters. I killed my first coyote with a 1500 in .223 that my dad bought when I was a kid, and one of the most accurate rifles I’ve ever owned was a heavy-barreled Model 1500 with a laminated thumbhole stock in .308 Win.

Like many rifles, the 1500 comes in a variety of configurations and price ranges—including carbon-fiber barrels and high-end stocks. One of the base models that fits this category perfectly is the Kuiu Verde in .308 Win. The rifle features a tactical gray Cerakote finish, sporter-weight barrel, and a Hogue Kuiu-camo stock with a wide fore-end, meaty grip, and soft recoil pad.

The Howa Model 1500 action is a simple two-lug push-feed action—much like the Remington 700. Unlike the 700, it features an M-16-style extractor, but does have a single plunger ejector on the bolt face. The recoil lug is machined into the action, and Howa’s trigger group is attached to the action with a single Allen screw.

Sitting in the stock, the barrel channel is even, and the barrel is free floated completely back to the receiver. The stock is beefy, but comfortable to shoot. It has a wide fore-end, and a thick, nearly vertical grip which makes a perpendicular pull on the trigger easy.

The barrel has a slightly recessed crown, and the muzzle is threaded, although it’s notable that the thread pitch is ½-inch x 28 (a threading that is most common with .22-caliber chamberings) rather than the more common 5/8-inch x 24. The muzzle is ready to be fitted with either a brake or suppressor. Because the barrel is a relatively light sporter weight, expect major point-of-impact shifts when adding a can.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (29 groups): .866 inches

Average 20-shot Group Size (9 types of ammo): 1.32 inches

The Savage Model 110 is a stalwart of the mid-priced hunting rifle category and has been since its introduction in 1963. In fact, it was one of the major competitors that pushed Winchester to adopt a push-feed design for the Model 70 in 1964, according to Jack O’Connor’s writings at the time.

The Model 110 is a simple push-feed, bolt-action rifle that features a second set of lugs behind the forward set. This could still be considered a two-lug bolt because only the forward lugs rotate and lock into the receiver, but the rear ones spin freely around the bolt body and remain in the raceways while the bolt is locked into battery. The bolt handle is cast, and the bolt features a small plunger ejector and an extractor that’s fitted into the right-hand lug (something the push-feed Winchester Model 70 used as well).

The Savage Model 110 is a hunting rifle that was designed to be affordable and accurate, and it carries a reputation for both. The Model 110 Storm that I tested features a stainless-steel receiver and barrel, and a detachable 4-round magazine. I like the design of the magazine because it’s durable, but I did notice that the stainless-finish bottom plate has picked up some surface spot rusting simply from the ambient humidity. The loaded magazine takes firm pressure to insert into the rifle, but it springs free with authority when the magazine release is pressed.

The rifle features a 3-position tang safety that locks the bolt in its most rearward position. It also uses Savage’s Accutrigger—a user-adjustable trigger with a center safety tab. It’s a well-liked and crisp-breaking trigger that certainly aids with the shootability of the rifle.

The Trail Hunter Lite model features a fluted barrel that weighs less than the Trail Hunter model that features a pretty heavy barrel. It’s not an ultralight gun, but on par with many other standard bolt-action hunting rifles. This is one of the more affordable Model 110s, and its coatings and stock allow it to hold up to the worst elements. Along with its accuracy, these make it a wonderful value.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (15 groups): 1.96 inches

If you notice the resemblance between the Weatherby Vanguard series and the Howa 1500, it’s because they are very similar. Howa makes the barreled actions for the Vanguard line, though Weatherby finishes them in Sheridan, Wyo. by adding the stock, trigger, barrel fluting, finishes, etc. The Vanguard series was introduced in 1970 to offer a lower-priced option than the premium Mark V line, and firmly fits the bill for a quality mid-priced hunting rifle.

Like the Model 1500, the Vanguard is a two-lug push-feed action—nearly identical except for a few differences. One is that the Vanguard’s bolt features three small gas vent holes that are visible on the ejecting side when the bolt is closed. The Model 1500 only has the forward hole. Additionally, the Model 1500 has three larger vent holes in the bolt body that point down towards the magazine when the bolt is closed. The Vanguard only has one.

The Vanguard First Lite features a relatively slender, high-quality synthetic stock. The fore-end is slightly widened at the bottom with a slimming taper closer to the barrel. The Monte Carlo comb provides a comfortable and firm cheek weld, and the subtle texturing on the grip and fore-end make the rifle easy to handle and hold. The stock is finished with First Lite Cipher camouflage pattern.

One notable feature is the rifle’s Cerakote finish, which is even, good-looking, and done in-house at their Sheridan, Wyoming factory. The rifle includes both a slim radial muzzle brake and thread protector—both machined to fit the barrel profile perfectly. The fit is precise, and it’s hard to see the seam when the muzzle brake or thread protector are tightened.

In an apples-to-apples comparison, it’s probably not fair to shoot a fluted, sporter-weight 6.5-300 Wby Mag. against similar-class rifles in .308 Win. The 6.5-300 is an incredibly fast, flat-shooting cartridge, but it will heat up a barrel quickly and is generally much less forgiving than cartridges like the .308 Win. and 6.5 Creedmoor. However, the only sample Weatherby had available at the time was chambered for 6.5-300, and I was excited to see how it would fare. The rifle held its own.

Average Five-Shot Group Size (29 groups): 1.28 inches

New for 2022, the CZ 600 series was a complete divergence from their previous actions and, following the CZ 600 Alpha, the CZ 600 American is a traditionally-styled wood-stocked version. It has a three-lug, push-feed action that uses a detachable box magazine. Our sample was chambered in .308 Winchester and featured a sporter-contoured barrel, anti-corrosion finish, and a checkered Turkish Walnut stock. It comes with a threaded muzzle, but it’s 9/16×24 rather than the American standard 5/8-24 and will require an adapter for use with most suppressors.

Read More: Full Review of the CZ 600 American

The CZ 600 American features an exceptionally idiot-proof adjustable trigger and its heft makes it very comfortable to shoot. The trigger features four adjustment positions similar to those on Sako rifles. It also features an over-sized bolt knob that makes running the short-throw action a breeze. The American isn’t light, but it’s not exceptionally heavy or long barreled either. It would make a great all-around woods rifle for any hunter.

The safety mechanism on the CZ 600 is interesting, as it’s a thru-tang safety that you press down into the tang to disengage, and up from the bottom to engage. The safety locks the bolt, but there is a bolt release button that can be pressed to open the bolt while the rifle is on safe.

The biggest takeaway from accuracy testing mid-priced hunting rifles is that they are generally a step above the budget rifles in accuracy. They will shoot a wider variety of loads with better consistency, but you still might have to spend some time on the bench to find what they really like. Several of the mid-priced rifles have MOA accuracy guarantees for three-shot groups, and I found them all to satisfy their claims.

Most rifles in this price block do fall short of the accuracy of premium rifles when it comes to five-shot groups over time, but this probably won’t bother the average hunter. Many people will claim that their mid-priced rifles will shoot just as accurately as any rifle in the $2,000 to $4,000 range, but that’s usually not true. Especially since we’ve started using larger sample sizes (20-shot group aggregates), we see that more expensive rifles are generally much more consistent than budget guns. That said, All of these are plenty accurate enough, so pick one that best meets your needs and get out and hunt.

The OL editors pick the best deer hunting rifles on the market.

Tyler Freel is a Staff Writer for Outdoor Life. He lives in Fairbanks, Alaska and has been covering a variety of topics for OL for more than a decade. From backpack sheep hunting adventure stories to DIY tips to gear and gun reviews, he covers it all with a perspective that’s based in experience.

#8280. Why Mule Deer (Not Whitetails) Are North America’s Greatest Game Animal

Published Nov 12, 2026 8:56 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

I’ve always been a big woods whitetail hunter. I grew up in New England, where deer hunting meant tracking, still hunting, and roving through endless miles of mixed hardwoods and thick pine forests looking to bag a ridge-running mountain buck. It’s one of my greatest passions and what I truly love to do.

So when I moved to Southwest Montana in my late 20s and discovered that the bulk of whitetail hunting there was isolated to wide-open river bottoms and agricultural fields — rather than the surrounding snow-capped mountains and rocky canyons that appealed to my big-woods sensibilities — I was sorely disappointed. Yet, there was another critter hiding among those picturesque peaks that my local friends assured me would give all the rugged hunting adventure I could ever ask for: the mule deer.

Truth be told, I wasn’t all that impressed with mule deer when I first saw them. They came sedately down to the river when I was fishing and strolled up the driveway to my cabin like demure livestock, as self-assured and unafraid as the cows I saw in the surrounding fields. While I thought they were beautiful and cool-looking animals, they just didn’t spark that same feeling of mystery and lust for adventure that their Eastern whitetail cousins had.

I honestly felt like I would miss my beloved big-woods whitetail bucks when hunting season rolled around, but I still decided to give these bulky, floppy-eared deer a try. Little did I know that by the time my first Western hunting season ended, mule deer would change me as a hunter forever.

One of the interesting things about mule deer is that they’re a relatively new species. They evolved around the end of the Ice Age when whitetail deer from what is now the Eastern U.S. pushed past melting glaciers to meet and breed with the blacktails of the West Coast, creating a hybridized species of hardy, adaptable deer that soon populated the recently-formed Rocky Mountains. This makes the mule deer a purely North American big-game animal that has been shaped and forged by the rugged mountains, plains, and deserts of the West.

Because of the harshness of these environments, mule deer have more to worry about than your average Eastern whitetail. First, they are constantly harassed by predators like wolves, grizzly bears, and especially mountain lions. In Colorado, which has the highest mule deer population of any state at roughly 416,000 animals, it’s estimated that lions kill between 100,000 and 200,000 mule deer each year. This can make mule deer extremely cagey and hard to approach, as they are on constant alert, making them a significant challenge for hunters. It also makes them an incredibly fun and worthy opponent that pushes you and forces you to up your game.

As mule deer contend with brutal winters, scorching summers, sparse feed, and limited water sources, they have no choice but to be roaming foragers. They require large expanses of wilderness dotted with multiple food and water sources in order to survive.

Whitetails have an average home range of around 300 to 600 acres, where they will often spend their entire lives. Muleys, by contrast, have both summer and winter ranges. These deer can travel as far as 50 miles in just a few days to move from their summer to winter grounds. One particular herd in Wyoming migrates from the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem in the northwest corner of the state all the way to southern Wyoming’s Red Desert every year. It’s a 480-mile round trip that makes this herd the farthest migrating big-game animal in the Lower 48.

The result of all this moving and adapting means that you can find mule deer in a variety of different terrains. From mountain forests and grass-rich bottomlands to boulder-strewn canyons and scrubby deserts, anywhere with sufficient forage and water is likely to hold a mule deer or two, so long as it’s the right time for them to be there.

This last point is critical, as mule deer hunting is often a game of “here today and gone tomorrow.” In some ways, it’s similar to chasing migrating waterfowl or even herds of caribou. Once you find them, you often have a short window of time to fill your tag. For hunters who love to witness these migrations, and who enjoy exploring wild and beautiful country, the mule deer is the perfect beast.

There’s a rugged romance to mule deer hunting. It reminds one of those long ago days before trail cams, tree stands, and target bucks infiltrated our hunting culture — a time when going out and harvesting an animal was done with a little know-how, a reliable rifle, and a good pair of boots.

While there are private ranch outfits and other scenarios (especially around agricultural areas) where it’s possible to pattern a single trophy mule deer buck, it’s an entirely different story on the vast public land tracts of the West. On public ground, a mule deer you see in the evening may be ten miles away by the next day. Setting up a stand and waiting for him to come back is pointless. To be a successful DIY mule deer hunter, you typically have to seek the deer out and go after them rather than sit around and wait for them to come to you.

This can turn muley hunting hunting into a drawn-out game of walking and exploring, where you climb up steep mountainsides and crawl over rocks, following tracks and other sign through thick brush and dense timber. It often means hiking deep into the backcountry and studying big sections of terrain where you might spend hours and even days just watching the landscape and taking your opportunities as you find them. In short, it’s everything deer hunting should be.

Most mule deer aficionados choose the spot-and-stalk method, where you climb to the highest point you can find and then glass the surrounding terrain with binoculars and spotting scopes trying to find an approachable buck. It’s a style of hunting that requires immense patience. You search for food sources and bedding areas and then pick apart the hillsides and brushy valleys trying to make a deer appear before your eyes.

Other mule deer hunters choose to still hunt, tracking the deer through thick timber and snow. This method gets at the very core of hunting, as it requires you to move slowly and quietly through the forest shadows like a predator would, trying to spot a buck before it spots you and bounds away out of sight and out of reach.

Both methods require little equipment beyond a good pair of boots, a sharp knife, an accurate rifle, and a quality pack, which is essential. Because once you hike into good muley territory, there’s a good chance you could come out heavy.

Hunters who do their homework and put in the miles will eventually get opportunities on mule deer. Unlike some other big-game species, which can have sparse or isolated populations, mule deer herds tend to be dense. Their populations do fluctuate, and mule deer have their own conservation challenges, including habitat loss, chronic wasting disease, and other isuses. But these habitual herd animals will often return to good food and water sources year after year, giving knowledgeable hunters some chances at success.

Looking at the numbers in Montana, Colorado, and Idaho, success rates for mule deer hunters seem relatively low, averaging around 10 to 18 percent. The bulk of that harvest comes from areas along migration routes, however, where 25 to 45 percent of hunters are actually successful. Outfitters and guides who set up in these areas, especially those with private land connections, can boast client success rates between 85 and 98 percent. This shows that once you find a lonely corner of land with mule deer in it, you’re likely to find a lot of them. And this is especially true during the rut.

Usually occurring between the second and third week of November in most places, the rut is when mule deer bucks give up their normally solo existence and begin keying in on does. Like whitetails, muley bucks are usually separated from does for most of the year, choosing to travel alone or in small bachelor groups. But once the rut begins and they start seeking out hot does, their habits change.

The rut doesn’t necessarily make them more receptive to calls or scents, like whitetails. But it does mean that so long as you find a few does and keep them in sight, it won’t be long before a buck comes along. Their focus on the doe is often so intense that they’ll ignore everything else around them — including hunters — and if you can avoid scaring off his ladies, you can sometimes make moves in plain sight of a rutty mule deer buck without spooking him off.

It’ll be a good buck, too. Even younger mule deer sport a branched set of antlers and a heavy body, and after spending so much time hiking and looking for them, every hard-earned muley buck feels like a trophy.

By the last week of my first season hunting mule deer, I was desperate. Those cheeky and seemingly un-spookable deer I had seen grazing along the roadsides and strolling nonchalantly across my front lawn during the summer had disappeared once autumn rolled around. In their place was a wary and flighty animal that seemed to bounce away and vanish into the terrain as soon as I scrambled after them. It was an intensely frustrating experience as the deer always seemed to be just out of my reach.

I had almost given up when, around last light on the last day of the Montana hunting season, I glassed a small group of deer feeding in a steep canyon. I grabbed my rifle and crawled up the near vertical canyon walls, popping my head over a small crest to see a doe and a nice 4X4 buck looking at me from 150 yards. Shouldering my rifle, I got the crosshairs on the buck’s shoulder and squeezed the trigger just as the deer started to bound away, dropping him in his tracks. As I walked up and held his antlers in my hands, I could tell something inside me was different.

Nowadays, when I happen across a nice whitetail buck while hunting in the West, I usually won’t even raise my gun. Whitetails will always hold a special place in my heart, but I am now and forever will be a muley man.

Everyone is “pretty tired” of you responding to what you are with an exhausted, “I just felt like running” in a goofy accent. It’s OK; we’ve all been there. And Trail Runner’s resident doodler and creative character costume expert, Bobby Peavey, has your back. He’s put together a curated list of archetypes from your local run club and Instagram feed that are sure to be a hit this spooky season.

This costume is perfect for your most bonk-vulnerable friends.  Dress them up as Bonkenstein and enjoy a night of constantly bringing them back from the dead with salty and sweet snacks.

Do you have the patience of a saint and the multitasking skills of Leslie Knope? Then the Race Director costume is the perfect choice for you. Your night is going to consist of making sure there are ample snacks for all, that trick or treating/holiday party schedules stay on track, that everybody stays safe and healthy, and about a dozen other things that everyone else surely overlooks.

When you select this costume for the spookiest night of the year, the assignment is clear: only speak in the past tense for the entire night. You’re full of nostalgia and cynical disdain for anything modern. You’re basically the Uncle Rico of the evening.

Time to update your watch to the current model, recharge your heart rate strap, and cover every inch of exposed skin with wearable storage.  Because the funnest part of your Halloween is going to be teaching all your friends about the newest and techiest gear on the market.

For this costume, it is crucial that you log more photos than miles.  You are in this costume purely for the likes and kudos. If you exit Zone 1 at any point, you’re doing it wrong.

No pacer or muling needed with this costume. Thanks to your vampire diet and a steady dose of nipple chafing, you’ve got all the nutrition you need to conquer any ultra distance!

#8275. To Win the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Try Being … Vulnerable?

Author Dan England spoke with five members of Team USA after they won the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship on October 22. A rough start forced the team to abandon the fundamentals of competition and ask for help, be honest about their problems, and sacrifice for others. It paid off: the U.S. came from behind to defeat Australia and Belgium, who took second and third, respectively.

Early into the second night of the 2026 Big’s Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, Mark Dowdle turned to U.S. teammate Levi Yoder and admitted that he was so tired he might fall asleep and into the nearby ditch. Yoder replied that he was so tired he was hallucinating and might wind up in that same ditch.

Before the start, Harvey Lewis, a two-time individual backyard ultra world champion whom many on the U.S. squad thought of as their de facto captain, told his teammates to lean on one another. But Dowdle hesitated the first day, and so, he thought, did many others. It made sense: Backyard ultras are usually individual events predicated on you staying strong while others give up.

For the uninitiated, backyard ultra rules are pretty simple: Run a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour, until only one remains. (That runner must complete one final loop, also called a yard, to be declared the winner.) At the Backyard Ultra World Team Championship, which alternates every other year with the individual championship, each participating country simultaneously hosts its own backyard ultra with 15 runners. The team with the most cumulative laps wins.

Typically at backyard ultras, competitors are wolves looking for the elk with a limp. No one wants to look weak. No one demonstrated this formidable exterior better than Dowdle in the Last Soul Ultra this April, when his gamesmanship created the event’s most talked-about moment. But his competitive side was ubiquitous among the 15 elite backyard runners on Team USA. They each won backyard ultras to qualify; they were wolves, not elk.

Yet Team USA struggled from the start. With daytime temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, it felt warmer than they thought it would. The course was hilly, with over 400 feet of climbing per loop, costing them a minute or two per loop in a format where extra seconds are precious. Indeed, over the first 40 laps when all runners from all 67 countries were still in the race, the U.S. had the slowest average lap speed of 52:21—nearly seven minutes slower than the fastest country, Slovakia.

Struggling through that second night, the U.S. decided to try a different tactic. They decided to be vulnerable.

Lewis urged the team to be honest about how they were feeling because there was a good chance others could help. It took Dowdle a bit to believe, even after watching how others supported each other.

“It did take encouragement from my team to even be more of a teammate,” Dowdle told Trail Runner.

But Dowdle was enthused when, after his admission that he was struggling, Yoder suggested that they look out for each other over the next 3 miles they had to complete to keep going. Dowdle got the message: This would be a different backyard than he’d ever run before. They talked to each other through the loop and by the end they had caught up to their teammates.

“That turned the corner for me,” Dowdle said. “In a normal race, I would never say that I was falling asleep to another runner. You just would never give up that information. But that opened the door for me to be more vocal about how I was doing.”

Several other members of the U.S. squad admitted that being honest with each other and asking for help when they needed it was key to them winning the world title. Instead of acting like individuals in a last-man-standing race, they were a unit. That helped many of them run farther than they ever had before—eight Americans ran over 80 yards, or 333.3 miles—when it looked like Australia might literally run away with victory.

“When some were feeling strong, we would help those who were not feeling OK,” said Megan Smyth, who set a PR with 82 yards and was the last woman standing. “I’m pretty sure that’s how so many of us got over 80 yards.”

The backyard, despite its do-or-die nature, lends itself to camaraderie because of the way runners all start the next 4.167-mile loop together on the hour, every hour. Jon Noll qualified for Team USA by running over 440 miles at the individual world championship last year. Even there most competitors congratulated each other after each lap. “The ultra community, in general, is not exactly a cutthroat environment for the most part,” Noll said. He especially felt that sense of camaraderie this time as the miles piled up.

This is why Smyth loves the backyard format.

“There’s no incentive to win a lap, so you really do wind up cheering for each other,” Smyth said.

Still, Team USA had to get comfortable with each other in a hurry. Even with seven returning members from the third-place 2024 team it was a little awkward at first: Some had previously competed against each other, and some called each other friends. Some were rivals. Other first-timers felt a sense of awe: Smyth had imposter syndrome, which doesn’t make it easy to talk about, say, a sore ankle.

But she also welcomed the unique race set up. If a typical backyard ultra can feel crowded and chaotic, the team race with its 15 competitors feels sparse, even intimate. Smyth got her wish right away.

“I haven’t gotten to do true team running since my cross-country days,” she said. “It was just a magical experience.”

A couple team meetings over Zoom, as well as an in-person meeting before the race, helped shoo away some of the awkwardness, Lewis thought. But Smyth said Lewis helped bring the team together during the event, too, with little (even corny) things like running in a fighter jet formation and chanting “U.S.A!” for a lap.

Smyth remembers walking at night and nearly falling asleep before the Ron Express came up behind her. Ron Wireman, competing in his second team championship, struggled early in the race and needed help from others. That first night, he was eager to pay his teammates back and named himself after a train to help them through the dark.

“He said, ‘MEGAN ARE YOU AWAKE?,’” Smyth said.

Smyth, just like Dowdle, learned how to ask for help. Later in the race, as the prospect of doing another lap on the steep trail, she requested a “hill sherpa.”

The team cohesion would be tested right away as Lewis insisted they answer a question democratically: Should they run the road or the trail?

Team USA competes on the original Big’s Backyard Ultra course in mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell’s literal backyard in Bell Buckle, Tennessee. On odd years during the individual championship, racers run a trail loop during the day and a road loop at night. This time it was runners’ choice throughout the race.

The road was flatter and easier, but the hard, smooth surface can be problematic for trail runners. Smyth, for instance, said she didn’t bring many pairs of road shoes. But Laz recently made “improvements” to the trail loop that made it steeper, tougher, and slower. The precious minutes saved on the road loop could be the difference between having time to recover, fuel, sleep, and even go to the bathroom, and to DNF.

“There isn’t a lot of wiggle room in a backyard,” Lewis said.

Communication was key as the team tried to accommodate runners struggling with the trail by adding more laps on the road.

“We were changing things as the race went on,” Noll said. “Sometimes you didn’t know what course you were doing [on the next lap]. Mentally that can be hard.”

Ultimately, the back and forth paid off. Eventually emphasizing the road over the trail helped the team squeeze yards from people who may not have been able to continue otherwise.

“If we hadn’t moved to the road, I don’t know if we would have won the race,” Lewis said.

As the third day burned off its final few hours, Australia had a commanding lead of 58 yards over the U.S. The Aussies still had 11 runners in the race; the U.S. was down to 9. Nicholas Steel kept announcing to his U.S. teammates just how far behind they were. More than one American admitted later that they found these updates annoying. Dowdle told himself he didn’t care and tried to enjoy the experience.

But backyard veterans will tell you that the race doesn’t end at hour 70; that’s really when it starts. One Aussie dropped at yard 70, another at 72, two at 73, and two more at 75. By yard 80, nine Aussies had dropped. They had only two runners left—a precarious place to be, given the final runner can only complete one additional lap after the penultimate runner drops. Sure enough, Australia was out by yard 88. We’re not being judgy about this: They were on their third day of running without sleep. But that brutal attrition gave the U.S. a shot.

Suddenly Steel’s updates were inspiring. They would need Dowdle and Noll, the workhorses, to keep doing their magic. But the Americans realized that they could win if they got at least half their runners to yard 75 and several past yard 80.

“The possibility that we could catch up lit a fire under my belly,” Dowdle said, “and I remember thinking, ‘Oh, maybe I do care.’”

Even the Americans who dropped relatively early decided to stay at the campsite to cheer. This was big: Dowdle finished one lap with 15 seconds to go, riding the wave of exhortation to get him across the line in time.

Lewis did what he could to keep as many runners out there as possible. He ran with those who were close to dropping, even to his detriment. At times he finished the lap with less than three minutes to go. Lewis, famously, sleeps for a few minutes after every loop, but running with others meant he wasn’t able to do that. Ultimately, he went out for yard 84 but didn’t finish it, a result that Lewis found disappointing.

“I didn’t have my own rhythm because I was helping others,” Lewis said. “My ultimate goal was to be there for the team, so I sacrificed myself and my own best race for that.”

That kind of support from teammates, along with the competitive boost the Americans got chasing down Australia, helped push some to their backyard ultra PRs. Nick Petterson made it to 84 yards, 19 more than his previous best. That’s nearly a full day more of running.

“The team needed you, and that was a really easy thing to grab onto,” Petterson said. “We needed everyone to crank up the numbers. That motivation outside of just myself was really helpful.”

Petterson thrives off that external focus anyway. During backyards, he enjoys asking others how they’re doing, even though it’s not always reciprocated.

“The team factor was a major driver when times got hard for me,” he said. “I might have gone out earlier if it wasn’t for that.”

Yoder made it 86 yards, 11 more than his qualifying mark. Ryan Snickles went 69 yards after qualifying with 55. Smyth set a PR by five yards and quit only after her ankle swelled like a balloon. Jeff Walker got 75 yards, 30 more than his qualifier. Even Steel seemed inspired by his own updates. He went 94 yards—177% of his 53-yard qualifier.

Ultimately the U.S. won by a landslide with 1,120 yards to Australia’s 1,069.

It’s the second world title for Team USA in this rapidly developing sub-sport. When the U.S. won in 2022, it was with only 860 yards. Belgium, which has won the other two team titles, took third this year—although two of their runners set the individual backyard ultra world record of 124 yards, or 516.7 miles over five days of running.

“When other runners are hanging on longer,” Lewis said, “it impacts everyone to hang on longer.”

Ultimately, Dowdle was the last American standing with 107 yards—a personal best by 13 yards, or 54 miles. Noll got the assist with 106 yards. Despite his initial reticence, Dowdle says he values moments with his teammates more than his individual national title.

“There was one lap where I broke down crying,” Dowdle said, “and Nick Petterson saw me and put his arm around me and was just with me during that time.”

Dowdle wouldn’t want the backyard format to be flooded with team events, but he wants to go back:

“I’m bummed that you have to wait two years for it again.”
