#8272. The Best Budget Shotguns of 2026

For budget-conscious hunters who need a reliable pump under $500, the Mossberg Maverick 88 or Remington 870 Express are the proven choices. For hunters who want an inertia semi-auto without the Benelli price tag, the Stoeger M3000 is the standout pick. For those who can stretch closer to $1,000, the Beretta A300 Outlander and Winchester SX4 represent the category's best value-to-performance ratio.

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Shotguns digest more shells in a season than most rifles will in a lifetime. They get knocked around in the uplands, and splattered with mud in the marsh, and shot and shot and shot at the range. A lot of people don’t like the idea of spending any more than necessary on a gun that has to take such abuse. This list is for them, the practical among us, who will skip a frill here, an engraved pheasant there, in order to maximize their bang for the buck. What follows are nine shotguns that represent extremely good values in their categories. One of them is most likely the best budget shotgun you can buy for the type of hunting you do.

Made in Mexico, the Maverick 88 is a budget Mossberg 500, which seems redundant. It’s essentially the same gun as the Model 500 but with a crossbolt safety in place of the top safety. The Maverick 88 also starts below $300. For that, you get a lock, stock, barrel, and not much else. Well, you get one choke tube and a middle bead, too. I have shot 25 straight on the skeet field with a Model 88, which suggests they shoot where you point them, and I’ve seen them at work in the field, too. They come in black plastic, 3-inch 12- and 20 gauges, in full-size and scaled-down Bantam models.

Friends don’t let friends shoot cheap gas semiautos. They are a headache, unless they are the Maverick SA. This plain Turkish-made gas gun is slim, it’s light, and it does nothing but work. The design is outdated; you have to switch between two different pistons depending on whether you’re shooting light or heavy loads, but outside of that minor inconvenience, the SA delivers reliable performance so long as you break it in with a box or two of heavy loads, and don’t try to make it shoot super-light target ammo. It’s light, listed at 6 ¾ pounds in 3-inch 12 gauge, but fairly soft-kicking. It comes in walnut and black synthetic models with spacers to adjust stock length. This gun joins the 20-, 28-gauge, and .410 SAs already in the Mossberg line.

If you want an inertia gun but don’t want to shell out for a Benelli, the Spandau S2 offers a clone of the old-style Benelli M2 at a great price. It looks like an M2, works very well, and I can’t bump mine out of battery. I shot the 12-gauge turkey version for the 2026 gun test and loved it enough that I’m taking it to the woods next spring. The Turkish-made S2 accepts M2 parts, which is a bonus, since there are a ton of aftermarket add-ons for M2s. Even without Benelli parts, it’s a good gun on its own. It comes in 3-inch 12- and 20-gauges, with 24- or 28-inch barrels, and starts at a ridiculously low price. There are also combo sets with 24- and 28-inch barrels.

When people ask me what they should buy for a first shotgun, I point them to the A300. It’s based on second-generation technology, but in this case, it’s a budget version of the excellent Beretta 391, simplified, changed a little, and made in the United States. The least expensive model is the synthetic version, which features spacers that let you adjust the stock length up to an inch to fit smaller shooters, plus a version of Beretta’s Kick-Off recoil reducer. The gas system is famously reliable, and the gun shoots all loads without adjustment. It comes in just below $1000, at $999.

The latest in the family of Browning/Winchester semiautos spawned by the Browning Gold back in the ’90s, the X4 is made as a price-point gun, but it still comes packed with features. A redesign of the X3, it features a larger square safety, bolt handle, and bolt release button for easier use in cold weather. It has a bright, TruGlo bead, too, for those who like them, and inside it has the same excellent, reliable, easy-care, soft-shooting gas system of the Gold/X2/X3 family. It comes in 12 gauge, black synthetic at just over $1000.

The ACE represents an excellent buy in an inertia gun. Well-made in a very modern Turkish factory, it features deep-drilled barrels for better patterns, a trigger group that you can remove with the push of a button, and a bolt that can’t be bumped out of battery. The two-piece receiver gives you easy access to the action if you need to maintain it in the field. The “Airy” recoil pad works, and the gun shoots a very flat 50/50 pattern. After a couple of early bobbles, mine has hit its stride and become very reliable. The gun also comes in an ACE version without the square-backed receiver, and both are made in 3 ½-inch 12, 3-inch 20, and 3-inch 28 gauges. They come in wood and synthetic models.

The CZ Drake’s price tag reads like a typo. No O/U should cost as little as it does, yet it’s a solid gun that gives you all the advantages of a break action—two chokes, compact balance—at low semiauto pricing. Made in Turkey, the Drake comes in 12, 20, 28, and .410. It doesn’t have much in the way of engraving or fancy wood, and it has extractors that lift spent shells instead of kicking them out like ejectors. In short, it’s a bare-bones O/U that works, and that’s no small thing for $629 complete with hard case and five choke tubes.

The current version of the Orion, Weatherby’s long-time entry-level O/U, is a solid, dependable Turkish-made O/U. It has a low-profile action and a racy Prince of Wales grip. The Grade A walnut stock of the Matte Blue version is matte-finished to match the matte metal. The gun comes in 12- and 20-gauges, with a choice of 26- or 28-inch barrels in 12-gauge and 28-inch in 20. The barrel has a nicely subdued brass bead, and ventilated top and mid-ribs. In all, it’s an excellent value, and if you want to step up to traditional Weatherby glossiness, you can pay $100 more for the Orion I.

As the price of O/Us climbs, the Instinct holds the line at the sub-$2000 price point. The entry-level Instinct, the L model, features a case-colored receiver and Grade A satin-walnut wood. The guns have Prince of Wales grips, rounded forends, and vent top and mid-ribs. They come with a full set of tubes and a small fiber-optic bead. The 12-gauge weighs in around 7 pounds; the 20 is 6 ½, just right for carrying and shooting in the uplands. If you want a lighter gun, you’ll have to pay more for the alloy-framed Instinct SL.

Used models are the best budget shotguns going. The original buyer takes the depreciation hit, you get a deal, and as a bonus, someone else puts the first ding in the stock, saving you the anguish of worrying about it. If it weren’t for used guns, I’d hardly have any guns at all. Still, you have to be careful. Do your homework. The Blue Book of Gun Values is your guide to how much you should pay. It lists virtually every gun made and its price across a range of conditions.

Buy from a dealer who stands behind what they sell. Be sure you know what the return policy is before you buy. If you buy from an online seller, use only those with good ratings, and make sure there’s an inspection period, typically three days. Find out if inspection includes test-firing.

Check the gun carefully for function. I recently bought a Model 12 Winchester with a slide release that was very difficult to press (it’s a thing with Model 12s), and I negotiated the necessary repairs as part of the price. See if the choke tubes come out. I picked up a Mossberg 835 turkey gun, and when I checked it out, I found the choke tube was rusted in place. The gun was already dirt-cheap, but the store knocked another big chunk off the price when I pointed out the stuck tube.

Look for signs like marred screws that shows someone who didn’t know what they were doing has been poking around inside. Be sure neither the barrel nor the stock has been cut down, and look for signs of refinishing. If you need to, have a gunsmith look the gun over, just as you might take a used car to your mechanic. He can spot problems and keep you from buying what looks like a great budget shotgun but is actually a lemon.

Finally, consider resale value. Someday you may want to move on from the gun even though right now you’re smitten with it. I’m terrible about this, but I’m learning. A little while ago, I passed up a terrific deal on an older Browning Citori skeet gun with great wood and a full set of sub-gauge tubes. But it had 26-inch barrels, and the current trend is toward longer ones. I knew if and when I soured on the gun, the short barrels would make it tough to sell, so I let it go. Whether you are buying new or used, a budget means you have a limited amount to spend. And whether that’s a few hundred dollars or a couple thousand, you want to get the most for your money.

“Never sell a gun,” some sage told me years ago. While it seemed like sound advice at the time, it’s not practical. Guns pile up. You have to thin the herd occasionally. Sometimes you need money right away for emergencies; other times you want to make room for something new. There are several ways to sell a gun, from taking it to a gun store or pawn shop to selling it at auction or through private sales.

The Blue Book of Gun Values is updated annually. It’s the standard most buyers and sellers rely on. You can also search online auction sites to see how much guns like yours have sold for.

If you sell a gun to a gun shop, you get money right away—but you might receive only half the gun’s value or even less. Stores have overhead, and they can’t give you the full value of the gun if they want to make any money on the resale. Scopes and other accessories rarely add much to a gun’s price. If you think you might need them in the future, take them off and sell the gun by itself. You’ll generally get a better deal if you trade the gun toward something at the shop that you want. If you need money right away, sell the gun, take your lumps graciously on the price, and walk out the door with cash in hand.

Ask if your gun shop sells on consignment. They’ll work with you to set the price, display the gun, sell it, and take a commission when the gun sells. Some guns go right away, while I’ve seen others sit on the rack for a year or more until someone meets the seller’s price.

You’ll reach the widest possible market if you sell online through GunBroker.com or a similar site. Take lots of pictures, including any scratches, dents, and dings, and be scrupulously honest in your description to minimize the chance of returns. You’ll be responsible for shipping the gun, and the auction site will take a commission when the gun sells.

Private sales (where legal; see below) will get you the most money for your gun. Ideally, you’ll sell it to a friend who wants it, and you’re done with no hassle. Failing that, advertise the gun locally—the bulletin boards at shooting ranges are good places— and sell it. Only ask top dollar if you’re willing to wait a long time for your money. Again, let the Blue Book be your guide.

Be sure you know your state’s laws. A growing number of states require private sales to go through a Federal Firearms License (FFL) holder who can perform background checks. Laws for selling handguns are often stricter than laws governing long gun sales. Be careful and know the law.

The new Backcountry Cottonwoods kit. (Photo: Backcountry)

#8269. Backyard Ultras Are Booming. Here’s Why.

In quite the feat of boots-on-the-ground journalism, author Dan England raced Jess’ Backyard Ultra on August 9, 2024. (Don’t ask him about the race name grammar.) He also spoke with backyard ultra mastermind Gary “Lazarus Lake” Cantrell, several other backyard ultra race directors, and key backyard ultra runners, including Harvey Lewis and Maggie Guterl. What he found is that the format of running a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until only one runner remains is about so much more than running in circles. Since this article was originally published on Outside Run in 2024, backyard ultras have further entered the mainstream with the rise of figures like Mark Dowdle, Belgium resetting the world record, and Team USA winning the 2026 Backyard Ultra World Team Championship.

It’s 8:55 P.M. on Friday, August 9, and I’m with a small group of runners huddled together in a tent on a farm near Greeley, Colorado, that momentarily shelters us from our bad life decisions.

Outside the tent awaits pouring rain and a mushy race course complete with the “Plank of Doom”—a pink makeshift “bridge” adorned in purple twinkle lights suspended four feet over a drainage ditch full of stormwater.

Before the starting gun of this backyard ultra goes off in five minutes, Jessy Nelson needs to make an announcement. I’m assuming it will be about safety. Instead, she tells us that she is not a narcissist.

Yes, Jess’ Backyard Ultra does carry her name. But she named the race for about a dozen friends, all named Jess. (Seriously!). She met them all in an online chat group during a 1,000-kilometer Great Virtual Race Across The States.

Nelson started the race on her farm for them in 2021 with the hope that one Jess could run far enough to qualify for Big’s Backyard Ultra—the original Bell Buckle, Tennessee, “backyard ultra” event that pioneered a quirky new kind of endurance racing format in which runners must complete a 4.167-mile loop on the hour, every hour until they can no longer accomplish the task.

For the record, this event is Jess’ Big Backyard Ultra, not Jessy’s. Understand?

We nod as the rain comes down harder. It would be a fun, goofy, quaint little race that seems to match the aesthetic of many backyard ultras across the world, except it’s been raining for three days, transforming the dirt roads on which we will run into what seems like gooey Jello pudding.

Nelson is worried. The Plank of Doom is seriously dangerous, she tells us. Sure, it’s pink and twinkly, but the four-foot fall that could result with any misstep could mean a broken ankle or, according to Nelson’s narrowed eyes, instant death. Nelson is so serious about the plank that she forces the four of us competing to vote to keep it on the course instead of bypassing it through a paved road 100 yards to the south. We vote to keep it, 3-1.

It’s hard to take anything Nelson says seriously, given that this is a race seemingly held on the set of Little House on the Prairie and that a stuffed toy squirrel named Skittles awaits us in a rocking chair at the turnaround to our 4-ish-mile loop. One of the Jesses befriended a squirrel in her backyard, you see, and that’s a tribute to her. Nelson once befriended an eagle, who would follow her during her daily 10-mile loops around her property. But now, she presumes, the eagle is taking cover. We are about to do the opposite.

Nelson’s odd race is now one of an estimated 500 backyard ultras held around the world that are certified by concept creator Gary Cantrell. You may know him as Lazarus Lake, or simply Laz. He is  probably the sport’s most famous race director and certainly  the quirkiest. Cantrell is known first and foremost for creating the Barkley Marathons, a grueling 100-plus-mile largely off-trail race in Tennessee that’s considered to be the world’s hardest running race to complete. While there’s only one Barkley Marathons, Cantrell’s backyard race format has boomed over the past five years or so.

There is no predefined end length or time in a backyard ultra, as long as multiple runners can complete each 4.167-mile loop within an hour. (Cantrell chose that peculiar distance because running 4.167 miles per hour is exactly what it takes to run 100 miles in 24 hours.) A race ends when only one runner remains to complete a lap and is declared the winner, while all other runners are relegated to did not finish (DNF) status with whatever total number of laps they are able to complete. The runner who completes the second-most laps in a race is often referred to as the “assist,” in the sense that their effort is ultimately what determines how long the race is allowed to continue.

Most backyard races are not like Cantrell’s Big’s Backyard Ultra, which, even though it maintains a grassroots feel, has gained worldwide fame and is filled with elite runners. Most backyard races are more like Nelson’s: small, fun and grueling little get-togethers that last a couple days and bring most runners to tears. Most backyard race directors are like Nelson, too; they have“real” jobs outside of race directing and simply love the format and camaraderie their events foster amid runners of all ability levels pushing  themselves beyond what they ever thought possible.

When Cantrell started his race and named it after his pit bull, Big, in 2012, he hoped to have enough interest for just one event. He was pleasantly surprised when people asked if there would be another race the following  year. Now tens of thousands will likely tune in to the livestream to watch this year’s race on October 19. Cantrell guesstimates more than 25,000 people have run in a backyard ultra event this year, and those are just in the races he’s certified: He knows there are probably dozens more who don’t bother with the paperwork.

“The continued growth really has been a surprise for me,” Cantrell said. Indeed, there are backyard races in 83 countries now.  Even the renowned Tarahumara tribe of Indigenous people from Chihuahua, Mexico, (aka the Raramuri people, who were profiled in the 2009 New York Times bestseller Born to Run,) have their own race, Cantrell noted.

Cantrell relishes putting on the world’s hardest events, almost to a sadistic degree. Only 20 individuals have finished the Barkley Marathons since he began it in 1986. It’s a race as ominous as its location, Frozen Head State Park in Tennessee. The race, over 100 miles with a staggering 65,000-feet-plus of elevation gain, is a miserable quest for survival through thorn-infested bramble, often terrible weather, and ridiculously steep hills on a “course” with no real route.

He started Big’s as another way to test people, and at times, it resembles Stephen King’s The Long Walk, a fictional horror story about 100 walkers who are forced to trudge hundreds of miles and are shot when they quit. Big’s format is also horrifyingly simple: Run 4.167 miles, a “yard,” in under an hour, and then line up and do it again, and again, and again, on the hour, until one person is left. No breaks from the on-the-hour start are allowed, not even to use the porta-potty, but if you finish the yard early, you can eat and drink to your heart’s content, sleep a few minutes, and yes, answer nature’s call. Last year’s winner, accomplished Cinncinnati ultrarunner Harvey Lewis, set a world record by running 450 miles over 108 hours—or four and a half days.

Cantrell now finds himself surprised not only by the race format’s popularity but also the allure many runners have found in the design. These backyard races are, like Nelson’s race, more about community and the comradery of people pushing each other to go farther than they ever have than about fighting your competitors to the near death. While the format becomes exponentially more grueling over time as variables like sleep deprivation escalate, for the first 24 hours or so, the backyard ultra format is an approachable way for many to cover a very long distance. And Cantrell admits that he likes what these mom and pop backyard races have become.

“There are a lot of aspects to it that I didn’t really consider,” he said. “I do know we get a lot of people who never thought they could ever run an ultra. It’s a race for everyone.”

Cantrell thought of the idea for a backyard race close to 50 years ago, when he was in high school struggling to keep up with the fast kids on his track team during interval workouts. He noticed by the end of an interval he was often a little closer to their heels.

“I’d get left in the dust early, but eventually, I’d wear them down,” he said. “So in a 4-mph race, I thought I could beat everybody.”

The idea stayed in the recesses of his mind until he could do something about it on his property in central Tennessee. He didn’t have the money to put on a big race, but with the format, all he needed was a stopwatch.

“This format doesn’t require very much,” Cantrell said. “I think that’s why it’s caught on.”

It’s also caught on because it’s spectator-friendly—both online and in person—perhaps more so than any other race not on a track. It not only made a household name out of Lewis but acted as a coming-out party for Courtney Dauwalter when the two went head-to-head for nearly 20 hours in 2020 and ran a total of 283 miles before Dauwalter outlasted him by a lap and won. Cantrell said this was another aspect of the race he didn’t consider, and it’s partly what makes it fun.

“Women are on an equal competitive footing with men,” he said, and indeed, Maggie Guterl also won Big’s Backyard Ultra, now considered the format’s national championship, in 2019.

The format, Cantrell said, is supposed to measure willpower, not VO2 max or speed or other aspects of physiological talent. There are enough races for that. Instead, Big’s measures grit—the one thing he had over those speedy, more talented guys on the track in high school.

“The most challenging part,” Cantrell said, “should be the distance between the chair and the starting corral.”

Tens of thousands were captivated last year by Lewis’s win, his second at Big’s Backyard, which Cantrell now livestreams and provides real-time written commentary. Lewis was already well known for winning the 135-mile Badwater Ultramarathon in 2014, but he wasn’t taken seriously as a trail runner when he first entered Big’s in 2017, he said.

“I like the trails though,” Lewis said. “I’m very strategic. They were doing it wrong. Everyone was running up the first hill, and I was in the back, just walking up. The next day, everyone walked up the hill.”

Lewis kept going even after making a lap by just a second. He eventually gave in after 200 miles, taking the assist, but it made him wonder just how far he could go. He decided to devote part of his life to it.

“Big’s is so great,” Lewis said. “You’re walking into an ultimate game board, with strategy, perseverance, and skill level. The course itself is nothing special, and it’s usually that way with a lot of them. The genius is behind the format.”

Lewis races at Big’s to win, no doubt, but as a teacher at the School for Creative and Performing Arts in Cincinnati his living does not depend on it. (Good thing, as there’s no prize money anyway.), Despite his competitive drive, he’s learned to relish in the non-competitive moments on the course and treasures his two assists as much as his wins.

Last year, he says his goal was as much to help get runners through the third night as it was to outlast them all. He remembers 2020 mostly for the way he and Dauwalter spent nearly a full day and night taking turns leading the race and pushing each other to approach 300 miles, a number that was, at the time, unheard of to run in this format. Lewis called it a “collaboration” instead of a race. It was a much-needed feel-good story during the pandemic delivered by two nice people.

“We were very encouraging of each other,” Lewis said.

This is one of the evolutions of the race that took Cantrell by surprise: Backyard races build community among runners with different ability levels because of the unique format. Many other ultras around the world are in intimidating places for beginners, but the accessible four-mile loop obliterates those fears.

Mandy Mullen, the owner of run.Windsor in Windsor, Colorado, changed the format from a 50K to a backyard race for her Weld Your Mettle ultramarathon because it helped foster that community aspect.

“There’s so much more to running than just running,” Mullen said. “In this the competition goes away, and it’s more teamwork. There’s zero of, ‘I want to beat this person.’”

Katie Stroud is the president of a running and walking club that’s existed since 1979 in Alice Springs, a small town in the desert of Australia. She hosted the second annual backyard ultra this year as a part of the races the club puts on.

“It’s such a terrific format for people to push their distance in such a wonderful and supportive way,” Stroud said. “It’s so much more than people running in circles.”

Indeed, Cantrell believes more people ran 100 miles in 24 hours, a benchmark so elite that races usually give out special belt buckles to those who do it, this year in backyard events than all the other ultramarathons around the world combined. The final two left standing this year in Alice Springs, Stroud said, were running buddies who just wanted to push each other to 100 miles.

“There are all these little moments like that in our event every year,” Stroud said. “It’s really cool to be there for that.”

Carl Worth was another one who caught the backyard bug. Even though he’d never run more than a half marathon, he ran the virtual backyard race during the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020 and astonished himself by covering 54 miles. He liked the camaraderie and community of backyard running so much he began organizing the Banana Slug Backyard Ultra the following year in Oregon’s Champoeg State Park.

At this year’s event, the winner ran for 49 hours and 200 miles for a “Silver Ticket,” which qualifies him for Big’s Backyard, since the Slug was one of the six events where the winner qualified him for the World Team Championships.

But Worth prefers not to focus only on the winner. During the race, he puts up a spreadsheet on a TV—he’s a software engineer by trade—and posts everyone’s longest distance they’ve run. Whenever they break it, and many do, they can ring a bell, a tradition that Cantrell established at his own race. At this year’s Banana Slug event, 34 runners surpassed their personal bests.

“It’s a really satisfying thing to put on as a race director,” Worth said. “You get to see some amazing things.”

This is true for Jess’ Backyard Ultra as well. The sun rises, illuminating the gray sky and shining some welcome light on our muddy trails. Nelson decides to take a small nap at the house. Our fourth competitor rolled her ankle in the wee hours of the morning, making my friend, Bret Naber, the winner after 30 miles, but we decided to run through the night and see how far we could go. At 9 A.M., after 12 hours and 50 miles of running through the mud, we go home for a shower and some sleep.

This year’s Big’s Backyard Ultra on October 19 is the biannual international team competition, called the World Satellite Backyard Team Competition. Team USA will compete at Cantrell’s event in Tennessee, and the 15-member U.S. roster will have at least two women, Megan Eckert, who won the Saguaro Showdown Backyard Ultra in Mesa, Arizona, and Jennifer Russo, who won Ohio’s Backyard Ultra, as well as Lewis and Scott Martin, the three-time winner of the Banana Slug race put on by Worth.

Cantrell said there are 68 national teams, the members of which will compete simultaneously in backyard ultras in their home countries to earn points for their teams. It’s much like the Olympics—with each country enjoying a home field advantage—and it makes you wonder if this event will finally get ultrarunning there.

“I think you have to reasonably see how it goes,” Cantrell said. “A lot of things start up, and they are really popular, and then they fade out. Maybe somebody more politically skilled than me could get it there.”

But Cantrell’s favorite part about the race format isn’t the superstars, even if his own includes some of the most elite ultrarunners in the world. It’s that time isn’t a factor. It’s about the distance you run, and if you run a personal best, you get recognized for it, even if you finish 30 seconds before the bell.

“The age groups in other races are won by the same people over and over,” Cantrell said. “But in this one, everyone has their day.”

#8268. How to Hunt the Best Day of the Rut No. 5: November 13

If you suffer from friggatriskaidekaphobia (fear of Friday the 13th), this Best Day of the Rut could come with a little apprehension. But for most whitetail hunters, a mid-November Friday should stir up anything but dread. After all, this is the peak of the rut, and almost anything can happen.

Several years ago, on this very day, I shot a mature buck on the edge of a cornfield just 15 minutes into my hunt as he stole a quick sip of water from a mud puddle and continued cruising along the stalks. As I got down and checked my arrow for blood a few moments later, an even larger buck charged in and almost ran me over. Intoxicated by rut hormones and trying to decipher if I was a threat or his next mate, he locked eyes with me for what seemed like minutes before crashing off through the corn.

As wild and exciting as the peak of the whitetail rut can be, it can also be taxing on both deer and hunters. Bucks have now been either searching for or chasing does for weeks, and many hunters have been working just as hard in pursuit of the. But if you haven’t found success yet, don’t lose heart. November 13th is my pick for the No. 1, overall, best day of the entire 2026 rut. So, lock in for a great hunt on this Friday, because the frenzy of the whitetail rut is in full swing.

Related: The 7 Best Days of the 2026 Whitetail Rut

The estrus bell curve is now at its height, meaning the largest portion of does on the landscape are currently in estrus and ready to breed. The action should be on fire, with one caveat—so long as you can find it. Scrapes have largely been abandoned for some time, exchanged for full-out seeking and chasing of does by testosterone-driven bucks. And peak-breeding is, of course, when the highest percentage bucks catch up to those does. Referred to as “the lockdown,” this is a period when bucks sequester does in attempts to guard and breed them, which makes seeing them from stand near impossible if you’re not in just the right spot.

On top of this, factors like weather and local herd dynamics also determine how intense the rut is perceived by hunters. Warm temperatures can drive activity to the nighttime, putting a damper on daylight activity, while areas with a skewed buck-to-doe ratios can see decreased chasing due to the vast breeding options bucks have. But rest assured, one thing is true—the rut is happening and is at this apex. So, here’s how you can break through the lockdown and put yourself in the middle of the action on this challenging, yet most promising Best Day of the 2026 Whitetail Rut.

Two factors push deer into heavy cover more than any others: the peak rut and hunting pressure. Since the first is definitely happening now, and the second is happening in many areas, picking an isolated bedding pocket for an all-day sit is a prime rut strategy. If you have a sanctuary on private land, now is one of the few times to consider entering this sanctum. For the public-land junkies, your pre-scouted, thick-cover bedding areas are by far your best bet for daylight action. Plany your Eentry and exit routes carefully and try to get settled an hour or more before light shooting light. This helps ensure that you’ll beat all deer back to these secluded haunts, and allows them to filter back to your bedding ambush totally alerted. One often-overlooked detail is the color of light you use when entering in the dark. Whitetail studies at the University of Georgia show white light appears 18 times brighter to deer than to humans, but red is next to impossible for them to see. So, if you need it, use a red headlamp, and put extra effort into planning an ultra-silent setup—two things that can make or break an early-morning entry.

What exactly should you be looking for in a prime rut bedding area? According to renown public-land whitetail expert John Eberhart, you should focus on “thick, hard-to-access, secluded areas where multiple trails converge and with ample shooting lanes. Bucks will push does back into these areas and cruise within them at midday, which is exactly where you need to be,” he says. Eberhart adds that the majority of bucks he’s killed have come during this stage of the rut, in these thick-cover areas, and often during midday hours.

If you’re not seeing deer in range, try a calling sequence to mimic a chase. An estrus doe bleat followed by a few excited grunts can bring any buck within earshot right to your tree. And don’t worry if the hours drag on and movement. This is exactly why you need to have ample food, water, and patience to wait it out, because a rut hunt in a bedding pocket can go from boring to big-buck-down in a matter of seconds.

Related: How to Rattle In Whitetail Bucks

If the prospect of sitting in the same spot all day doesn’t appeal to you, an good alternate play is to get down at midday and move to a transition zone outside of bedding cover or between bedding cover and evening food. Setup on the edge of thick cover to catch deer traffic and leverage the nightly deer movement toward a larger food source. This is exactly what I did when I hunted the edge of that standing corn several years ago. I was able to setup my sticks, platform, and saddle as several deer meandered among the rows just 60 yards from me. It’s also what brought the bigger buck running to me. Bucks are keyed up now, and when they cannot see far in thick cover, they must rely on their ears and can be easily fooled. Use this to your advantage by calling or rattling in these conditions to pull a buck out of nearby cover and into one of your shooting lanes.

I caught some of this intense rut behavior in a similar transition zone on public land a few years ago. Sitting in a pinch point surrounded by walls of thick slash, I watched several bucks chase a doe in and out of a small opening and ultimately had a front-row seat to the largest buck breeding her. Afterward, he looked around, blinked a couple times, and then bolted in back into the cover to find another doe. Right now, bucks know their job and don’t waste a minute getting to it, which could bring him right to you if you are in one of these right places at the just right time—which should be this Friday.

I would never suggest blowing up a hunting area on a Hail Mary if you think a little patience will pay off later. However, if you’re working with limited time, having eyes on a shooter buck is information you may want to act on. We’ve all been there. You spot a buck locked down and bedded with a doe through our binoculars while sitting in a tree well out of range. But if you have a few factors in your favor, you absolutely can make a move. A visual barrier like a hill or dense cover and some cover sound, such as an afternoon wind, can disguise your movements, and turn these situations into big opportunities. Just make sure to take your time and keep an eye peeled on those deer, especially the doe—the savior of many a brain-dead rutting buck in mid-November.

#8267. I’ve Owned Dozens of Benchmade Knives—These Are the Best

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more

Benchmade knives have long been a staple for hunters, anglers, and outdoorsmen. The Oregon-based company makes quality blades that are sharp, versatile, and durable. The number one gripe people have with it is the price—and understandably so. Most of their knives are expensive, and there is no way around it. So, are these knives worth the premium price tag? Yes. You just need to make sure you’re buying the right blade for the right application.

I’ll admit that I was late to the scene. In fact, I didn’t get my first Benchmade knife until last fall, right before hunting season. I was sent a Raghorn—made for skinning and quartering big game animals—to test in the field. At the end of the season, I was so impressed with the Raghorn that I started to explore other blades in the collection.

Fast forward to almost a year later, and I have more Benchmade knives than I’d care to admit. But each serves a specific purpose, and dedicated outdoorsmen should pay close attention to these knives. They’re game-changers in the field.

The Benchmade Bugout is the perfect knife. It features everything you need in an EDC knife and nothing you don’t. Throughout my testing, the Bugout was what I carried the most. In fact, I had to force myself not to clip it to my pocket every morning to make sure I tested the other knives thoroughly. And after two months of carrying various EDC knives—Benchmade and other brands—the Bugout stood alone.

This knife is lightweight, sharp, and a perfect length for everyday carry. I use it to open packages, cut fishing line, and repair gear. My good friend, a former fisheries biologist, carried this knife on the job every single day for over two years. He used it for motor maintenance, boat repair, electrical work, and any other tasks he encountered on the water. And the durable stainless steel or cerakote finish makes this a great option for carrying on the water—just make sure to rinse it if you use it for saltwater applications.

As I said before, I clip this to my pocket every morning. And the lightweight design makes it almost unnoticeable—even on light athletic shorts. To top it off, this is one of the most affordable Benchmade knives. The price plus the ergonomic design make the Bugout a solid EDC option.

The Benchmade Narrows is a premium EDC knife, and the price reflects that. What makes it so expensive? For starters, it is the thinnest knife Benchmade has ever made, only measuring .28 inches in thickness. This design also makes it the most compact knife I’ve ever carried.

The appeal of the Narrows is the slim build that makes carrying it almost unnoticeable. Benchmade accomplished this by redesigning the axis lock and substituting the liners for a new lock stud and torsion spring. That terminology won’t mean anything to most people, but it’s important to note how they developed such a thin frame without sacrificing strength or durability.

This knife is king for those who spend time in the backcountry and are looking to save space. And while Benchmade reduced the thickness of the frame, they kept a longer 3.43-inch blade. This durable stainless steel blade increases the knife’s versatility beyond EDC uses, and I wouldn’t hesitate to carry it with me on hunts. It is a do-it-all knife. The titanium handle is lightweight, comfortable, and grips the hand well.

At almost $600, this isn’t a purchase for someone looking for a typical EDC knife. The Narrows is made for situations where space management is crucial—backpackers, hikers, hunters, etc. This knife cuts weight and saves space while offering the versatility of a longer, stronger blade.

Think of the Taggedout as the Bugout of the hunting world. It is a “jack of all trades, master of none” type of knife. And I very much mean that as a positive. I carried the Taggedout during my big game hunts, waterfowl hunts, turkey hunts, and upland hunts last season. I used it to help dress a mule deer and breast out dozens of ducks. I like the lightweight design of this folder, and it works well as a general camp knife, but can still perform in-the-field tasks.

Benchmade is also offering two new Taggedout models this year. The first features a new handle, a premium stainless steel blade, and a thumb stud. The second, which releases in September, will have a Magnacut steel blade—the first Benchmade hunt knife to feature this new stainless steel that is taking the knife world by storm. The Magnacut model will also include a lightweight carbon fiber handle.

While the new models have better materials and some nice improvements, I’m not sure if it’s worth the extra money. I love my original Taggedout, and its versatility is unmatched. For $180, this is one of the best value knives in the Benchmade lineup.

You’re looking at the best hunting knife I’ve ever carried. The Raghorn is an ultra-lightweight full tang fixed-blade skinning knife. I carried mine during a seven-day elk hunt and a five-day mule deer hunt. This knife made easy work of skinning and quartering my buck, and I was impressed with the control of the blade. This steadiness of the fixed blade knife is enhanced by the milled finger grip on top of the blade, which allows for increased precision and control.

The carbon fiber handle and steel blade make for a lightweight (3.56 oz) knife. A strong and lightweight fixed blade is a huge benefit in the backcountry, where every ounce matters. I like the high-vis orange cerakote finish on the blade for safety reasons, which really makes a difference if you place the knife down, especially in low-light conditions. My Raghorn came razor sharp out of the box and sliced a piece of paper in half like butter. The blade retained a sharp edge even after I skinned and quartered a mule deer. And while $380 is a lot of money, this knife is worth every penny. My only complaint is that the sheath doesn’t fit a belt, and you need to buy a Tek-Lok belt clip to secure the knife to your hip.

Big game hunters who process their own harvest need to have a Meatcrafter. I use mine every time I pull a piece of wild game out of the freezer. It slices through meat with ease and is perfect for trimming fat. But its best use is deboning and processing game after a hunt. The blade has just enough flexibility to move around the bone and ensure you get the most meat.

I even used my Meatcrafter to process over a dozen iguanas after a hunt in Southern Florida. Now, if you’ve never skinned an iguana, you should know their skin is like leather. The Meatcrafter was the only knife in the house that could cut the tough skin without ruining the meat. I also bring this knife on summer camping trips, and it performs just as well at base camp. Like most Benchmade knives, it is on the pricier side. But if you process and cook a lot of wild game, this knife is well worth the cost.

I’m no chef, but this knife makes preparing meals more efficient and enjoyable. The Custom Station is an all-purpose culinary knife that works just as well at camp as it does in the kitchen. Slicing, chopping, and preparing meat is easy with this sharp blade and comfortable carbon handle. Besides its ergonomic design and quality build, I love that this knife is compact and light enough to bring to camp. I’ve prepared various wild game and everyday meals with this knife, and it is the best kitchen blade I own.

The basic Station comes in at $325, but you can splurge for more custom options with artwork on the blade and handle.

This is one of the lightest and most durable out of the front automatic knives available. With a simple push of the button, the 3.51-inch blade quickly releases from the handle. The Shootout only weighs 2.80 ounces, and it is perfect for everyday carry applications.

Originally designed for law enforcement, this automatic knife features easy deployment whether with your weak hand or in a stressful situation. It operates from a double-action spine fire release button towards the front of the handle. The biggest concern with automatic knives is safety, and Benchmade stepped it up a level. If something is directly in front of the blade when you hit the release, it will instantly pop off the track and go loose. This safety precaution eases my mind while I have it in my pocket. Benchmade also added two new colors and a comfortable grivory handle to the Shootout for 2023.

When shopping for expensive knives, especially for outdoor-specific pursuits, it is critical to consider the knife’s intended purpose. I chose every knife on this list for a reason. Some are more versatile than others, but I use each knife for different tasks. I tested them in the field, marsh, and/or kitchen and judged them on their performance at a specific task rather than against each other.

Big game hunting knives were tested in the field, skinning and quartering big game animals. The waterfowl knife was tested by breasting mallards, and the butchering pick was chosen after processing two mule deer. Culinary knives were tested in the kitchen while preparing various wild game meals.

The rest of the lineup features everyday carry (EDC) knives. Which means there is more overlap and competition between the models. To narrow down the winners, I carried each knife for over a week and performed everyday tasks like opening boxes, repairing gear, car maintenance, and anything else you’d use a pocket knife for. I evaluated the Benchmade EDC knives in the following categories:

By the end of the test, specific knives edged out others, highlighting the strengths and weaknesses of each. My biggest takeaway from over a year of testing was that the right blade for the job makes a big difference. Everyone should identify a specific need for a knife before spending good money on one.

Benchmade knives are an investment, and you should have a specific need before you buy one. Whether that’s hunting, camping, everyday carry, or cooking—your knife should be tailored to tasks you need to accomplish. The following considerations will help point you in the right direction.

Are you looking for a knife to dress big game animals? Or maybe you need something to help clean dozens of ducks. Backpackers might be looking for something lightweight and slim to save space. This is the thought process you have to work through before choosing a knife. Many of the Benchmade knives on this list—the Raghorn, Taggedout, Flyway, Meatcrafter, and Station—are built for particular tasks. People looking for blades to fill niche hunting, camping, and cooking roles should give strong consideration to these knives.

The Benchmade everyday carry options are a bit different. You’re going to pay more money for a Benchmade EDC knife than elsewhere—that’s just a fact. What you need to ask yourself is, are the knives worth the money for what I need them to do? And if you require a durable, lightweight, sharp knife every single day, then yes, they are worth it. The Bugout, Shootout, and the rest of the Benchmade EDC options are high-quality knives that are extremely sharp and useful in everyday scenarios.

Benchmade offers a lifetime factory resharpening program. Mail your knife back to Benchmade (no matter how long after you bought it), and they will sharpen it free of charge. And while you should sharpen your knife throughout its lifespan, it doesn’t hurt to send it back to have it professionally sharpened. After all, it’s free.

Just because Benchmade knives are high-quality and expensive doesn’t mean they’re rust-proof. It is important to properly clean and dry your knives to prevent rust from forming. If it rusts, rust polish and a microfiber cloth will remove any spots.

All Benchmade knives are made at their factory in Oregon City.

Yes. Benchmade makes some of the most durable knives available. The blades are made from high-quality steel and premium handle components and hardware.

Benchmade is known for making some of the best hunting, camping, EDC, and culinary knives. Choosing a knife should be based on application and purpose. Determine what you need from your knife and start looking for a blade fit for the task. When it comes to big game hunting, the Raghorn stands alone. Every dedicated bird hunter needs a Flyway, and the Station is great for meal preparation. But the most versatile knife from Benchmade is the Bugout. It is the perfect EDC design and well worth the money.

#8266. The 7 Items That Got Me Through October (and the Rest of Fall)

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Oh October, the month of mystery. Here in Boulder, Colorado, it’s when you wake up in the dark not knowing if it will be warm, cold, raining, or windy. The only thing you do know every morning is there will be even more much-larger-than-life-sized skeletons poking out of peoples’ lawns. (Why has this become a thing? As my friend Clare said on a run the other day, “people are desecrating their lawns with plastic trash!”)

Anyway, it’s a tricky time of year for running. Head out the door overdressed and you will end up a puddle of sweat that, depending on the weather, ultimately makes you cold. Leave underdressed, as I did for a tempo run two weeks ago, and your limbs will feel like they’ve been cursed by a witch who’s turned them to immovable ice.

But tricky conditions can be solved with treats. My trusty associate editor is, in his words, “going to the desert to do something stupid.” (Go Cade!) That leaves just me to round up our gear of the month. Here are the five items I kept packed in my Janji Ultrahauler (another piece of gear I can’t live without!) so I was ready for whatever I woke up to:

Kilian Jornet’s fledgling shoe and apparel company has stuck to relatively technical alpine equipment—until now with the Nnormal Cadi. This do-everything trail shoe is exceptionally comfortable thanks to a padded heel collar and tongue and a cushy midsole with 37 mm stack in the heel, 31 mm in the forefoot. It’s got a nice wide toe box (an obsession of mine as I work on my foot strength and toe splay). And with a Vibram Megagrip outsole it’s tacky on all terrain and in all conditions. I also appreciate the mesh upper, which is breathable on hot days and dries quickly on wet ones. It’s the only shoe I brought on a trip recently, which means I found myself wearing it for a 12-mile run around the Charles River in Boston—definitely not as energetic as your typical road trainer these days, but it got the job done just fine. It’s just a solid, dependable shoe.

It’s rained A LOT in Boulder this month. And by a lot, I mean more than zero times. I know I’ve lived here for too long because I’ve gotten soft and the only thing that got me through more than zero very dark, very wet mornings was this rain jacket from Arc’teryx. That’s because it’s actually waterproof. But it’s also super lightweight and breathable, meaning you don’t incinerate in your own body heat and end up wet anyway. Plus one for the cinch on the hood so you can actually keep it on your head while you’re running and another bonus for the vents under the armpits, which help moderate body heat. I know $450 is an obscene amount to spend on anything, but this is definitely a case of you get what you pay for.

When it comes to running pants and tights I am very, very picky. They can’t suffocate my waist, but they also need to stay put. They can’t bunch around the knees, but they also can’t be so baggy that the pant legs rub into each other. The Janji Altas Multi Pant is one of the few pieces that passes my stringent test. They are supremely comfortable thanks to a wide elastic waistband, and a drawstring lets you dial in the fit. They’re loose enough to allow for full range of motion, but they’re streamlined enough that I can wear them for harder efforts without getting annoyed. Why I really love them for this time of year is they are lightweight and breathable, providing just the right amount of insulation. And even better, they have nearly knee-length ankle zips so I often wear them for the warm up and zip them off for intervals—no shoe removal required.

There is something so comforting and luxurious about tucking into a comfy vest for a fall outing. Enter this fleece-lined vest from 7Mesh. It’s super breathable yet cozy thanks to a soft, woven outer layer paired with the light and ultrasoft fleece lining. I’ve been loving it for colder runs when a jacket feels like too much but a long sleeve isn’t quite enough. And I’ve also been loving it on the bike—especially because the vest folds into itself via a big back pocket, revealing little straps that let you fix it to your bike frame when you’re not wearing it.

Not too cold and not too warm, snug but not tight, these gloves are  a shoulder-season star. They’re so lightweight that I don’t think twice about wearing them for the start of a run before the sun rises and stashing them in a pocket as I warm up with the ground. I can use my phone with them on, carry my ballot (the midterms are on Tuesday!), as well as maneuver zippers and, if desperate, tie shoes. Plus the colors and patterns instantly boost my mood. (They came in so many fun options!)

One-star review for the name. Zero stars for the logo branded on the top of the collar. And yet, five stars for these socks. They are just that comfy and moisture-wicking. I am pretty skeptical of overengineered gear, but CEP has me thinking maybe there is something to developing stuff in a lab. These socks provide a gentle amount of compression and arch support while also being ventilated in all the places you want it. In other words: they stay put, and they keep my feet comfortable for a wide range of temperatures—perfect for fall running. Most importantly, my feet do not slip in my shoes. I repeat: no slippage here. My friend saw me running in them the other day and he said he also loves these socks so much that he ordered five pairs. Oh and they come in approximately one billion colorways.

I know, I know, it’s a crime to spend more than $50 on a hair product—much less two products. But hear me out: Colorado is savage on my wavy hair. When left unchecked, the dry air and harsh sun leech out every last drop of moisture, turning my hair into a wiry mess. Add in the rainy days of October (or my annual pilgrimage to Hawaii) and in years past I am ripping out chunks of matted hair every time I shower. Enter this fancy shampoo and conditioner. I am not exaggerating when I say this stuff has revolutionized my hair’s life. For the first time in 13 years since I moved here, my hair feels soft. And I can actually get a brush through it when I get out of the shower! You better believe I will be buying it again.

#8265. Skiers, Your Eyes Need More Protection Than You Think. Here’s What Doctors Say.

Catie Evans had been skiing for days along the Continental Divide in Colorado when she woke up with swollen eyes.

After logging multiple 12-hour days back-to-back, all while wearing glacier glasses, the avid backcountry skier figured she was just tired. But as she skinned toward Dead Dog Couloir on 14,267-foot Torrey’s Peak, she remembers, “I started to feel like somebody had thrown sand in my eyes.”

Eventually, with her eyes watering, she had to ski down with one eye covered, squinting out of the other with her friends guiding her.

Later, Evans tried to troubleshoot. Had she damaged her glasses without realizing it? Did she miss news of a recall? Or, throughout the multi-day trip, had she taken them off more than she thought, slowly racking up UV exposure in the process?

She’s still not sure. But, she’s not the only skier to experience snow blindness, and her experience illustrates the importance of eye protection at high altitude. While we often discuss features like fit, contrast, and style when it comes to choosing goggles, sometimes we don’t spend as much time thinking about what they’re protecting us from. So, we called up a few eye doctors to ask all of your burning questions about eye safety on the slopes.

While you might associate sun damage with summer days, skiers are constantly enjoying a double-dose of UV radiation thanks to the strength of the sun above combined with the reflective snow below. And, that exposure increases by roughly 4 to 5 percent for every 1,000-foot increase in elevation thanks to the gradually-thinning atmosphere.

Never let temperature or overcast conditions fool you; those invisible rays are always shining down, and they’ll pierce right through the clouds into your unsuspecting eyeballs.

We Tested 29 Pairs of Goggles. These are the 10 Best for the 2026-’27 Ski Season.

“Whenever we’re outside, (UV) rays can damage the surface of the eye as well as the cornea and lens,”  explained Dr. Becky Leenheer, spokesperson for the American Academy of Ophthalmology spokesperson, an assistant professor at the University of New Mexico, and an ophthalmologist herself.

Children, she said, are especially vulnerable. “Over time, cumulative UV exposure raises the risk of cataracts and of growths on the eye’s surface.”

Dr. Thomas Litzinger, an avid skier and ophthalmologist at ReVision Lasik and Cataract Surgery in Ohio, noted that the scariest potential consequence of continued exposure is cancers of the eye or the skin around it.

These conditions develop gradually, Leenheer said, but you shouldn’t ignore short-term discomfort either. Issues like photokeratitis (snow blindness), which is basically a burn to the corneal surface, hurts like heck and can contribute to further problems, though you may not feel them developing in the moment. Going forward, they’re a sign to protect your eyes better next time.

Here’s the good news: Almost any pair of goggles on the market should protect you from these risks. To be sure, look for claims like “100% UV (or UVA and UVB) Protection” or “UV400.”

One caveat is that goggles are not regulated in the United States. While any reputable company should be safe, we make no promises about the $20 goggles you found on Amazon. Litzinger added that the European Union does regulate goggles, and the label CE (Conformité Européenne) denotes that a pair meets EU standards.

Beyond UV protection, he explained, choosing goggles comes down to preference, or safety in the sense that better visual quality and field-of-view may help you avoid other accidents.

He notes that one common misconception is conflating UV protection with Visible Light Transmission (VLT). This factor determines how much brightness your goggles let in, but has no bearing on UV protection.

“There is no correlation between darker lenses and higher UV blocking,” added Dr. Cameron Cutler, an optometrist at Summit Vision in Frisco, Colorado. “Tint color does not matter, buy what you like!”

Features such as different tints, anti-fog measures, and lens shapes may promise improvements when it comes to comfort and visual quality, but they also don’t impact sun exposure itself.

Litzinger added that some skiers mistake glare complications for snow blindness, but this is another misconception. Though glare can be painful, or even reduce one’s ability to see, the cause is excessive brightness and likely choosing the wrong VLT for the conditions, not UV exposure.

As unpleasant as glare is, you can rest assured you’re protected from a UV standpoint with quality goggles.

Some companies do try to mitigate this issue by offering tinted, high-contrast or polarized lenses for a more comfortable ride. But be aware the latter poses a trade-off many skiers opt against, Cutler noted, as it can hide dangerous icy patches as well as glare.

Overall, Litzinger said, “It’s pretty important as skiers and riders to match your lens to the conditions to really discern contrast and terrain.” Additionally, Leenheer said, skiers should make sure their goggles are impact-resistant and fit snugly to protect you from wind, snow, and excess sunlight.

But, choosing the wrong ones (provided they have UV protection) won’t lead to any long-term eye damage, and neither will opting for budget goggles. “On the UV front, cheap and expensive are on the same playing field,” Litzinger said, adding that expensive goggles may distinguish themselves in other ways including fit, durability, and optical quality.

While some glasses and contacts block UV rays too, Cutler noted that full-coverage goggles offer the most protection for your eyes, as well as the sensitive skin around them.

That said, you’re only protected if you’re wearing them.

Plenty of eye damage occurs when skiers stop for lunch or a beer, take off the Oakleys, and expose their eyes to all those UV rays they’ve been avoiding all day, Cutler noted. So, even once you’ve taken off your skis, be aware of your environment and ready to rock eye protection for as long as you’re outdoors.

#8263. New Interior Department Plan Prioritizes Public Land Sell Offs and Data Center Construction

The Department of Interior has released a “strategic plan” that could guide the agency for the next four years, and it includes the proposed sale of federally managed public lands to states, local municipalities, and tribes. The plan to offload public lands—or “shrink the federal estate”, as the DOI’s 2026-2030 Strategic Plan puts it—comes roughly 500 days after Utah Sen. Mike Lee sparked a major national backlash with his failed plan to sell some 3.2 million acres of public lands throughout the western U.S. in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act of 2025.

“The Department will work to decrease the size of the federal estate by offering to states, localities and Tribes the opportunity to purchase federal lands,” reads a paragraph on page 16 of the 28-page plan. “Through these sales, the Department will be able to focus its resources on primary federal responsibilities and nationally significant federal lands.”

The Department of Interior manages more than 500 million acres of public lands via the Bureau of Land Management (BLM), The US Fish & Wildlife Service (USFWS), and the National Park Service (NPS). According to reporting in the Washington Sun, this marks the first time that the DOI has ever announced intentions to offload public lands in a strategic draft plan. And it breaks “with 50 years of precedent that largely limited land sales.”

In addition to public land sell offs, the DOI’s new strategic plan, announced by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum on November 11, would end the use of the popular Land and Water Conservation Fund (LWCF) to acquire new public lands. The Congress created LWCF in 1964 to reinvest offshore oil and gas revenues into public lands and outdoor recreation. The fund receives $900 million every year from oil and gas projects. It was fully refunded and reauthorized in 2020 with the passage of the Great American Outdoors Act.

The plan also announced that the DOI will further consolidate its workforce. This comes as the agency has already shed more than 20 percent of its workforce or more than 13,000 employees, largely through efforts pushed by the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE).

Another goal of the plan is to use public lands that do remain in the federal estate to supply materials and energy needed to construct data centers. “By developing reliable and up-to-date inventories of national resource assets, Interior will help ensure a stable domestic supply of energy, critical minerals, raw building materials and other important resources to build and power homes, data centers and long-term strength of the American economy,” the plan goes on to state. “In addition to advanced mapping, Super Intelligence and scientific data will enable the Department to expand and develop our inventory of potential resources. Together, these efforts will help the U.S. understand and actively manage its natural wealth, encourage innovation and support future development.”

The plan stops short of announcing any specific data centers sites proposed for public lands. However, there are already multiple efforts underway to permit data centers on BLM lands throughout the West. One such data center project near Boulder City, Nevada, which F&S reported on last August, was approved by the agency before a Federal Appeals Board overturned that decision.

A November 6 report from Pro Publica revealed that the Trump Administration’s US Geological Survey (USGS) has determined that some 91.3 million acres of public land managed by the Interior Department have the potential to host data centers. The states listed in the USGS report are Alaska, Arizona, California, Idaho, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Utah, Washington, and Wyoming. The Pro Publica report also pinpoints Sec. Burgum’s personal investments in the AI industry at somewhere between $18.1 million and $64.4 million.

#8262. How Joe “Stringbean” McConaughy (Finally) Broke the John Muir Trail FKT

Joe McConaughy thought he would probably start a bit slower than François D’Haene when he went after the Frenchman’s record on the John Muir Trail (JMT) this September. He guessed he’d be maybe 20 or 30 minutes behind in the early miles.

But when McConaughy got to Kearsarge Pass around mile 40, he was an hour off of D’Haene, who ran the Fastest Known Time (FKT) on the 223-mile trail through California’s Sierra Nevada in 2017, just months after winning UTMB for the third time.

“That was definitely a bit of a crack in the armor,” McConaughy told Trail Runner. “But I told myself that maybe he went out at more of a race effort, while my pace was better for a multi-day FKT.”

McConaughy, known by his thru-hiking trail name, “Stringbean,” has more than a few multiday FKTs to his name. He’s set records on the Pacific Crest Trail, Appalachian Trail, Long Trail, and Arizona Trail. And he had two prior record attempts on the JMT, one of which earned him an unsupported FKT.

“I thought my experience could help me beat him,” McConaughy said.

As he chased the ghost of the JMT’s past, McConaughy drew from his many multi-day FKTs and races. All of the miles and mistakes, successes and failures, and lessons and growth along the way helped him ultimately establish a new FKT of 2 days, 16 hours, and 15 seconds, taking nearly three and a half hours off a time that had stood for nearly a decade.

In rock climbing, climbers talk about “flashing” a route. It’s when they successfully climb the whole thing on their first attempt—without any practice or “beta” to help. McConaughy’s JMT effort was pretty much the opposite of flashing. The 35-year-old Seattle-based endurance coach was incredibly familiar with every mile of the JMT. Prior to his record setting attempt this fall, he’d covered the trail four times—the first in 2014—including the two prior FKT attempts. He’d also spent five summers guiding backpacking trips in the Sierra.

So when McConaughy ended up in a blizzard on Muir Pass with snowflakes landing in his eyeballs, it didn’t really stress him out or slow him down. If anything, it helped him move faster as he wanted to get up and over to warmer ground.

“I’ve seen the worst that the Sierra can throw at you,” he said, citing thunderstorms, blizzards, and rugged terrain. “I didn’t have to do a bunch of mental gymnastics, worrying about things I hadn’t experienced before. Instead, I could devote all of my energy to things that actually were issues.”

Most of McConaughy’s issues during the record attempt were ones he expected to occur, was prepared for, and could handle. “The long climbs were long climbs and some of the descents take decades,” he said. But after numerous JMT attempts he knew “it could feel much harder.” A little over a day into his attempt he was two hours ahead of D’Haene’s splits.

The JMT is far from the only goal for which McConaughy’s persistence has paid off. He took seven swings at earning a Golden Ticket into the Western States 100 before clinching one at the Black Canyon 100K on his eighth try in 2025. He’s also raced the Cocodona 250 three times and has a trio of Barkley Marathons starts.

“I like to think I’m more fun than a project-er, but when I look back, that’s pretty much my entire running career,” he said. “I feel like it gives me purpose. I want to do routes that inspire me and motivate me and take what I’ve done wrong, or what I feel like I could improve on, and continue to experiment, tinker, and optimize.”

He’s not as intense as a rock climber going after a seemingly impossible objective like the Dawn Wall, he swears. Rather, it’s about finding the sweet spot where he’s pushing himself to grow but having fun doing it. He’s not training to be the best at any given race or record attempt; he’s training to be the best version of himself for years to come.

“I get a lot of joy from sticking with the process, training with a smile, putting in the work to make a difference, and looking for opportunities to rise like a phoenix and perform the best that I can,”  McConaughy said.

Caroline Himbert, who is coached by McConaughy and set her own unsupported FKT on the JMT this July, helped pace McConaughy on the JMT this fall. “He goes back to things he’s failed at and tries to continuously learn and grow; he loves the science and spreadsheets and takes things seriously,” Himbert said. “But at the same time, he doesn’t take things too seriously and he keeps things fluid and fun.”

As evidenced by the fact that it stood for nine years, the JMT record was stout. D’Haene is known for bringing a newfound level of professionalism to FKT attempts, with a full support staff, set of pacers, and film crew. But rather than seeing the competitive level of the record as a deterrent, McConaughy saw it as part of the draw.

“It’s the granddaddy of FKTs,” he said. “More people have attempted the JMT FKT than pretty much any other premier route that exists—and the fact that François [D’Haene] and Darcy [Piceu] were the [previous] record holders is an ode to the level of attention and competitiveness that it’s gotten.”

On his first attempt in 2022, McConaughy set an unsupported record of three days and one hour. But Jeff Garmire beat it by 13 minutes just 25 days later.

McConaughy knew he could do better, so he tried to reclaim the record in 2024. But he hallucinated in the final miles and wound up off-trail on a class-four scramble, much closer to life-and-limb-threatening risk than he’d anticipated. It was a wake-up call for McConaughy, who always considers what he’s asking of others when he chases a big goal. He’s now the father of a 6-month-old and knew he couldn’t end up in a similar situation—or worse—if he went back.

“That experience made me really rethink what the record meant to me and ask myself if I wanted to do it again,” he said, adding that it felt reckless to go for another unsupported record. But after much reflection, and many conversations with his wife Katie, he decided he had to go back.

“I knew I couldn’t exist as an athlete without trying to put my stamp on the JMT,” he said. “This was my third time [attempting the FKT] on this trail and I wanted to give it my all, and use my best tips and tricks from every other effort to get the record.”

McConaughy showed up with a 12-tab spreadsheet and 12 years of beta to guide his effort this fall. He thought some of the greatest opportunities for improvement lay in fueling, pacing, and recruiting an all-star crew to help him out. In his unsupported-style attempts, he’d had to carry all of his own food and gear with no supply restocks along the way.

At Cocodona in 2025, McConaughy hit a wall that no amount of carbs could fix. He thought he knew how he needed to fuel to compete for the win. He’d done sweat testing and was experimenting with high-carb fueling. But he ended up with GI distress and struggled to breathe. He still finished in a respectable fourth place, but it was far from the finish he wanted.

He started working with nutritionist Meredith Terranova, who suggested he was likely hypernatremic—too high of blood sodium concentration—during Cocodona. He wondered if trying to optimize his performance through a data-driven approach with high carb fueling and sweat tests meant he’d stopped listening to his body.

So on the JMT he turned to real food like trail mix, purees, and waffles, especially on the big climbs—of which there is no shortage with 38,000 feet of elevation gain to cover. He also used recovery drink mixes and fat- and protein-based fuels from his nutrition sponsor, Näak.

“I feel like sticking to more whole food was the biggest learning and the biggest difference maker in my performance,” he said.

He also made up ground through a smarter sleep strategy. In his 2022 attempt, in which he finished six hours behind D’Haene’s record time, McConaughy slept for six hours. He knew there was an opportunity to trim down time spent resting while still sleeping enough to avoid dangerous hallucinations.

He settled on taking a mere 40 minutes of sleep beneath a pine tree on Bear Ridge—around 28 hours in. He thought it might be prudent to get at least an hour but he decided to push it a little with 40 minutes, figuring he could always nap later if he needed it. When he got to his third night out on the trail he was still running strong, cracking jokes, and appreciating his surroundings, Himbert said.

“You could tell he was having a good time and he was a ball of energy,” she said. “I was with him more towards the end, and he was still moving so well. I think that’s the key with this trail; it’s so challenging but if you can still move well towards the end then you can crack these times. I think Joe really nailed it, and it went close to perfect.”

McConaughy’s crew was one of his greatest assets. He learned some things about crewing the JMT after his crew missed him at Kearsarge Pass during his Pacific Crest Trail FKT in 2014. The PCT overlaps with the JMT for about 170 miles. He had to keep going on the PCT for two days with no sleeping bag, only a half-day’s worth of calories, and nothing warmer than a thin windbreaker. “We didn’t really know what we were doing,” he said. Hence the 12-tab spreadsheet this go-around, which was largely for the benefit of his crew and the complicated logistics of supporting a record-attempt on the JMT.

Part of the beauty of the JMT is that it offers an uninterrupted tour of backcountry wilderness. The trail only crosses the road twice over the course of the entire 223 miles. That’s also what makes it a bear to support. Meeting McConaughy on the trail required hiking several miles and thousands of feet of climbing to deliver food and gear. Pacers ran monster sections—usually around 40 miles at a time. But his crew of pacers was up for the challenge, with a collective résumé that boasted JMT FKTs, podium finishes, and 200-mile runs.

“Tara Dower talked about being a vessel on the Appalachian Trail, and I certainly had a similar experience on the JMT,” McConaughy said. “I was able to appreciate the beauty of where I was and the excitement of doing this absurd endurance thing because my crew was always filling my cup instead of making me pour things out to keep going.”

One thing that McConaughy has learned time and time again, is that he runs best when his cup is full.

“Gratitude and joy are the greatest performance-enhancing drugs,” he said.

While he was running, he thought about Katie, who was home solo-parenting so he could acclimatize to the altitude and run for 64 straight hours. He thought about his parents, who enabled him to get outside and run cross-country from a young age. He thought about the people who have supported his running career, and the friends who traveled to the Sierra to help him through the 223-mile journey. And he thought about the Sierra themselves, the mountains that have kept him coming back time and time again for the last 12 years.

“I run my worst when I’m thinking about how far behind someone’s splits I am,” he said. “When I caught myself doing that on the JMT, I thought, ‘This is doing more harm than good. You need to move forward at your own pace, and focus on the things that really matter.’”

After shaving over three hours off such a long-standing record, McConaughy hopes that he’s reached an end with his JMT FKT attempts. With all of the time and effort he has dedicated to the JMT, it feels a bit like a fairytale ending: “The princess was saved,” he said.

Now, he’s ready for a new goal, one he’s ready to chase to fuel his performance and fill his cup

“It’s one of those moments where I realize I’m maybe more capable than I thought I was,” he said. “And that makes it exciting to go back to Cocodona, or Western States, or another FKT, or any number of things to see what I can do.”
