And it performs, too: The 2.5-layer NanoPro fabric kept our tester dry even after she wore it under a heavy pack in 50-degree temperatures, but was still tough enough that it didn’t fray after heavy use.

Weight: 25.4 oz (men’s) / 25.0 oz (women’s) Sizes: Men’s S-XXL / Women’s XS-3XL

Pros and Cons + Soft and supple + Lots of venting options + Easy to repair and actually recyclable – Heavy and bulky – Too warm for summer weather

The Velez Adventure Smock is not the lightest jacket in our test: The jacket, which eschews a waterproof-breathable membrane for a DWR-treated polyester face backed by wicking fabric, is better suited for colder-season temperatures. So what makes it a good jacket for hikers who run hot? In shoulder-season conditions, it breathes and maintains its waterproofing better than most traditional three-layer rain shells. Venting helps, too: Biceps zippers and a horizontal front flap across the torso make it easy to dump heat quickly before users get too steamy.

Weight: 1.8 oz (men’s) Sizes: Men’s XS-XXL

Pros and Cons + Ultralight + Surprisingly durable + Surprisingly weatherproof – No hood or chest pocket – Tight fit

At 1.8 ounces, this gossamer hoodless jacket is a reliable friend for mountain runners, fastpackers, and anyone who values velocity. The 10-denier recycled nylon exterior packs up to (literally) pocket size, and while we wouldn’t bet on it to keep you bone-dry through a multi-day storm, it handled surprise desert downpours without batting an eye. Breathability is exceptional, which our tester confirmed after a full day of biking along the Grand Canyon’s South Rim.

First, understand you may have to compromise. While waterproof-breathable membranes are almost ubiquitous, most jackets prioritize waterproofing over breathability, or vice versa. Jackets that can weather a downpour without so much as wetting out may not breathe well, and those that breathe well may be better for scattered showers than the kind of rain that makes you start thinking about building an ark.

Pay attention not just to the breathability of the jacket itself, but to the venting options, too. Even the most breathable fabrics can’t dump heat as well as a set of pit zips or mesh-backed pockets that expose your underlayers to fresh air. Packability is more important than you might think, too: If you’re consistently hot, having a jacket that you can ball up and stick inside your pack without a second thought is a better move than carrying a heavy, bulky one.

Our lead testers for men’s and women’s rain jackets are Drew Zieff and Elizabeth Kwak. Our gear editors pulled these recommendations from their original testing notes and scores to recommend the best rain jackets for hikers who overheat.

#8225. A Woman Was Swept Off an Oregon Beach and Left Clinging to Rocks Offshore. A Lifeguard Rescued Her in the Darkness.

Rocky sea stacks rise along Oregon’s southern coast, where a woman was swept into the ocean by massive waves at Secret Beach on November 8. (Photo: Juan Pablo Jim/Getty)

A woman was rescued from the ocean after powerful waves swept her off a beach in southern Oregon on November 8, leaving her clinging to rocks offshore as darkness fell.

The woman had been walking along Secret Beach, a secluded stretch of rocky coastline roughly 20 miles north of the California border, when a swell pulled her into the ocean, according to a statement posted to Facebook by Curry County Aquatic Safety. Unable to reach her, the woman’s husband called 911 around 5:18 P.M. The report did not name the woman.

When a Curry County sheriff’s deputy arrived at the scene, the woman had been swept 200 feet down the coastline, where she was stranded on rocks roughly 50 to 70 feet offshore.

“People want to come see the waves, and we have a lot of great scenic viewpoints for them,” Luke Martinez, an aquatic safety officer and lifeguard with Curry County Aquatic Safety, told Outside. “Unfortunately, people sometimes get stuck in bad spots, and that was the case Sunday night.”

The National Weather Service had issued a high surf warning for Oregon’s southern coast that day, forecasting breaking waves of 25 to 33 feet.

Martinez told Outside that he and fellow lifeguard Shannon Ingram responded to the emergency as large waves continued crashing onto the beach.

“It was pretty unruly,” Martinez said. “There was huge surf. The tide was out, and we couldn’t see much, but there were surges occurring up and down the beach.”

Ingram reached the shoreline ahead of Martinez just after sunset. Wearing a wetsuit and a safety helmet, she determined she could safely enter the churning water and made her way to the stranded woman. She checked her for injuries, secured her with a rescue tube, and brought her back to shore.

The woman was able to walk off the beach with assistance before being taken to a hospital for further evaluation.

“It was a good ending to something that could have been pretty bad,” Martinez said.

Secret Beach sits along the Samuel H. Boardman State Scenic Corridor, a 12-mile stretch of coastline dotted with rocky cliffs, secluded beaches, and offshore rock formations. Martinez noted that the area has surged in popularity due to social media, even though its rugged geography poses serious risks.

“We live along a really rugged coastline,” Martinez said. “It’s similar to people visiting the mountains and climbing 14ers. Not everybody realizes the dangers involved.”

Curry County Aquatic Safety has just two lifeguards—Martinez and Ingram—covering roughly 100 miles of coastline and several rivers. On November 8, they spent much of the day advising beachgoers about the unusually powerful surf, emphasizing that volatile conditions can catch people off guard before help can arrive.

“Beachgoers will be watching the smaller waves, thinking they understand how far the water is reaching up the beach,” Martinez explained. “Then that longer-period swell arrives and surges much farther up the beach than the waves they’ve been watching. During these events, our beaches can become dangerous for anybody, including experienced surfers or swimmers.”

Massive waves are a recurring hazard along the Pacific coast from October through March, when winter storms generate the largest swells, according to the state of Oregon. During major storms, offshore waves can exceed 30 feet.

Also on November 8, videos captured similar scenes elsewhere along the coast. Footage from Cannon Beach showed a young girl nearly being swept into the ocean, while another video from Winchester Bay showed two people scrambling to escape incoming waves as their dog was swept into the water. The dog was later rescued.

Another round of massive surf is expected to batter the Oregon coastline in mid-November. A National Weather Service warning projects breaking waves reaching 30 to 35 feet November 13 and 14. The agency is urging visitors to stay off beaches, rocks, jetties, and piers while the high swells continue.

#8223. Iran Executed a Mountaineer for Alleged Violence in Anti-Government Protests. Hundreds More Face the Same Fate.

Ali Sina Mostafavi (Photo: Courtesy of Iran Human Rights)

Ali Sina Mostafavi dreamed of climbing Everest. In 2019, he trekked to its Base Camp. Under a photo of him pointing to the summit, he wrote on Instagram in English: “Top of the world. I promise to come back to you.”

Mostafavi never fulfilled his promise. On October 14, he was executed by the Iranian authorities in Kerman Central Prison.

The 38-year-old is one of at least 39 people to have been executed in connection with Iran’s anti-government protests last winter, and one of six athletes among them.

Dr. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, an ice climber and co-founder of the Norway-based Human Rights for Sport, told Climbing, “From a human rights perspective, every single aspect of this case is an absolute violation. The state has not made any credible, independently verifiable evidence public.”

Born in 1987 in Bam County, southeastern Iran, Mostafavi was a professional mountaineer and a member of the Speeco mountaineering club in his home city of Kerman. He called mountains ‘the love of his life,’ according to Abdollahkhani.

Mostafavi climbed two of Iran’s highest peaks, Damavand (5,610m/18,410ft) and Alam-Kuh (4,850m/15,910ft). In 2016, he ascended Mount Kazbek (5,054m/16,581ft) in Georgia.

In 2019, Mostafavi traveled to Nepal and summited Island Peak (6,189m/20,305ft) and trekked to Everest Base Camp. In 2022, he attempted Ama Dablam (6,812m/22,349ft), reaching 6,600m/21,654ft.

Mostafavi was married and had a 13-year-old daughter, Respina. Alongside his climbing career, he was an accomplished musician who played the tar, a traditional Persian lute. Friends spoke of his sensitive, artistic spirit, and his deep love for mountains, music, and animals—notably, his beloved cat and dog.

On his Instagram account, @everest_coldhell, his bio reads: ‘Mount Explorer. Love the nature. Musician.’

In December 2025, Iran’s economic crisis sparked street protests that developed into nationwide demonstrations against the Islamic Republic’s repressive regime, which enforces compulsory hijab laws restricting women’s autonomy, conducts violent crackdowns on protests, issues arbitrary arrests, and employs the use of torture.

In an attempt to suppress dissent, authorities used lethal force, killing thousands and arresting tens of thousands of protesters. The human rights organization Amnesty International called this “the deadliest period of repression by the Iranian authorities” in its decades of monitoring the country.

Following the assassination of Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei by US-Israeli airstrikes on February 28, Iran’s government intensified repressive crackdowns on dissent under the pretext of “wartime conditions.”

By October, at least 106 people arrested during the January protests had received death sentences, according to documentation by human rights organization Hengaw.

Iran carries out the world’s second-highest number of executions after China. In 2025, its government executed at least 2,159 people, the highest figure recorded by Amnesty International since 1981.

On Instagram, Mostafavi expressed support for Iran’s former Crown Prince Reza Pahlavi, an exiled dissident who calls for a secular, democratic, and liberal Iran, describing him as “the only saviour of the homeland.” Two sources claim that Mostafavi’s family were set to move abroad before the 2022 ‘Woman, Life, Freedom’ protests began, but he ultimately chose to remain to fight for Iran’s future.

One obituary claims that he had been arrested twice in recent years for political activism and had spent time in Kerman Prison. This January, the mountaineer joined protests alongside millions of Iranians.

IranWire, an independent pro-democracy outlet, reported that Mostafavi was arrested three months later on April 25 alongside his wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé, while his mother’s home was also raided.

Mostafavi was reportedly beaten during his arrest and was forced to sign confession papers to release his family members. It is not known whether he had access to an independent lawyer, a right frequently denied to defendants in political and national security cases in Iran.

The Iranian judiciary’s account of the case was published by state-aligned media outlets including Mizan News Agency, Tasnim News Agency, the IRIB, and Tabnak. The allegations have not been independently verified.

The Judiciary of Iran claimed that Mostafavi had participated in the widespread anti-government protests in January, and that he was a member of the “Immortal Guards,” an armed wing of exiled dissident Reza Pahlavi’s group.

The judiciary also alleged that Mostafavi had shot and injured two civilians, fired at security forces, and possessed firearms, ammunition, and Molotov cocktails. It further accused him of communicating with foreign media and sharing footage of missile strike locations during the US-Iran war.

Mostafavi was convicted of the capital offense of moharebeh, or “enmity against God,” alongside several charges relating to alleged violence, weapons possession, and communication with hostile media. The evidence against him has not been made public.

The judiciary reported that the fiancé of Mostafavi’s sister received a prison sentence of 12 years and seven months for alleged cooperation, while he, his wife, and his sister were also sentenced to seven months in prison for posting content deemed as propaganda against the regime.

An appeal against Mostafavi’s death sentence was rejected. IranWire reported that he was transferred to solitary confinement the night before his execution and that family members were summoned. The judiciary announced that he was hanged at dawn in Kerman Central Prison on October 14. According to IranWire, Mostafavi asked the prison guards to pass along a message to the judge: “I did not wage war against God, nor did I commit moharebeh that you should charge me with it; my fight was with you.”

That evening, state-aligned outlet Tabnak published footage purporting to show Mostafavi’s arrest, weapons allegedly found in his possession, and a confession to a planned attack on Kerman Airport. IranWire reported that the confession appeared to have been made under duress and spliced together with unverified footage. Amnesty International has also identified signs of forced confessions in 18 videos of Iranian prisoners arrested between February and May 2026, during the same period as Mostafavi’s arrest.

Shortly after his death, a video of Mostafavi’s young daughter crying on her father’s grave, accompanied by their cat, circulated on social media.

Human rights groups have voiced concerns about Mostafavi’s case in the context of widespread forced confessions and sham trials lacking due process in Iran.

“The complete absence of forensic evidence or transparent court records confirms that his conviction rested entirely on forced confessions extracted under coercion rather than any objective proof,” Abdollahkhani said.

She explained that the arrest of Mostafavi’s wife, his sister, and his sister’s fiancé fits an established pattern of authorities using family members as leverage.

“The Islamic Republic routinely arrests close relatives and uses threats of torture or sexual violence to force athletes into making false confessions in a desperate bid to save their loved ones,” she said.

According to Human Rights for Sport, at least eight other mountaineers’ lives are at risk.

Maryam Hadavand Siri, a 42-year-old mother of two, led the Mountaineering Board of Pakdasht County in Tehran Province. She was arrested during the January protests, transferred to Evin Prison, and sentenced to death in April, without access to an independent lawyer. Following an appeal, her case was referred to the Supreme Court for review.

Social media activist and mountaineer Fatemeh Jami was arrested at her home on June 30 by Cyber Police officers. She was transferred to Gorgan Prison, where she remains detained without access to a lawyer or medical assistance.

Tara (Shirin) Masoudi, a member of the Razhan Mountaineering Group in Mahabad, was arrested on August 19. She was transferred to a detention centre and later released on bail. She is awaiting a final verdict.

Mohammad Hakimpour, Mostafa Ghaderi, Mohammad Saleh Hosseini, Hossein Abdollahi, and Khaled Rahimi—all members of climbing clubs in Saqqez—were arrested on October 8. According to Human Rights for Sport, they were subjected to physical abuse in detention and have been denied access to legal counsel, family visits, and telephone calls.

Abdollahkhani urges climbers to raise awareness of Mostafavi’s execution and the status of the eight other mountaineers, and to contact national federations, sports governing bodies, the International Climbing and Mountaineering Federation (UIAA), and the International Olympic Committee (IOC).

“How is it possible that a member of the climbing community is at risk of execution on alleged political charges, while the global climbing world stays silent?” she asked.

On October 30, Human Rights for Sport published an open letter to the UIAA executive board and athlete commission. In the letter, Abdollahkhani asks the UIAA to appeal directly to Iran’s national mountaineering federation, along with its Ministry of Sport and National Olympic Committee, to stop further executions and advocate for the release of imprisoned climbers.

#8222. Is an AI Data Center Coming to a National Park Near You? This New Map Shows Where.

(Photo: Courtesy of More Than Just Parks)

As America grapples with the rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence data centers, two brothers have set out to map infrastructure project proposals nationwide—including those near public lands and national parks.

Will Pattiz is the cofounder of More Than Just Parks, an independent public lands publication that tracks AI data centers. According to his research, at least 14 proposed data center projects are within ten miles of a national park boundary. His data also shows that 38 sites are planned within 25 miles of a national park, and 131 are within 50 miles.

“The basic idea is that a lot of these [projects] are being done under the cloak of darkness or secrecy, and we want folks to know where they’re coming in and who’s building them,” Pattiz, a resident of Portland, Oregon, told Outside. “The stance that we take is that we don’t want them on public lands.”

“Places like Utah, for example, have a huge amount of data center projects and some of the biggest ones that are being proposed,” Pattiz said. “Just depending on the size and scale, they take up a massive amount of resources and will have impacts on public lands one way or the other, whether it’s taking water or the land itself.”

Data centers are rapidly popping up across the United States, fueled by the computing needs of artificial intelligence and cloud-based software. These centers house massive servers, data storage systems, and networking equipment, and they require sizable amounts of electricity and water to run and maintain the hardware.

“The question that we want to see asked is: ‘What is the public benefit from this?’” Pattiz said. “So far, the ones that have been proposed on public lands, there’s no public benefit that’s been outlined.”

To use Pattiz’s map, a user inputs their zip code, and the site shows the closest data center or proposed facility. The site then suggests how the center will affect utility costs, as well as the groups that support the center.

“You can go through that discovery process yourself to decide whether you support [the center] or not, because these are things that are going to impact all of us, and you can decide where you land on that,” Pattiz said.

The map auto-populates as more information becomes available. As of this writing, the tool reflects 2,086 data centers, 741 of which are still in the proposal phase. Of those, 77 are located within ten miles of protected land like national parks, wildlife refuges, and wilderness or conservation areas. Roughly half are in the American West.

In Virginia, 97 data centers are proposed, and 12 are within 25 miles of Shenandoah National Park.

At least 25 data centers are proposed in Indiana, according to the map, and eight are located within 25 miles of Indiana Dunes National Park.

The map also includes several construction proposals that are extremely close to iconic National Park Service sites.

Arizona alone has 26 active proposals, with three within 25 miles of a national park. In January, the City of Page sold roughly 500 acres to developers planning to build a $10 billion data center next to Horseshoe Bend, an iconic viewpoint along the Colorado River. The 500-acre parcel was previously protected for outdoor recreation. According to the City of Page, the proposal is undergoing public review and has not yet been formally adopted, but a planning and zoning meeting is scheduled for November 17.

According to Pattiz’s map, the center is also located about five miles from the northeastern edge of Grand Canyon National Park near Lees Ferry.

Just outside of Price, Utah, Pattiz found that a company called Valar Atomics applied for more than 9,000 acres of Bureau of Land Management land for data center buildouts, including permits for hundreds of small nuclear reactors, a fuel plant, and nuclear waste storage.

According to a report published by NPR, the so-called Project Beehive would produce about 9.6 gigawatts of power for data centers. Currently, the entire state of Utah produces less than half of that on average, NPR reports.

The land is about two hours from both Arches and Canyonlands National Parks.

Located about 40 miles from Zion National Park, Antelope Data Center is slated for development as part of a 640-acre, 1.5-gigawatt project that will include an on-site natural gas power plant, according to The Salt Lake Tribune. The Iron County Commission approved a conditional use permit in June 2026.

Large-scale data center rollouts represent an inflection point in American history, Pattiz said. As construction crews have erected these centers, they have become political lightning rods in American towns and cities.

Pattiz believes that giving Americans transparent, readily available information about where big tech is breaking ground will help them track what developers are building in their backyards.

“At the end of the day, data is data,” he added. “Whether or not there’s a need for these things is a totally separate question from where they’re being built and what impact they’re going to have on you and the places that you love.”

Hiking boots have lost some ground to trail runners and low-cut shoes over the past decade, but don’t write them off just yet: If you have weak ankles or are prone to stumbles, an old-school hiking boot may be exactly what you need, especially if your trips often involve rough terrain or heavier loads. Besides providing protection from rolls and twists, a mid-cut boot can help lower your injury risk by supporting your foot and ankle and easing the fatigue and soreness that builds up over the course of a long backpacking trip.

We’ve gone through our favorite hiking boots of 2026 and picked our seven faves for hikers with problem ankles, four from our men’s list and three from our women’s roundup, both curated by Blair Braverman, the expert reviewer at our sibling site Backpacker. All earned our testers’ approval over hundreds of trail miles, so you can confidently buy the best hiking boot for your weak ankles.

Think of the Arc’teryx Konseal Trek as James Bond’s car: Its slick looks conceal “an arsenal of protection,” as our reviewer noted. Among its tricks: a bonded Gore-Tex membrane that provides waterproofing while keeping the boot slim; a mid-height, lightly-padded cuff outfitted with a Kevlar exterior for durability even on talus-strewn slopes; and a carbon fiber shank worked into the EVA midsole, so your ride is both comfortable and stable. Read the full review.

First, look at the cuff: You want an upper that’s stiff enough to support your joint if you stumble or step on a loose rock, but not so stiff that you can’t maintain a natural stride on the tail. Which of those you prioritize depends on your objectives: Long days on relatively smooth trail call for softer support, while stiffer boots may help prevent injury on steep, loose ascents. Pay attention to the padding on the cuff, which should cradle your ankle rather than squeeze it.

Midsole construction can also make a big difference in how a boot feels on the trail: An EVA midsole will feel bouncier and softer, more akin to a running shoe, while a PU midsole will provide a somewhat stiffer, more supportive ride, though often at a weight penalty. A shank, often made of a material like carbon fiber, will provide additional stiffness and structural support to the sole, though it should still allow your foot to flex naturally.

Finally, pay attention to the outsole; while it may not play a role in supporting your ankle directly, a grippy tread can help prevent stumbles and slips, which can lead to injuries. Softer rubber will grip better on hard surfaces, though it will shorten the boot’s lifespan as it wears away faster. A harder, less pliable rubber may feel more slippery on surfaces like slickrock, but can grip well on soft trail, allowing its tread to “bite” into the path.

Mostly we just let our testers do what they do best: walk. We called in dozens of different hiking boots and shoes and handed them out to 15 testers with instructions to put on some serious miles. They took short hikes and 30-mile backpacking trips, on-trail and off. They scrambled up peaks and down canyons, logging more than 700 miles in total. As they trekked along, we asked them to consider everything from fit to grip, cushioning to stability.

Because pack weight can influence all these variables, we had them hike with both light loads and heavy packs. And to understand how boots and shoes performed in different weather conditions and environments, we spread testers and samples across the continent, from coastal British Columbia to New England’s windy summits.

After at least two testers have tried every shoe, we have them fill out a detailed questionnaire. Then we send them back out with more shoes. The process is ongoing and endless. With every review we compare the results to all the other hikers we’ve tested over the years. Because ultimately we’re not just looking for the best new hiking boots for weak ankles, we want the best hiking boots for weak ankles, period.

Category manager Wisconsin-based Blair Braverman is a long-distance dogsledder who loves hiking whenever she’s not mushing. Her longest backpacking trip was the 400-mile Oregon Coast Trail, and her favorite is Colorado’s Four-Pass Loop.

#8219. This New Book Strives to Help Climbers Rewire Their Mental Game

(Photo: Left: Sam Douglas Jones / Right: Vertebrate Publishing)

We all do it: Eyeing other climbers and comparing ourselves to them. Wishing we were better at dynos, heel hooks, or some other elusive climbing move. Loading ourselves with shoulds when it comes to training or grades.

Even non-performance-oriented climbers like me tend to be guilty of at least some negative thoughts when we’re up on the wall. It’s hard not to think that way when so many highly specific levels dominate the sport. This makes the idea of progression almost impossible to resist, even if you claim to do it only for fun.

There is something about the progress ladder of the Yosemite Decimal System. Its slash grades, letter addendums, and pluses and minuses tempt you to try and tick routes with higher grades. The same goes for the V-scale, as well as many other grading scales. We often ask “What if?” questions about breaking into a harder grade. And we often define ourselves by the grades we climb. “I’m a V10 boulderer,” someone might say, or “I’m a 5.10 climber.”

Meanwhile, when I’m skiing or mountain biking, there are essentially only four, color-coded levels, green through double black. Compared to climbing, I find it rare for someone to ask what color run I skied or trail I rode—and did I make it down without falling? But after someone climbs a route, one of the first questions might be what the grade was. And did you send it?

As the sport continues to grow, two British climbers have noticed that the expansion of training content has far outpaced the rise of mindset content when it comes to climbing. And they agree that climbing tends to be uniquely progress-oriented compared to other sports.

“It’s great to see the growth in top-end performance climbing, but for a lot of people, that might come with a lot of pressure to perform the same way,” says Louis Parkinson, the founder of the coaching company Catalyst Climbing, a climber of over 20 years, and co-author of the new book Get a Grip.

To write a self-help book for climbers focused exclusively on mindset, Parkinson teamed up with Joel Robertson, an MA MBACP psychotherapist and climber. Nicknamed “The Climbing Therapist,” Robertson insists that their book isn’t only for elite or performance-oriented athletes. That’s because he believes climbers at any level can experience the pressure and negative thought patterns that the sport can induce. He also sees negative mentality extending beyond the sport.

“If you’re being brutal to yourself at the crag or in the gym in ways that are holding you back in climbing, then you’re almost certainly doing that to yourself at family Christmas or at work or whatever,” Robertson says. “Mental health and climbing mindset are not separate, right? Let’s treat them the same. That’s the whole ethos of the book.”

Both Parkinson and Robertson admit that they are far from perfect when it comes to their own mentality. They emphasize that a healthy climbing mindset requires continuous work, rather than a one-time solution.

A former competitive climber, Parkinson recalls a period where he stopped enjoying climbing. This triggered an identity crisis of sorts, since he had oriented his entire life and career around the sport. “If I stop climbing, then I don’t know who I am,” Parkinson recalls thinking.

Eventually, Parkinson realized that his lack of enjoyment stemmed from the immense pressure he was putting on himself to continuously improve. When he couldn’t perform up to his own standards, he became “really, really upset.” Once he eased off the unrealistic expectations he was holding himself too, the joy came back. Parkinson’s past struggle echoes a similar experience of Chris Sharma. Earlier this year, he talked with Climbing about letting go of grades in order to send Biographie, the world’s first 5.15.

Robertson, primarily a casual indoor boulderer, shares a more recent experience from a couple weeks ago. After three sessions, he flashed his gym project. In the midst of some celebratory fist pumps, however, he watched in mild horror as someone else came and flashed his project as their warm-up. “It’s so classic,” Robertson says of this common climbing predicament. “I genuinely felt way less good about the achievement and not just the achievement, but myself.”

To avoid comparing yourself to others in a negative way, one suggestion Get a Grip offers is to think about your climbing friends. Do you love and value them because of their climbing ability, or because of who they are? Most people care about each of their friends as a person, not in terms of their climbing abilities. When you start to compare yourself to others, or base your self-worth on whether you, for example, sent your project, try to view yourself as you would your friend instead.

Robertson and Parkinson also suggest focusing on comparisons that are accurate and valuable, rather than grounded in envy or self-pity. Instead of thinking, “Damn, I wish I could climb like that,” ask, “What could I learn from watching someone else that I could apply in my own climbing?”

One of the critical ways to work on climbing mindset is to cultivate more awareness around our own thoughts, according to Robertson and Parkinson. Rather than becoming bogged down in the thought, attempt to view the thought impartially. Try reframing the thought, or compartmentalizing it. “Rather than ‘I am anxious,’ it’s ‘a part of me is anxious,’” Robertson explains. This can help you get some distance between yourself and a fleeting notion or emotion.

Throughout the book, reflections from pro climbers bring more color and insight to what a strong mindset looks like. In one of my favorite sections, British boulderer and competitive climber Shauna Coxsey talks about asking questions instead of making statements. An “exploratory mindset,” as Robertson and Parkinson term it, will fuel you with curiosity rather than pressure. “People often think I’m a very motivated person, but I would disagree,” Coxsey writes after sharing her focus on curiosity. “I think I’m a very committed person. For me, motivation and commitment have to go hand in hand because it’s impossible to be motivated all the time.”

Another standout pro mindset cameo comes from another British boulderer and comp climber: Hamish McArthur. Essentially, he reveals that he more or less blacks out when he climbs hard. This allows him to enter the coveted flow state that so many of us seek. “The times when I’ve performed at my best, I don’t really have any memory of what it was like,” he writes.

I took a lot away from the book in terms of how to edit and take control of my internal monologue. But I was left with one nagging question: How can we all climb more like McArthur, and find that elusive flow state?

“Just think less. It’s easy!” Parkinson joked with me. “No, it’s really hard. It’s insanely difficult.” Parkinson clarifies that achieving a mindset like McArthur’s requires a long-term commitment to honing your meditation skills so you can quiet your mind and just climb. But the lessons in Get a Grip can help get you started.

Vertebrate Publishing released Get a Grip on October 8. You can find a copy from Catalyst Climbing, Amazon, and wherever books are sold. Climbers can also listen to Get a Grip as an audiobook narrated by Parkinson.

#8218. New Research Finds That Slower Running May Be Good for Your Brain. A Neuroscientist Weighs In.

It’s easy, as a runner, to slip into an all-or-nothing mindset. There may have been times when you’ve caught yourself thinking, “What’s the point of going on a run if I can’t commit to at least 3 miles?” or “If I’m going to run this slow, I might as well walk—or skip it altogether.”

The reality is that something is almost always better than nothing, and running, even very slowly for a short time, can boost your brain and mood.

In Aug. 2026, researchers in Japan set out to discover if very light intensity running would affect the brain, especially the parts that are involved with executive functioning. They weren’t curious about the effect of very light intensity running over time; rather, they wanted to know if a single bout of light intensity running—just one workout—could yield noteworthy brain benefits.

For their study, researchers recruited 24 young and healthy adults, including 13 males and 11 females, with the average ages of 23.38 and 20.55, respectively.

The main experiment included a control (CON) day and a very slow running (SRUN) day, with every participant engaging in both days. For the CON session, participants sat on a chair on an unmoving treadmill for ten minutes.

Before the SRUN session, maximal oxygen uptake (VO2peak) was measured for each participant to determine a very slow run speed that would elicit 35 percent VO2peak. Then, participants ran on the treadmill for ten minutes at their predetermined very slow speeds.

Males averaged 3.39 mph, and females averaged 2.40 mph. While these are easily walking speeds, the researchers observed that participants were able to maintain running form.

Before and immediately after each session, participants completed the following: The Color-Word Stroop task (CWST) to measure inhibitory control and the Two-Dimensional Mood Scale (TDMS) to measure pleasurable moods.

For the CWST task, participants were shown two rows of letters on a monitor and had to determine (by pressing “yes” or “no”) if the color of the letters in the top row matched the color name written in the bottom row.

There were three conditions: Neutral, Congruent, or Incongruent. For the neutral condition, Xs were written on the top row in a particular color, and the name of that color was written in black on the bottom row.

For the congruent condition, the word “red” was written in red in the top row and, in the bottom row, the word red was written in black. The incongruent condition was included to introduce cognitive interference. In that condition, the word in the top row did not match the colors of the letters, but the bottom row still had the name of the upper row letters’ colors written in black.

For each trial, in which either the neutral, congruent, or incongruent condition was displayed, participants would, as quickly as possible, press either “yes” or “no” to report whether or not the color of the letters in the top row matched the color row in the bottom row.

Participants were given three practice sessions to make sure they understood how to perform the task.

So, what does CWST measure? It directly measures something called Stroop interference, which is the difference in reaction time between the incongruent and neutral conditions.

Essentially, Stroop interference is a way to assess executive function, with lower values indicating higher executive functioning. In this study, Stroop interference was lower after participants ran versus the seated control setting.

The TDMS assessed participants’ arousal and pleasure states. Participants were asked to rate the following eight descriptors on a scale from 0 (“I’m not experiencing this at all”) to 5 (“I’m currently feeling this way quite extremely”): energetic, lively, lethargic, listless, relaxed, calm, irritated, and nervous.

The results indicated that immediately following the short and very slow run, participants reported feeling more energized and content than after the control setting.

But what effect does ten minutes of slow running have on brain activity? To examine this, researchers used a non-invasive brain imaging technique called functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). fNIRS measures changes in hemoglobin throughout the brain’s cortex, which corresponds with cortical activity.

For this study, participants wore an fNIRS cap with electrodes while they performed the CWST task, five minutes after running. As hypothesized, very slow running can generate increased activity in multiple subregions of the prefrontal cortex—namely, the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, the left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, and the right and left frontopolar areas.

Activation of these brain regions keeps us sharp and functioning well day to day; the prefrontal cortex is involved with executive functions such as managing competing goals, decision-making, reasoning, and self-control.

There was one more variable that the researchers were curious about: head acceleration. Even among smooth runners that glide across the ground, the head moves vertically with each step.

A previous study suggested that this mechanical force may underlie some of the psychological benefits of running by impacting neurotransmitter activity. So, the researchers of the current study sought to explore that more. They found that even the small head acceleration that occurs during very slow running was positively correlated with the amount of post-run pleasure the participants reported.

As is the case with every study, there were a few limitations. First, electrodes (such as on the fNIRS device) can pick up signals other than neural activation, such as skin blood flow. The researchers minimized this potential by carefully designing their protocol and checking if the data made sense. Second, head acceleration is obviously different between seated controls and running conditions, so a third, walking group would enhance future experiments.

Here’s the main takeaway: a single, ten-minute run at a very slow, almost walking pace may be enough to boost short-term cognitive performance and elevate your mood.

Consider what this means if you’re returning to running after an injury or illness. Or, perhaps you’re in a new season of life, and you can’t, realistically, carve out more than a few minutes to move your body. This study encourages all of us to keep running, no matter how fast or far we go.

#8217. Georgia’s Entire 78-Mile Appalachian Trail Section Will Require Bear Canisters in 2027

A hiker carries a bear canister on the Appalachian Trail. (Photo: Courtesy Appalachian Trail Conservancy)

Hikers on Georgia’s stretch of the Appalachian Trail will need to store their food in a hard-sided canister next year according to a new order from the U.S. Forest Service, a change that follows years of rising bear encounters on the southern miles of the AT.

In a press release, the USFS said that the rule would take effect January 1, and would apply to anyone camping in a 1-mile-wide corridor along the entire 78-mile section of the AT, including hikers staying in shelters. The requirement is year-round and also applies to the AT Approach Trail.

Alternative food-storage methods like bear hangs and Ursacks will not be allowed. Hikers who violate the order could face a fine of up to $5,000 or 6 months in jail.

“With the Appalachian Trail going through the heart of North Georgia’s black bear habitat, we want the hikers who flock here to understand how incredibly valuable these public lands are—for people and for wildlife,” Chattahoochee-Oconee National Forest Supervisor Judy Toppins said. “Finding a balance that protects hikers, wildlife, and forest health is our goal.”

As visitation to the Appalachian Trail has risen in recent years, human-bear conflicts have too, with a 2025 survey by the Appalachian Trail Conservancy finding that bear reports had risen by 75 percent that year alone. A disproportionate amount of those run-ins happen in Georgia: Morgan Sommerville, the ATC’s director of visitor use management, said that while just 3.5 percent of the AT lies in Georgia, the state accounted for more than 12 percent of its bear encounters.

The new requirements represent the largest expansion of food storage rules on the trail yet. Previously, only a few short segments required a canister, such as the 5-mile segment between Jarrard and Neel Gaps in Georgia’s Blood Mountain Wilderness. Hikers who didn’t want to tote a hard-sided container could simply avoid camping in many of those.

“The ATC has recommended that overnight campers on the Trail carry a bear-resistant food storage container since 2017 because of how adept bears have become at defeating traditional food hangs and other storage methods,” Somerville said. “This new order along the AT in Georgia will require all overnight hikers and backpackers to use reliable food storage gear—a hard-sided bear canister—on their AT adventures, which will protect themselves and the bears that call the AT home.”

Getting AT thru- and section-hikers to embrace the new guidelines could be a challenge. While the ATC has recommended for almost 10 years that hikers carry bear canisters, data suggests that few do. A 2025 survey by The Trek found that 13.6 percent used a canister, compared to 43 percent who used a bear hang and 32.3 percent who chose the riskiest option and slept with their food.

#8216. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the villages of Shimsal and Khyber jointly installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#8215. Are Ultralight, Ultrastrong Dyneema Rain Mitts Worth Hikers’ Money? We Tested Them.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Gimmick or Gamechanger, the Backpacker editors test hiking gadgets to see what’s worth your money—and what’s a waste of it.

I’ve backpacked in my fair share of nasty conditions. On Vancouver Island’s West Coast Trail, I trudged through a downpour so heavy that I had to wring out my pants by the time I got to camp. In Gates of the Arctic National Park, I wore neoprene socks over my Darn Toughs to trap some warmth in my feet as I slogged through boggy tundra. Wet conditions, even when temperatures are mild, can be the most difficult in which to stay warm and comfortable. Looking back, I wish I had packed some rain mitts on those trips.

Most backpackers aren’t carrying waterproof overmitts. They serve a niche purpose of keeping your hands dry in wet but warm(ish) weather. In truly cold conditions, you need heavy-duty gloves. For summer showers, you can usually go without gloves or mitts entirely. But for hikes in steady rain with temperatures in the 40s and 50s? Rain mitts can work wonders to maintain comfort while taking up minimal space and weight in your pack.

As a hiker based in the PNW, I was excited when I came across a pair of ultralight rain mitts from cottage brand High Tail Designs, which is known for colorful printed fabrics and artist collaborations. Made for use alone or with a liner glove for warmth, they employ a blend of Dyneema Composite Fabric (DCF) and Dyneema Hybrid Fabric and weigh roughly an ounce per pair. They also run a whopping $105. What sets them apart from most other rain mitts on the market is the material and the fun aesthetics. Few other brands use Dyneema for hiking apparel; it shows up mostly in products like backpacks and shelters where strength is paramount. It’s also unusual to see Dyneema in colors other than black at white, as the material is difficult to dye.

Because it doesn’t absorb moisture, Dyneema dries faster than other waterproof materials like treated nylon. This also means it doesn’t stretch or bag out when exposed to lots of water. The flipside is that it doesn’t breathe—a Dyneema rain jacket would dry faster than a Gore-Tex one, but you’d likely be soaked from the inside after a few minutes of hiking. I wondered how those competing properties would work in a pair of rain mitts.

Off the bat, I was a fan of how the mitts protected my hands on rainy hikes. The fully taped seams kept moisture at bay, and I appreciated the large pull loops and cinchable shock cord wrists. They’re oversized for use with or without liners, so dexterity is limited, but that’s expected with any kind of mitts.

Other rain mitts, like those made with Gore-Tex, boast some level of breathability. These, in comparison, are basically a vapor barrier for your hands. They’re not meant to be breathable, and I found myself surprisingly unbothered by this. Hiking in a downpour with temperatures in the mid-50s, they kept my hands comfortable and dry, and I didn’t work up enough of a sweat over an hour to feel clammy inside. And since I care more about keeping my hands warm than dry, I don’t mind that these aren’t designed to breathe.

But does the fact that they’re made of Dyneema make them better than other rain mitts? What makes Dyneema appealing for outdoor gear is its remarkable strength-to-weight ratio, which can make all the difference in heavy-duty gear like backpacks and shelters. But it is invariably more expensive than other materials. In a small product like mittens, the weight savings become almost negligible, and the added tensile strength seems frivolous for the cost.

I haven’t done enough long-term testing of these mitts to speak to their durability over time, but I’m skeptical that they truly outlast similar products made from treated nylon. Generally, DCF is more tear-resistant than nylon, but it can also be more susceptible to abrasions and pinholes. While my pair hasn’t shown any signs of deterioration yet, the properties of DCF seem like overkill for a mitt where treated nylon will do.

Which brings me to the price. High Tail Designs’ rain mitts are $105 per pair. At 30 grams per pair (size small/medium), they are among the lightest rain mitts out there—but not by much. The Helium UL Rain Mitt from Outdoor Research costs half as much at $55, though it weighs twice as much at 68 grams per pair. Black Diamond’s UL Overmitts weigh a few grams less (23 grams for a size small) and are still more affordable at $70. I haven’t personally tested either of those mitts, but they are comparable in weight and function at a much lower price point.

As someone who hikes in everything from a drizzle to a deluge, I’m a rain mitt convert. I’ll be wearing these all winter long for lowland romps where fully weatherproof, insulated gloves are overkill but liners alone would soak through. They’ll also have a place in my pack on wet overnights or long-distance summer hikes where I need some just-in-case protection and don’t want to pack heavy gloves.

In my opinion, rain mitts as a category are a gamechanger. But it’s extremely hard to justify $105 for a pair made from the highest-end ultralight materials when there are cheaper options on the market that function similarly. For that reason, Dyneema rain mitts feel more like a gimmick. However, if you’re someone who puts a high value on style, that added cost may be worth it. High Tail Designs sells rain mitts in 11 different patterns; their company ethos is all about self-expression on the trail, and their colorful designs support real artists.

#8213. Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park Named 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year

Voyageurs National Park Dark Sky. (Photo: Daniel Dendler)

For people living beneath the artificial glow of city lights, a sky filled with thousands of stars can seem like something out of science fiction. According to a recent National Park Service report, 80 percent of Americans cannot see the Milky Way from their homes.

But at Minnesota’s Voyageurs National Park, a roughly five-hour drive from Minneapolis, some of the darkest skies in the country reveal the heavens in dazzling detail. And thanks to the park’s growing lineup of in-person and virtual programs, you don’t have to travel to the North Woods to experience the magic.

This week, Voyageurs received one of the highest honors in conservation: DarkSky International’s 2026 Dark Sky Place of the Year award. The annual award honors individuals and organizations dedicated to protecting nighttime environments. Voyageurs is only the second American national park to receive the award; the first was Grand Canyon National Park in 2019.

“What makes this award so meaningful is that it isn’t about Voyageurs being a beautiful place to see the stars. We were certified as an International Dark Sky Park in 2020 for that,” Christina Hausman Rhode, executive director of Voyageurs Conservancy, its nonprofit partner of the park, told Outside.

Since earning its International Dark Sky Park certification in 2020, Voyageurs has introduced some 8,300 students to the wonders overhead through its Virtual Dark Sky Classroom, welcomed nearly 6,000 people to Park After Dark and other nighttime programs, and drawn more than 1,300 visitors to six annual Star Parties. Add to that roughly 40,000 students nationwide who participate in Boreal Stargazing Week each year, and it’s clear the park’s reach extends well beyond its 218,000-acre boundary.

This honor recognizes what has happened since, Rhode added: “A shared commitment by the National Park Service, Voyageurs Conservancy, and our gateway communities to protect these skies and share them with as many people as possible.“

Voyageurs also stands out because it’s about 40 percent water—covered by interconnected glacial lakes—a fact that adds to its stargazing prowess. Sweeping views are unobstructed by foothills, and its 30 calm lake surfaces act as mirrors reflecting the constellations and making the dark-sky experience all the more impressive. This is no Great Smoky Mountains National Park with its 12 million annual visitors either. With roughly 200,000 visitors each year, Voyageurs offers plenty of wide open space to take in the starscape.

“Voyageurs doesn’t just protect some of the darkest skies remaining in North America,” Ruskin Hartley, CEO and executive director of DarkSky International, told Outside via email. “It’s the people behind that protection.”

Hartley said that from the land managers and rangers to community partners, there’s a shared commitment at the park to preserve the night through responsible lighting, as well as to share the park’s wonders with the public.

The recognition comes at the end of a particularly challenging year for wilderness conservation in northern Minnesota. In April, Congress passed and President Donald Trump signed a resolution that reversed a 20-year mining ban covering roughly 350 square miles of Superior National Forest near the neighboring Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness. The move reopened the door to proposed copper and nickel mining operations.

The threat to Voyageurs? Well, what happens in the Boundary Waters doesn’t necessarily stay in the Boundary Waters. The two protected landscapes are linked by the Rainy River watershed, a sprawling network of lakes, rivers, and wetlands. (Incidentally, the Boundary Waters and Voyageurs, along with Ontario’s Quetico Provincial Park, form one of the world’s largest dark-sky regions.)

“Copper mining from a proposed Twin Metals mine would absolutely impact Voyageurs,” says Libby London, communications director for the nonprofit Save the Boundary Waters.

Once pollution reaches the water, it can spread quickly for several hundred miles, explains Pete Marshall, communications director for Friends of the Boundary Waters Wilderness, another nonprofit organization that’s been advocating for the Boundary Waters area for 50 years. Governor Tim Walz signed an executive order in August to block the state from permitting copper mines in the watershed, but that order expires three months after Walz leaves office.

In July, lightning-sparked wildfires fueled by hot and windy conditions forced the rare closure of Boundary’s entire million-acre wilderness, upending summer travel plans and prompting evacuations. Out of an abundance of caution, Voyageurs officials banned campfires and charcoal grills for six weeks.

Against that backdrop, Voyageurs’ Dark Sky Place of the Year award is a welcome conservation victory.

Protecting the night sky at Voyageurs has required more than simply keeping the lights off, of course. The park has had to rethink how it uses light in the first place. Under a new lighting management plan, outdoor fixtures were replaced with dark-sky-friendly alternatives that direct light downward rather than into the sky. National Park Service staff also began regularly visiting five locations throughout the park to measure the darkness using a sky quality meter, a device that measures the brightness of the night sky. On a scale where 22.0 represents the darkest natural night sky, Voyageurs averages an impressive 21.45—meaning that when the sun goes down, the stars really do come out.

And while the award puts Voyageurs in the spotlight, the park’s greatest achievement may be what happens when the lights stay out. For Rhode and the Voyageurs Conservancy, the hope is that the recognition inspires others to look up—and take action.

#8212. Hike of the Week: Explore a Wilderness With Wolves and Endless Flat-Topped Peaks

The Flat Tops Wilderness Area in northwestern Colorado is one of my favorite places to drop off-grid. Among its basalt peaks and sweeping valleys are some of the state’s best trails, in my opinion. Its “hidden-gem” days are long gone—lots of people, especially those from Colorado’s Western Slope, recreate here. Yet, you can still find areas where you’re the only human for miles.

That solitude can be intoxicating. The 10.9-mile out-and-back to Marvine Lakes via the Marvine Trail could easily be a dayhike. But when I visited with a group of friends this summer, we wanted to spend time marinating in the scenery, lounging on the lakes’ shoreline with some beers, and enjoying a nice bagged meal with friends. I saw more wildlife on that trip than I have on any other in a long time: We crossed paths with elk, mule deer, beavers, and a silver-colored canid that looked much bigger than any coyote I’ve ever seen. Was it a wolf? I can’t say with certainty, but the Flat Tops is one of the areas where Colorado’s wolf reintroduction program has been most successful.

The trail starts at East Marvine Campground, about 35 miles east of Meeker. When we arrived, several outfitters were saddling horses and preparing to ride out with their groups. The trail is multi-use, though mountain bikes and motorized vehicles are not permitted in wilderness areas. Dogs are allowed, and leashes are not required. But hikers should stay both stay horse- and bear-aware.

The hike itself isn’t too strenuous, climbing just 1,045 feet over the 5.4 miles to the lakes. It passes small beaver ponds, pops out into meadows where you might catch a glimpse of browsing elk or deer, and winds through thick old-growth pine and spruce forest. The hike follows pristine Marvine Creek the entire way. Water is never an issue as long as you’ve got a means of purifying it.

When you arrive at lower Marvine Lake, you’ll find turquoise water reflecting the stratigraphy of the towering cliffs that hem the valley. The trail splits and goes around both sides of the lake, passing dispersed camping spots. We picked one on the very far end of lower Marvine Lake, between it and upper Marvine Lake. Our group hung out well past dark, expecting the kind of stars that only the remote corners of the Rockies can deliver. We were not disappointed.

We hiked out the next day, retracing our footsteps to the trailhead. If you wanted a longer hike, the Marvine Trail extends deeper east into the Flat Tops Wilderness Area and connects to an entire trail network. Following it all the way out to Twin Lakes and returning via the East Marvine Lakes Trail would make a 22.5-mile loop and end at the same trailhead you started at, with more alpine ponds and lakes along the way.

#8210. The Best College Ski Towns in the U.S.

Big Sky and Lone Peak (Photo: Aerial_Views / Getty)

In today’s fast-paced, instant-gratification-obsessed world, it’s harder than ever for colleges to grab a young person’s attention. Don’t get us wrong, they’re trying, turning to drastic measures like on-campus waterparks, steakhouses, and even valet parking to attract a rising crop of future graduates.

But what if colleges had a taller, more natural card to play? For some mountain lovers, the idea of a college experience that combines curriculum with outdoor adventure is a prime way to push the needle. The prospect has made university towns like Burlington, Vermont, and Salt Lake City, Utah, into winter sports juggernauts, but it has also brought smaller towns into the discussion, putting them on the map and putting their universities on the “must apply” list.

So, what’s the best U.S. college town for skiing and snowboarding? We considered a handful of factors (proximity is just the start, after all) to find that answer, region by region. That means more than just the skiing itself, but also the culture, cuisine, and community that come along with it, making these mountain paradises appeal to college students and graduates alike. When it comes to studying hard and shredding harder, here are the best places to earn those turns…err, degrees.

The sheer amount of ski areas and college towns in the Northeast is enough to overwhelm, but let’s keep it simple: there’s only one Burlington, Vermont. Perched on the edge of Lake Champlain, this four-season wonder is also home base for the University of Vermont, St. Michael’s College, and Champlain College—and a whole lot of skiers and boarders between the three. In addition to national championship-winning alpine and Nordic ski programs, UVM has also grown one of the strongest ski and snowboard clubs in the country. Mountains around Burlington are all about showing their student population love, serving up heavily discounted college season passes at resorts like Jay Peak, Sugarbush, Mad River Glen (skiers only), and Smugglers’ Notch. The days of the legendary Triple Major may be over (if you know, you know), but there are still plenty of cheap turns for the higher education crowd.

After a long day on the slopes, take a walk down Church Street for the ultimate cultural contrast. This pedestrian-only brick walkway echoes Europe with a uniquely New England appeal. Stop at the Church Street Tavern for a local brew and then trek to Bove’s for its famous Italian cuisine. Burlington is a music hotbed, so don’t forget to pay your respects at Higher Ground on your way out of town.

Lake Champlain—need we say more? This large body of freshwater is Burlington’s lifeblood, providing public beaches, public sailing centers, unmatched paddling access, and even some fun urban cliff jumping (we suggest Red Rocks for an evening plunge). The Green Mountains earn their name here in the summer, crisscrossed with hiking and biking trails that rival most any in the country. Camel’s Hump might be the crown jewel, but there are plenty of day hikes within a short drive of town.

You might not think of the Southeast as ski country, but don’t tell Boone, North Carolina. This college town is home to Appalachian State University and set at the foot of the Blue Ridge Mountains—one of the premier snow-sliding regions in the South. Boone is an easy drive from three formidable Southeast ski resorts, and Appalachian Ski Mountain is less than 15 minutes from campus. In addition to having one of the best ski schools on the East Coast, the local area has night skiing and four terrain parks. On select nights throughout the season, students can score $16 night skiing tickets as well. For the more advanced, Beech Mountain is just 45 minutes away, opening up a realm of on-hill possibilities.

If you’ve made it out to Beech Mountain, don’t sleep on the 5506’ Skybar—the highest elevation bar on the Eastern Seaboard. For those looking for a lower elevation reward, the town of Boone is known for its home-crafted beer scene and beautiful downtown. Grab a pint at Appalachian Mountain Brewing or size up a mocktail at Fizzed before checking out Blowing Rock Village south of Boone’s downtown.

Boone was a summer escape long before it became a winter destination, once considered the finest vacation retreat between Newport, Rhode Island, and Palm Beach, Florida. Nowadays residents live the best of both worlds, scoring winter turns before hitting the summertime bike trails at Rocky Knob Mountain Bike Park. Fly-fishing aficionados have their pick of honey holes along the Blue Ridge Parkway and local guides are friendly enough to share the goods, or at least some of them.

Set smack dab in the middle of one of the country’s most overlooked snowbelts, Marquette, Michigan, has the distinct pleasure of being both off the tourist map and in the crosshairs of winter’s biggest storms. The largest city on Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, Marquette is also a university town, welcoming students to Northern Michigan University every fall. But when snow starts to fall, this student population converts to bona fide powder hounds. Marquette Mountain sits within city borders and receives over 210 inches a year—making it one of the snowiest places east of the Mississippi. NMU students get a whole season of it for just $361.

If just enjoying the slopes isn’t enough, undergrads can also pursue an associate degree in ski area management. This unique program runs in conjunction with Gogebic Community College, a school that places students into five-month internships at actual ski resorts and has its own ski hill, Mount Zion, right on campus.

Marquette is where college bar and ski bar collide into one heck of an après evening. Grab a $2 mystery beer at the Wooden Nickel Bar or dive into a face-sized cocktail while taking over the jukebox at Remie’s. The Midwest does après different—and we’re all for it.

Set on the shores of Lake Superior, Marquette turns students into long-term residents. Presque Isle Park and the Black Rocks offer up stunning, cliffside trails and wild forest, while biking in the NTN trail systems features a little something for every ability level. Cutting right through town, the Iron Ore Heritage Trail stretches 47 miles across the region, connecting caves, ruins, and historical stops related to the area’s mining roots.

This pick’s a little spicy, but hear us out. Boulder and Crested Butte have the skiing and mountain biking thing on lock. Salt Lake City has mountain proximity in spades. But Durango? This college town has a bit of everything—minus the people and mountain-bound bustle. Home to Fort Lewis College, Durango sits in the cradle of Colorado’s San Juan Mountains, an overlooked corner of the state with some serious vertical relief. Students attending Fort Lewis have their pick of Purgatory, Wolf Creek, and Hesperus within an hour or so of campus, but for those seeking bucket-list turns, Silverton and Telluride are a respectable day trip. If class is letting out late, there’s even Chapman Hill, a small (but steep) community ski area at the edge of campus, which offers an entire season of skiing and riding for $130.

Durango is a locals’ town right down to its libations. While several breweries have popped up over the years (Animas, Steamworks, and Ska, to name a few), it’s hard to pass up a post-mountain beer at Anarchy Brewing Co. Aside from some seriously strong IPAs (we liked the Sex Panther), this spot is four-legged friendly and has good food served on its outdoor patio.

If you just can’t wait to wet your whistle, the town’s biggest cheat code is the Durango Hot Springs Resort and Spa. It may sound bougie, but this series of naturally heated pools is a hangout that will soothe the soul without breaking the bank. The facility offers beer and wine for purchase and is only 20 minutes from Purgatory Ski Resort.

It’s deals and access like this that keep Durangatangs in town after they graduate, but while winter is a highlight, this locale is all about summer recreation. The Animas River runs right through the heart of Durango, often dotted with rafters and flotillas of varying sizes. Further downstream, the town has its very own whitewater park, and Durango Whitewater is a direct feeder program to the U.S. Olympic whitewater teams.

Beyond the river, Durango features hundreds of miles of mountain biking trails ranging from flowy beginner to some of the gnarliest technical terrain in the West. In fact, in 2030 the town is slated to host the UCI Mountain Bike World Championships.

Set between Montana’s two biggest mountain resorts and home to a robust network of in-town Nordic skiing, Bozeman has quietly been cultivating its ski community for decades. Students at Montana State University can take a free shuttle bus to nearby Bridger Bowl or unlock a discounted season pass at Big Sky (though it won’t include Saturdays or tram access). But Montana State skiers and snowboarders are not just on-piste enthusiasts. For the backcountry curious, the school has a strong backcountry scene including a dedicated Backcountry Club for avalanche education, gear help, group trips, and networking with professionals in the nearby Custer Gallatin National Forest and beyond.

It just so happens that some of Montana’s most epic skiing is located above some of Montana’s most epic après bars, so lucky you. Grab a pint at Scissor Bill’s in Big Sky or sip a Cold Smoke Scotch Ale at the Grizzly Bar off the Bridger Bowl parking lot—either way, you can’t lose.

The key to a good night is making it back to Bozeman, though, where Main Street offers up one of the more fun Eagles Club experiences around, complete with cheap drinks and rowdy live music. The Zebra is another community staple, where college students, ranchers, and old-timers can mingle over good local tunes.

Bozeman is an outdoors town with a frontier soul. The changing demographics lean toward outdoor recreation, but there’s an underlying and common current dedicated to protecting and enjoying the wild places in its periphery, and it shows. Hyalite Canyon is home to some of the best ice climbing in the world, and hosts a slew of climbers, runners, Nordic skiers, and hikers year-round. The Gallatin and Madison Rivers and Bozeman Creek all pass through or near town as well, giving anglers and kayakers primo access right out the front door, and plenty of options for anyone looking to play a little midweek hooky.

This Northwest representative was a close call with Bellingham and its coastal charm, but there’s something about the high desert that just doesn’t quit. Bend didn’t start out as a college town, but with the arrival of Oregon State University’s Cascade Campus (and the continued local support for Central Oregon Community College), this outdoors hotspot has become one heck of a diploma destination. Just 30 minutes from the 360-degree volcano skiing and riding of Mount Bachelor, Bend is a college town wrapped in mountain pedigree. We’d be silly not to mention the extensive backcountry access in Deschutes National Forest, and the Olympians that have come out of Mount Bachelor’s powerhouse Nordic skiing program. All of that and 300-plus sunny days a year? Where do we enroll?

Ski bar legend has it that before après was a French word, it was a guiding light in Central Oregon. Kidding aside, few ski towns have as many post-ski food and beverage options as the mighty Bend. While the boom has curbed in recent years, there are still over 30 breweries and taprooms within Bend city limits. Crux Fermentation Project and Monkless Belgian Ales rest on the banks of the picturesque Deschutes River, but the cozy climes and kickass beer at Terranaut Beer won Oregon’s Small Brewery of the Year in 2025.

For folks who turn college degrees into outdoor family roots, there are few spots quite like Bend. With year-round river recreation (including a retractable surf wave co-designed with surfer Gerry Lopez) and multiple trail running and mountain biking trail systems around town, Bend residents don’t know how or care to sit still. Beyond city limits, Central Oregon is an absolute natural playground, whether it be rock climbing and hiking around Smith Rock State Park, wandering the woods around Sisters, or getting out on the water in Prineville. If your friend says they’ve gotten bored of Bend, it’s time to find a new friend.

As the growing season winds down, some plants benefit from a final tidy-up. But knowing what to cut – and what to leave alone – is crucial.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

While the cold weather and dropped leaves of November make it seem as if the gardening season is over, there’s still one task left: pruning. Certain plants benefit from a pre-winter trim, while others shouldn’t be touched with pruners until next year.

Some perennials should be cut back all the way right now, while other types of plants, like fruiting vines and certain shrubs, can be touched up more lightly. Exact timing for these tasks depends on your location, weather, and the plant.

Here, we’ll outline some late fall pruning basics and list some of the plants you can tidy up or trim back now, before winter fully takes hold. We also share which plants are better trimmed next season.

Peonies are notoriously susceptible to fungal diseases. The deciduous foliage will die back in fall and, if left in place, can allow fungal spores to overwinter and reinfect plants next year. Trim back foliage once the leaves have yellowed or browned, or earlier if they look diseased.

November is the right time for this chore in many places, but if you garden in a warmer climate, the timing might be later. Remove all of the foliage without cutting it too close to the plant’s crown.

Another herbaceous perennial common in many gardens, hostas die back in fall. Clearing away the spent foliage tidies up beds, makes spring cleaning easier, and prevents many pests and diseases from overwintering and spreading. Cut leaves back to the base without getting too close to or cutting into the crowns. As long as leaves are still green, keep them in place to collect energy. Wait until they die back.

Gardeners are often tempted to cut back the leaves of these early bloomers soon after flowering, but it’s important to wait. The green leaves continue collecting energy to store for next year’s flowers. As long as they are healthy, keep the leaves in place until they start dying back in fall. November is a typical time for pruning bearded irises in many gardens. Cut the fans back to four to six inches (10 to 15 cm).

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

As with irises, you don’t want to trim back leaves just because the plants have finished flowering. Let healthy, green leaves stay in place to gather energy. For many gardeners, daylily leaves will be ready to cut back by November. In warmer climates, you might not trim them back until December. Cut daylily leaves back to a few inches above the ground.

Summer-fruiting raspberries develop fruit on canes that are two years old. Once they’re done fruiting, these older canes use up energy that the plant could be using on new canes and next year’s fruit. Identify the older, woodier canes that fruited this year, and trim them back to the ground.

You’ll also see newer, greener canes. Do not cut these back, or you’ll lose next year’s berries. Tie them together or to a support, like a fence, to protect them from winter winds.

Grapevines need regular pruning to maintain their size and structure and to support abundant fruit production. Timing is important. The vines should be dormant, so they don’t lose too much sap or sprout fresh growth. You also don’t want to prune too late, after hard freezes turn vines too brittle to make clean cuts.

When you find the right time to prune your grapevines, remove dead, damaged, or poorly positioned vines and canes. Identify healthy, young vines and trim around these. Don’t remove all older wood, especially the main trunk and arms.

Lavender hedges that are cold-hardy, like English lavender, benefit from a late fall or early winter trim to maintain their shape and health and protect them from winter weather. Too much material left on the plants can accumulate snow and ice that damage the crowns. Trim these lavenders back by about a third before the real freezing weather begins.

Pro gardeners can't get enough of Felco pruners – and these scored top in our testing.

This handy sharpener keeps pruners in top condition for clean cuts.

This telescopic tool is brilliant for trimming trees and tall climbers – no ladders required.

While these are examples of plants you can and should tackle this time of year, there are also plants that should not be trimmed now.

As a good general rule, you can trim back damaged, dead, or diseased stems and branches from any plant at any time of year. However, harder maintenance pruning needs careful timing. These plants are examples of those that can take a hard trim as winter is about to set in. Most importantly, know which plants and varieties you have and what the best practices are for these before you begin any pruning project.

Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.
