#8206. New Research Shows How Much Altitude Actually Slows You Down

One of the all-time great topics for discussion on the Sunday long run is “What was so-and-so’s race performance really worth?” Andreas Almgren, for example, won this year’s New York Marathon by running the first half in 1:04:04 and the second half, including the hills of Central Park, in 1:01:57. What could he have run with a flatter course and more even pacing? Similarly, you can ponder the effects of factors like heat, wind, drafting, shoe design… and altitude.

Everyone understands that the thin air at high altitudes matters when you’re climbing Mount Everest, or even playing football in Denver. But the effects can also show up at much lower altitudes. I once spent a few months in Australia’s capital city, Canberra, which is only around 1,900 feet above sea level. I had a streak of disappointing road races—which only made sense once I realized that even at that altitude VO2 max is reduced by about five percent. Australian sports scientists had figured that out when they were setting up the Australian Institute of Sport in Canberra and noticed that their fancy new testing equipment seemed to produce abnormally low values.

This intrinsic worth of high-altitude performances is currently a hot topic because the NCAA voted over the summer to eliminate its altitude conversions for track and field qualifying standards. Until now, any performance at more than 3,000 feet above sea level was adjusted to account for the effects of less air resistance and lower oxygen levels. Sprint performances had time added, because thin air makes them faster; middle- and long-distance performances had time deducted, because the lack of oxygen made them slower.

The conversions were eliminated in part because, as the rules committee wrote, “there is no true science being applied” in formulating them. That makes a new study in the International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance slightly late to the party—but it’s interesting nonetheless. Atle Guttormsen and Simen Guttormsen of the Norwegian University of Life Sciences analyzed more than 900,000 individual performances from track meets at 382 NCAA indoor track venues over a 14-year period to determine exactly how much difference altitude makes.

The statistical analysis attempted to account for as many sources of variation as possible: the design of the track (e.g. banked or unbanked), how a given performance compared to the athlete’s other performances that season, how early or late in the season it was, and so on. (Conveniently, there’s no wind indoors.) Overall, they came up with an estimate for how much altitude affected various events per 1,000 meters of altitude (which is 3,281 feet).

Here’s the resulting data for six running events:

Up to 400 meters, athletes are faster at altitude. The effect at 60 meters is slightly smaller because (I’m assuming) they spend a large fraction of the race accelerating to top speed. At 200 meters, they’re about 0.4 to 0.5 percent faster than they would be at sea level. In the long jump, triple jump, and pole vault, all of which are speed-based (but not shown above), there’s a similar advantage.

The crossover, where lack of oxygen begins to outweigh lower aerodynamic drag, happens at race distances just beyond 400 meters. The negative effects of altitude climb steeply at distances of up to 3,000 meters, then level off. That’s because in these longer events, aerodynamic drag is mostly irrelevant, so the effects of altitude are purely negative. For distances of 3,000 meters and beyond, the negative effects of altitude in this dataset seem to be about 2.7 percent for every 1,000 meters of altitude. Note that 1,000 meters is just slightly more than 3,000 feet, where the NCAA’s altitude conversions used to kick in. That equates to a roughly 30-second disadvantage for 5,000-meter runners.

The most interesting point in this graph is the 800-meter data. Women experience a greater disadvantage than men at altitude: 0.92 percent versus 0.50 percent. Top NCAA men are running about 1:45, while top women are running about 2:00. Since they’re so close to the point where oxygen and aerodynamics balance out, that 15-second difference matters. The men are going faster, so they benefit more from the reduction in drag; the women are running for longer, so they suffer more from the lack of oxygen. The Guttormsens argue that the NCAA needs sex-specific conversion factors—but the argument is moot since the conversion factors have been scrapped, at least for now.

Assuming the oxygen-related penalty stays roughly constant at 2.7 percent beyond 3,000 meters, here’s what kind of slowdown you can expect in endurance events at various elevations:

The upshot: I can now tell myself that I was about 1.6 percent fitter than my half-marathon times in Canberra suggested. (I’ve been saying that for years anyway… but now I’ve got science!)

The problem is that altitude affects everyone differently. A few years ago, I wrote about a neat study showing that altitude-born South American cyclists perform relatively better in high-altitude race stages than European cyclists. Even though the Europeans were doing lots of altitude training camps, they couldn’t overcome the disadvantage of being born near sea level. Altitude response depends on a mix of genetics (where your ancestors lived), environment (where you live and/or train), and developmental factors (where you were born and grew up). This is another reason the NCAA cited in scrapping altitude conversion factors: the “right” conversion is different for everyone.

There’s even some evidence that trained endurance athletes are more susceptible to the negative effects of altitude than untrained people. That may be because their hearts pump blood so powerfully that it rushes past the lungs too quickly to pick up a full load of oxygen. This affects some athletes even at sea level, but becomes increasingly common as you climb in elevation.

Personally, Canberra isn’t the only history I’d like to revise: some of the most disappointing races of my life took place in Calgary (3,428 feet) and Edmonton (2,116 feet). These aren’t cities that anyone thinks of as “high-altitude,” but it’s clear that their elevation does have an effect—and that effect is bigger if you don’t realize that it exists, because in trying to stick with your expected pace you can burn yourself out early in the race. Knowing about these effects matters, and the new data gives you a starting point to make adjustments next time you head to the mountains—or even just the foothills.

For more Sweat Science, sign up for the email newsletter and check out my new book The Explorer’s Gene: Why We Seek Big Challenges, New Flavors, and the Blank Spots on the Map.

#8204. The Best Fitness Gifts for People Who Love to Sweat

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Smartwool Trail Run Nature Print Crew Socks

Fitness gear makes a particularly tricky gift because the people who use it most need it to cater to their (often intensely) personal needs. The good stuff works for many varied athletes, disappears during a workout, and keeps annoying little problems from becoming big ones, or makes recovery suck a bit less.

From blister-fighting socks to a $40 bandana that earns its hefty price tag, here are 13 gifts for people who would rather be sweating.

Giving socks for the holidays feels unimaginative—until those socks eliminate the hot spot that usually appears around mile 12. Smartwool uses 53 percent merino wool blended with synthetic fibers for durability and stretch, then reinforces high-wear areas with its Indestructawool construction. The 4 Degree Elite Fit System has targeted stretch zones to keep everything locked in place, while mesh zones improve breathability, and a nearly seamless toe reduces friction, making these absolute blister-mitigating machines. These are the best socks you could give.

The highest compliment I can give a running shirt is that I completely forgot about it on the run. Adidas built the ADI365 Climacool Iconic Tee around that goal, using lightweight performance material and targeted ventilation to move heat and sweat away from your skin during hard efforts. The athletic shape keeps excess fabric under control without squeezing you like a race singlet. At $35, it’s also refreshingly reasonable in a category where shirts now often cost twice that.

I have sacrificed dozens of reusable bottles to protein shakes with smells that became structurally bonded to the plastic and ruined everything poured into them after. RTIC attacks that problem with a ceramic-lined 18/8 stainless-steel interior designed to reduce lingering tastes and odors. Double-wall vacuum insulation keeps drinks cold for up to 24 hours, while a removable shaker helps mix powders. The chug lid gets a magnetic cap that stays out of your face while drinking. The whole setup is built for athletes who want one bottle to handle everything from water to protein shakes.

Forty dollars for a bandana sounds ridiculous until you use it every single day of a two-week climbing trip. Arc’teryx cuts the Sinsolo from ultralight 20-denier recycled nylon and adds breathable mesh sections, creating a one-ounce triangle that dries quickly and takes up basically no room. This makes the Sinsolo a utility player that can be worn as a headband, cover a burning neck from the sun, or be dunked in a creek to make an on-the-go swamp cooler.

Consuming a recovery drink should not feel like the final unpleasant interval of a workout. Tailwind’s mix wins because it goes down easily while still delivering meaningful nutrition with 20 grams of complete plant protein from fava and brown rice sources, enough carbohydrates to replenish glycogen, plus sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium. Just as importantly, it actually tastes good mixed with plain water, so recovery doesn’t require dragging out a blender when you’re already cooked.

Ciele helped transform running hats from disposable race swag into something runners happily collect. The GOCap SC earns the brand obsession with lightweight, fast-drying material, strategic ventilation, reflective details, and a pliable brim you can crush into luggage without ruining it. The soft design disappears on long runs and absolutely sucks sweat off foreheads. It also looks good enough that the recipient might keep wearing it after the run instead of immediately stuffing it into the bottom of a gym bag.

A 2.5-inch short leaves very little room for mediocre fabric or poor fit. Vuori uses its smooth BlissBlend Form knit, a 74 percent polyamide and 26 percent elastane blend with four-way stretch and moisture-wicking capability. The high-rise waistband gets subtle V shaping at the front and back, while the short inseam stays completely out of the way during yoga or Pilates. This short is minimal without feeling flimsy, and it’s polished enough to continue wearing after class.

A sports bra shouldn’t require a warmup just to pull over your head. Beyond Yoga’s Glowzone aims for support without sacrificing the incredibly soft, stretchy feel the brand is known for. Medium-impact construction makes it useful for less bouncy activities like studio work and lifting, while the streamlined shape layers easily under a tank. The Electric Fuchsia color injects joy into any workout.

The Moab XC’s large shield provides plenty of coverage, and Tifosi offers lens options designed to maintain effective contrast as light changes. I particularly like the pink-tinted lens for variable trail conditions because it makes terrain pop without turning shady woods into nighttime. The broad coverage also works beautifully on a mountain bike. They’re sport sunglasses, but they don’t make you look like you’re trying to win the Tour.

The Orosi leggings are the most organic-feeling leggings we’ve tested, and they still completely hold their own in the gym. Credit the substantial 10-ounce jersey made of 27 percent hemp, 61 percent organic cotton, and 12 percent spandex. That magic amalgam of fibers creates a softer, more natural hand while preserving enough stretch for yoga and strength work. A triangular gusset improves mobility, and flatlock seams help reduce irritation.

RENPHO’s Active Mini Thermacool shrinks percussion massage into a compact package, and adds hot and cold treatment options for another layer of recovery. Dialing up the heat while hammering tired quads adds a soothing element to an otherwise aggressive massage. It’s small enough that it doesn’t monopolize luggage space, which makes me much more likely to actually bring it when traveling.

Nathan takes a refreshingly straightforward approach to an often overcomplicated category with the AeroZip Hydration Vest. Four-way-stretch perforated fabric hugs the body, a full front zipper makes getting it on simple, and adjustable side cords dial in fit without leaving webbing or bungees flapping everywhere. Two 17-ounce HydraPak flasks ride on the chest, and the vest itself weighs just 4.8 ounces.

From warm up to recovery to everything else the rest of the day brings, this is a staple that every active guy needs in his closet. The soft performance four-way stretch knit that’s moisture-wicking and maximizes comfort all the same while the tapered leg and cuffed ankle create a clean, athletic look. The two inseam options make it a great gift, and the zippered pockets keep belongings secure from the gym to afternoon errands and beyond.

These feel a little ridiculous underfoot because of how well they buoy each stride. The Cloudmonster 3 Hyper combines On’s oversized CloudTec geometry with highly responsive Helion HF PEBA-based foam and a more durable, stable layer beneath it. There’s no rigid plate, so your stride rolls smoothly off the aggressive rocker rather than feeling controlled by mechanical stiffness. Zipping tender shrubs into plant covers keeps them cozy over winter, and here's everything you need to know to choose the right one for your zone.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A plant frost jacket is such a simple, straightforward way to keep plants alive and well over winter, and modern designs with drawstring bases and ventilating zips make it easier than ever to use them. When winterizing a garden, zippered plant jackets don’t only protect tender beauties like banana plants and tree ferns but can help to stop sensitive souls like olive trees from dropping their leaves in a cold snap, shield citrus trees from the occasional frost if you garden in zone 9, and prevent palms from rotting.

Fleece plant covers are also incredibly useful to cocoon early-blooming shrubs like camellia and magnolia if a frost hits just as they’re setting their buds, so you can save the flower show. Young fruit trees, too, can benefit from this extra layer to stop their thin bark splitting in freezing winter conditions, and a plant cover can shield all sorts of other plants from damage caused by snow, sleet and strong winds.

So, if you're getting ready to winterize plants as you prepare your garden for the onset of cold weather, plant jackets should be part of your plan. Not all fleece plant covers are created equal, however, so if you want them to actually work, you need to take a close look at their weight rating. The material used to make frost jackets comes in different weights and, just like comforters offer various levels of warmth, that directly impacts how well it will protect plants in winter, but also the more sunshine it'll block.

Horticultural fleece is a non-woven material typically made from polypropylene, and its weight determines how much protection it offers your plant, measured in grams per square meter (gsm) or ounces per square yard (oz/sq yd). Check the label or online description to find the rating. Any good-quality frost jacket will state the rating and the higher the number, the more insulation it will provide but also block more sunlight.

Armed with this knowledge, you can choose the exact right level of protection for whatever plant you’re winterizing in your USDA zone. While you need to ensure your plant is getting the right level of cold protection, you also need to cater for its sunlight needs.

Because these plants are dormant through winter in colder zones, they don’t need sunlight so you can safely use an ultra heavy-weight fleece to protect them. The fleece alone won’t be enough to protect banana plants (Musa basjoo) and tree ferns (Dicksonia antarctica) from the deep chill of colder zones but are still useful as a cover once you’ve packed layers of insulating straw around the plant. Not only will the fleece form a great barrier against wind and rain but it’ll keep the straw in place and that wrapped plant looking tidy.

Made from 95gsm or 2.8oz/sq yd non-woven material, these plant covers have rounded tops for a good fit and come in green, beige or white in four sizes: 31" x 25", 47" x 39", 71" x 47" and 94" x 79".

Because deciduous shrubs drop their leaves in fall, they don’t need any sunlight over winter to survive so you can safely zip them up in a heavy or ultra heavy-weight plant jacket, depending on the level of protection needed in your zone. This thicker material will also keep snow from weighing down and snapping brittle winter branches. Do choose a design with a zipper as well as a base drawstring so you can regularly open up the zip on milder days to let air circulate.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

In 60gsm or 1.77oz/sq yd non-woven fabric, these zippered plant jackets are made of a minimum 50% recycled material and come in four sizes: 23" x 23", 39" x 31", 71" x 47" and 83" x 71".

Hardy shrubs that flower early in the spring such as camellias and magnolias are typically tough enough to survive most winters without a jacket, but their flowerbuds are quickly killed by a late frost or cold snap. Throw on a medium- or heavy-weight plant jacket overnight to save those new buds from the frost.

Evergreen plants such as conifers still need sunlight and fresh air to survive through winter, so a medium-weight fleece is your best bet for general winterizing if your aim is to shield a hardy plant from snow, hail and wind damage. If you’re planning on leaving it on permanently through winter, use a medium-duty fleece for more tender evergreen olive and citrus trees and certain palms, too.

However, if you live in a colder climate you’ll need the increased protection of a heavy- or ultra heavy-weight fleece for these more tender plants. Either use this as an extra layer to throw on over the top of the permanent medium-weight layer in severe weather or, if you use this as the mainstay cover, you’ll need to keep unzipping it to allow sunshine and air in during milder daytime temperatures.

Most medium-duty fleeces are designed without a zipper but that’s not a problem: because the thinner material lets more air and sunlight through, they can safely be left in place.

Made of 32gsm or 0.95oz/sq yd breathable material, this medium-weight plant cover has a drawstring base and is available in three sizes: 32" x 32", 55" x 48" and 72" x 72".

No fleece jacket can generate heat, it can only insulate from the cold, so how you use it has a huge impact on how effectively it protects your plant in winter. Choose a design with both a drawstring and a zip as this not only makes the jacket quick and easy to pop on, but allows you to fit it closely and avoids the wind ripping it off.

Wherever possible, peg the plant jacket to the ground to catch any heat rising upwards. Soil holds onto considerable warmth from the sun, so make use of this natural radiator. Use bricks or stones to weigh the jacket base down, or peg it to the ground with landscape fabric pegs, choosing a product with gaskets to prevent the fabric tearing like these Galvanized Landscape Pins from Amazon.

Similarly, if you’re winterizing a plant in a container, use a frost jacket that’s big enough to fit around the pot, too, as this will protect the roots as well as trap any heat from the soil. Roots in planters are very vulnerable to freezing temperatures so consider wrapping the pot with bubble wrap first.

To prevent moisture building up under the cover and causing mold, make sure you buy a jacket marked as breathable, and open the zip on mild days to allow air to circulate.

While you don’t want to squash a plant into a cover, it’s a wise idea to fit the jacket around the plant to prevent it flapping in the wind and metal greenhouse clamps such as these from Amazon are invaluable to gather loose material or clip a jacket to existing plant supports.

Measuring 8’ x 8’ to fit bigger shrubs and trees, this ultra heavy-weight 80gsm or 2.4oz/yd cover comes with ties and stakes so it can be pinned securely to the ground in exposed gardens.

These ultra heavy-weight zippered covers are made from 75gsm or 2.2oz/sq yd patterned fabric and are available in a green or grey print in sizes 32"x24", 47"x32", 71"x47" and 83"x71".

Shaped for wide, bushy shrubs, this heavy-weight plant cover made of 50gsm or 1.5oz/sq yd fabric measures a generous 7' x 7' and is also available in an 8' square size.

#8202. 10 Simple Ways to Raise Kids Who Make Good Decisions

Ask any parent what it’s like to raise a kid today, and we’d likely tell you modern childhood seems much more complex—and perilous—than when we were young. Thanks to increased peer pressure, massive technological advances, and on-demand access to virtually anything via click or tap, kids today face a wider array of choices and decision-making opportunities than we did when we were their age.

As parents, we hope we’ve instilled strong values and resilience in our children so they’re always able to make good decisions. But how can we be sure they’ll do the right thing, especially when we’re not around? While there’s no magic formula, here are 10 tips to help your kid make smart decisions—even when you’re not there.

The earlier parents initiate conversations about how to make good decisions with their kids, the better. Explaining to your child what it means to make a good decision and why it’s important can set them up for future success. Kevin Zoromski, a psychologist and early childhood development expert says, “Give children choices as part of their day and as part of their typical routine. They will look forward to having some say over what they get to do in the household and you will establish their sense of responsibility as important decision-makers.”

Kids learn through observation and patterning the behaviors of people in their lives, especially their parents. Modeling good decision-making behavior will help reinforce your life lessons. Show your kid that you are honest, responsible, and accountable for your choices. “You are your child’s first and most important role model,” said mental health expert Ketsupa Jirakarn. “[Kids] are always observing and learning from you every day—even when you are unaware of it. So, make sure you practice what you preach.”

Let your kids know what you expect from them in terms of making smart decisions. For older kids, this could include things like always telling you where they are going, not using illicit substances like drugs and alcohol, and staying away from dangerous situations. “Children are more likely to accept the limits you set and are more likely to want to meet your expectations (i.e., be responsible) when you provide a warm, caring, and supportive relationship that underlies the discipline you impose,” according to a report from The Center for Parenting Education.

Give your child opportunities to practice smart decision-making. This could involve giving them small choices, such as what to wear to school or what to eat for dinner. It also could involve giving them bigger choices, such as whether to join a sports team or what to do with their allowance. By empowering your child to learn about the consequences of their choices through smaller actions, they will feel more empowered when making bigger decisions on their own.

When your kid makes a mistake, don’t immediately swoop in to fix the problem or resort immediately to punishment. Help them understand why a misstep was a consequence of not making the best decision, and then talk about how they can make a better choice next time. According to a report from the Harvard Graduate School of Education, “Reframing mistakes as opportunities from which we can learn—rather than failures alone—can help us feel like we are capable and in control. Reframing can also help us handle future mistakes more effectively.”

Learning how to think critically and independently requires self-awareness (i.e., knowing strengths, weaknesses, and values) as well as problem-solving skills. Encouraging your child to think through a decision and come up with a solution can further nurture and develop their critical thinking skills. “In childhood and adolescence, the body goes through many physical changes, but there are also many changes in how we think, feel, and behave, and in our motivations,” according to a report from Frontiers for Young Minds. It’s through repeated trial and error that kids develop the necessary skills to thrive into adulthood.

Some decisions have few consequences, while other decisions are highly consequential. Teaching your child the difference between big and small choices, and understanding the risks associated with some decisions will mitigate the chances of bad outcomes. For example, teach young kids about the risks of eating too much junk food or overdoing it with screen time, and teach older kids about the risks of cyberbullying and underage drinking.

Talk to your child about the choices they’re facing and help them understand the different options and the potential consequences of each choice. Teaching them how to evaluate information, identify biases, and make informed decisions as well as helping your child understand and manage their emotions and how to make decisions that are in line with their values will serve them well. “Emotional literacy starts at birth when babies can just bond with [their parents] and connect on just that level. And it continues to evolve,” said Dr. Michele Borba, parenting expert and author of Building Moral Intelligence: The Seven Essential Virtues that Teach Kids to Do the Right Thing.

As parents, being supportive and consistent with our reactions to our children’s choices will help ensure they make smart ones, even when we’re not present. If you sometimes let your child get away with making a bad decision, they will be less likely to take you seriously when you expect them to make good choices without you. Additionally, when your kid makes a good decision, be sure to praise and validate them. “Youth who experience more positive interactions with parents are better adjusted. Indeed, consistency in parenting—primarily consistency in discipline—has been linked to more positive youth outcomes,” according to a report from the National Institutes of Health.

It takes time for kids to learn how to make smart decisions. Don’t get discouraged if they don’t always and immediately make the right choices. Even when your kids are old enough to make decisions themselves, they still need your patience and understanding. Be there to talk to them, offer advice, and help them deal with the consequences of their decisions.

Bringing a little more joy to parenthood.

#8200. Great Hydration is About More than Just Electrolytes

Harmless Harvest shelf-stable coconut water. (Photo: Harmless Harvest)

Hydration comes up a lot when we talk about performance and recovery. Are you drinking enough water? Are you getting enough electrolytes? Are you tracking your fluid intake? It can be overwhelming to keep tabs of every statistic and ounce, but the hype around hydration isn’t without cause. Hydration is not only an essential component of pre-, mid- and post-workout performance. It’s an essential part of everyday life.

Electrolytes are a particular point of focus among performance athletes. Electrolytes are the minerals that help maintain the balance of fluids inside and outside your body’s cells. This is a critical consideration when it comes to high-exertion workouts where you’re losing lots of fluids through sweat.

The market is more saturated (pun intended) than ever with tablets, powders and pouches galore to help you optimize and maximize your electrolyte intake. But hydration doesn’t have to be as complicated as all that—and the conversation surrounding electrolytes doesn’t have to be reserved for elite athletes. It can be an everyday consideration for your morning walk, a quick out-and-back hike, or your daily commute to the office. And it all starts with a single coconut.

That’s the mission behind Harmless Harvest, a California-based company championing the coconut, turning a remarkable fruit into a remarkable lineup of products. It’s new pantry-friendly coconut water contains one ingredient: 100% coconut water with no added sugar or preservatives. The simplicity of their products ladder up to the simplicity of the brand’s philosophy—that great taste, quality ingredients, and premium tasting hydration should be for everyone to enjoy. Uncomplicated hydration doesn’t have to be a statistic for you to overanalyze—it can be an intentional and enjoyable part of your everyday life.

So what’s so great about a simple bottle of coconut water? Well, it’s just that: the simplicity. All on its own, coconut water delivers naturally occurring electrolytes, including potassium, to support everyday hydration. Unlike the formulated hydration drinks, tablets and powders that rely on added electrolytes, coconut water provides those muscle-supporting, fluid-balancing minerals into every bottle of Harmless Harvest coconut water naturally. Every bottle is made with a single ingredient with that naturally sweet coconut taste that’s completely delicious and refreshing.

From your pantry to wherever the day takes you, Harmless Harvest’s newest coconut water makes it easier than ever to keep great-tasting hydration close at hand. With no refrigeration required, you can keep bottles at room temperature until you’re ready to enjoy. Grab a bottle on the way to yoga, before a big day on the slopes, or just on the way to work. And unlike the traditional flash pasteurization commonly used by beverage producers, Harmless Harvest’s optimized heat treatment and micro-filtration preserves the fruit’s natural sweetness and nutrients, so you’re getting everything the mighty coconut has to offer.

Another question you might be asking is why is Harmless Harvest’s coconut water pink? Rather than using additives to control color variation from bottle to bottle, the company has embraced the pink hue that can come with the interaction between the coconut water’s antioxidants and natural elements like light and temperature.

Harmless Harvest’s commitment to sustainability and environmentally conscious practices extends beyond the bottle, too. The brand works with coconut growers in Thailand to source ethically farmed, non-GMO coconuts and also invests in initiatives that support farmers and their communities. These conscientious business practices aim to bring you products that you can sip with peace of mind.

Coconut water may not be the first thing you think to grab before a big workout or after a long run. It’s not a product that we typically associate with performance and recovery, but perhaps that’s the whole point. Don’t get us wrong, electrolytes are important, but in the age of optimization, where every mile, calorie and ounce of water is tracked, logged, and analyzed, it’s good to get back to the basics.

Being well-hydrated shouldn’t be reserved for when you’re pushing your body to its limits. Harmless Harvest’s mission is to show that just like general wellness, proper hydration goes beyond a numerical value—it’s about being mindful and listening to your body, one sip at a time.

Harmless Harvest creates delicious, premium coconut-based beverages and foods, crafted with care for people and the planet. Known for its naturally hydrating coconut water, the brand is committed to exceptional taste, responsibly sourced ingredients, and sustainable farming practices. Its mission is simple: make remarkable products while doing less harm and more good.

Most carved pumpkins tend to get binned or left rotting on the curb once the candles burn out. Yet that leftover gourdish grin is packed with benefits for your soil, future plants, and wildlife

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The first few days of November bring a familiar sorry sight, as pumpkins start piling up beside the trash cans, a few of them still grinning. Millions end up in landfills every year, where they break down without much air and give off greenhouse gases. That's a poor end for leftover Halloween pumpkins. In a garden, all that soft tissue could be breaking down into organic matter and feeding soil life – and that’s just the start.

If you took the time to grow pumpkins for Halloween, you know how much space, moisture, and fertilizer a single vine demands. All summer long, its leaves absorbed sunlight and pumped nutrients directly into its swollen fruit. Letting those nutrients leave your yard in a trash bag deprives your yard of valuable goodness that could be benefiting vegetable beds, feeding organisms and helping beneficial creatures. Even a carved pumpkin can have a second life as long as it hasn't been painted or coated.

Giving your post-Halloween gourds a productive second act is simple, fun, and satisfying. The only rule is that your fruit needs to be clean and free of contaminants. Any sections coated in craft paints, glitter, chemical sealants, or fake snow must be removed and tossed into the trash. Pull out any burnt candle stubs, melted wax, and battery-powered tea lights, and you are ready to put this fall bounty to work!

Turning post-holiday pumpkins into garden assets is a real no-brainer. Standard carving pumpkin varieties like Howden and Jack O' Lantern work especially well for the soil, because their flesh is tender and relatively easy to slice. Thicker, denser culinary and heirloom varieties (such as ribbed Cinderella, dusty-blue Jarrahdale, or warty Marina di Chioggia) offer firmer rinds that hold their shape for weeks, making them ideal where shape and rigidity are useful.

These fall projects work across every USDA hardiness zone, though local temperatures will determine how quickly your gourd decomposes. In cold northern regions (zones 3-5), freezing nights preserve carved pumpkins on porches longer, but freeze-thaw cycles eventually cause cell walls to collapse into watery slop, making early November the best time to act. In warm southern places (zones 8-10), elevated daytime temperatures accelerate mold and fruit flies, requiring immediate conversion into ground-based or wildlife-specific benefits.

Before tackling these projects, you need the right hand tools. A heavy-duty hori-hori knife is an excellent investment if you don’t have one, and can be used to simplify all kinds of cutting work. The Nisaku Hori-Hori from Amazon is great value and makes slicing through thick rinds a joy, and levers drainage holes through thick base walls without snapping. So find out exactly why your grinning pumpkin still has lots of goodness to give…

Tossing an intact pumpkin onto your compost heap can lead to disappointment. Its waxy rind acts like a raincoat, and depending on the variety and the weather, it could sit there for a long time with its skin intact. It needs breaking up first. Take a sharp spade or round-point shovel, and break the fruit down into fist-sized chunks to expose the flesh to soil bacteria and fungi.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

Because the tissue is roughly 90% water, this green compost source needs plenty of dry browns mixed in. Balance every bucket of chopped pumpkin with two buckets of carbon-rich browns, such as shredded leaves, straw, or torn cardboard to keep the pile aerated. Turn the heap now and then. If space is tight, a single-chamber tumbler like the Vivosun Outdoor Dual Chamber Tumbling Composter, available from Amazon speeds up heat decomposition in a more compact way.

If your compost heap is overflowing, try direct trench composting in an empty veg bed. Dig a trench 18-24 inches (45-61cm) deep, in a bed reserved for heavy-feeding spring crops like sweet corn, squash, or tomatoes. Fill the bottom with chopped chunks and stomp them down. Backfill with 12 inches (30cm) of clean soil. Don’t go shallower, or neighborhood raccoons may smell it and dig it back up. Loose, well-drained soil can break it down in 2-3 months, but if you have heavy clay soil, you may still hit chunks of pumpkin a year from now, so be patient.

A healthy, mature Halloween pumpkin contains hundreds of plump seeds loaded with goodness. If your pumpkin grew with vibrant color and a firm rind, these seeds are prime candidates for saving for next year. Strain the tangled seed mass in a colander and massage it under a stream of cold running tap water to strip away the pulp. Spread the cleaned seeds in a single layer over non-stick parchment paper, a fine metal screen, or a ceramic plate. Let them dry in a warm, well-ventilated room out of direct sunlight for 2-3 weeks.

To test for dryness, try bending one: if it flexes, it still retains moisture, but if it snaps in half, your seeds are ready to store. Slide your dried seeds into breathable kraft paper seed envelopes. Pour them into paper seed envelopes, like the Seed Packet Kraft Envelopes, available from Walmart in packs of 100. Write the variety and date on the front, and store in a cool, dark drawer. Word to the wise, though: modern carving pumpkins are typically hybrids that won’t go true to type. Also, bees can cross-pollinate squash varieties across neighborhood zucchinis, so next spring’s seedlings may produce some wacky, unpredictable gourds.

Songbirds burn through vital fat stores as November temperatures drop, and a firm pumpkin makes a wonderful natural feeding bowl (although it’s best to stick to uncarved porch pumpkins for this project). Cut your pumpkin in half across the middle, or slice the top third off. Using a sturdy spoon or hori-hori to scrape out the inner pulp and seeds, until the interior walls are clean. Poke 3-4 half-inch (1.25cm) drainage holes through the base using a large screwdriver.

Punch 3 evenly spaced holes along the thick top rim, thread some sturdy jute twine through, and hang the bowl from a sturdy tree limb or pergola beam. Alternatively, set the flat shell on a low wall, tree stump, or deck railing. Fill with black-oil sunflower seeds or a good seed blend, such as Pennington Wild Bird Food from The Home Depot. You can also use some of your rinsed and dried pumpkin seeds as extra treats. These nutritious kitchen scraps make a nourishing treat for cardinals, blue jays and titmice. Just inspect every few days: when the inner walls turn squishy or develop fuzz, take the feeder down and consign it to the compost heap.

If you have a solid (again, uncarved) ornamental pumpkin on your porch, you can turn it into a temporary planter. Carve a generous opening around the stem and scoop out the pulp and seeds. Using a long screwdriver, puncture 4-5 generous drainage holes through the bottom crust. If you need a good screwdriver, Black Canyon’s Phillips Extended Length Screwdriver with Soft Grip Ergonomic Handle from Walmart is an efficient way to punch through thick rinds. Elevate the pumpkin on some stone or a trivet for drainage, as sitting water will rot the base rapidly.

Fill the lower half of the pumpkin with light, free-draining potting soil, then tuck in your choice of cold-tolerant fall ornamentals. Some great options include dwarf flowering kales, ruffled ornamental cabbages, winter violas, pansies, and trailing English ivy. These cold-hardy choices will look fresh and colorful for 2-4 weeks. With wet soil sitting inside it, the pumpkin starts softening from the inside out, and a few freeze-thaw nights will hurry it along. When yours starts to sag, move the plants to a bed or regular pot, and compost the gourd.

Slugs and garden snails are a persistent menace in fall, but at night they seek shelter in dark, damp, sheltered crevices to conserve moisture. A curved chunk of pumpkin rind provides a perfect natural decoy. Take sections of rind, including leftover pieces from carving or scraps that have softened too much for bird feeders. Place them skin-side up on the soil, beside vulnerable vegetable rows, hosta crowns, or mulched borders. The sweet scent of decaying squash flesh will attract slugs from several feet away, luring them under the hollowed domes.

Early the following morning, flip the rinds over. You should find dozens of slugs, snails, and earwigs clinging to the flesh. Scrape them off into a bucket of warm soapy water, or feed them to backyard chickens. Reset the traps for several nights in a row. Every slug removed now is one fewer laying eggs. Once the rind collapses, compost it. Dust a little Harris Food Grade Diatomaceous Earth Powder, available from Amazon, around your traps to stop slugs escaping back into your beds.

This last one is a lovely eco-friendly bonus for anyone keen to support overwintering beneficial insects in their yard. As fall frosts intensify, beneficial predatory insects and pollinators seek sheltered crevices. Ground beetles, centipedes, roving rove beetles, lacewings, lady bugs, and solitary native bees are valuable allies in the organic garden, consuming thousands of aphids, slug eggs, and weed seeds. You can turn a hollowed pumpkin shell into a cozy winter sanctuary. Take an uncarved or cleanly carved pumpkin. Slice a wide entryway near the base (or prop the shell upside-down on a couple of flat stones to leave an open gap underneath).

Stuff the cavity with natural textural materials that create micro-tunnels and air pockets. Use bundles of dry hollow plant stems, bamboo canes, small pine cones, crumpled dry leaves, and coarse straw. You can buy Bell Nursery Mini Straw Bales from The Home Depot which can also be used as mulch for strawberries and other overwintering plants. Tuck your bug hotel beneath a thick hedge, under a quiet shrub border, or along a perennial bed out of wind and rain. The shell will slowly soften, insulating the center. By spring, it will return harmlessly to the soil, leaving your beneficial guardians safely in the mulch bed, ready to go to work.

Before you drag your hollowed Halloween pumpkins down to the street corner, hopefully these ideas show you that they could be working hard for your yard. These seasonal gourds are far more than short-lived porch decorations. By turning into a rich soil ingredient, feeding wild birds, constructing cozy shelters for beneficial beetles and stocking up on seeds to plant next year’s pumpkins, you keep valuable resources out of landfills and grab a head start on next year's growth. Once winter sets in, those leftover gourds may already be enriching your soil: a true win-win!

Need more ideas for getting the most from your plants, indoors and out, and looking for the best seasonal expert advice delivered straight to your inbox? Sign up for the free Gardening Know How Newsletter!

Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

#8197. ProArch: BA/Technical Product Manager

Headquarters: United States
URL: https://jobs.workable.com/company/u8TybTAE2YbYgRVFYov9t4/jobs-at-proarch

Partner Discovery & Requirements Analysis

  • Lead and document working sessions with clinical, finance, operations, product, and technical stakeholders to understand existing workflows, business rules, data requirements, and operational processes.
  • Translate manual and system-supported workflows into structured business and functional requirements.
  • Produce gap-analysis documentation mapping current-state processes and partner requirements to existing platform capabilities.
  • Classify requirements based on appropriate disposition, such as existing functionality, configuration, new development, acceptable operational workaround, shared platform enhancement, or out of scope.
  • Maintain a consistent backlog structure across implementations so requirements remain comparable, traceable, and reusable.

System Reconciliation & Technical Analysis

  • Analyze application logic, SQL, stored procedures, configuration parameters, integrations, and data flows to understand existing system behavior.
  • Determine whether business requirements can be satisfied through configuration, existing functionality, process changes, or new development.
  • Validate assumptions about platform behavior against available technical evidence and distinguish confirmed system behavior from inferred behavior.
  • Identify discrepancies between documented behavior, stakeholder expectations, system configuration, and implemented logic.
  • Trace business rules to underlying parameters, data elements, calculations, integrations, and system components.
  • Identify where behaviors are configurable versus hardcoded and assess the impact on future implementations.

Requirements Authoring

  • Write clear business and functional requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, assumptions, dependencies, open questions, and proposed workarounds.
  • Maintain appropriate separation between business-facing requirements and technical implementation details.
  • Ensure acceptance criteria reflect the agreed solution approach, including configuration changes, operational workarounds, or new functionality.
  • Apply a consistent standard for distinguishing standalone requirements from assumptions, configuration decisions, implementation details, or operational procedures.
  • Maintain traceability from business need through solution decision and development implementation.

Cross-Functional Facilitation & Governance

  • Facilitate requirements, solutioning, and review sessions across business, clinical, product, engineering, data, and operational teams.
  • Drive open questions toward resolution and update requirements and documentation to reflect confirmed decisions.
  • Identify ambiguity, conflicting requirements, downstream impacts, and cross-feature dependencies before development begins.
  • Prevent scope drift and ensure implementation-specific requirements do not unintentionally become platform-wide requirements.
  • Support prioritization and decision-making by clearly communicating business impact, implementation complexity, dependencies, and risk.

Ticket Creation & Scoping

  • Translate approved requirements into development-ready tickets containing problem statements, user stories, functional scope, acceptance criteria, dependencies, assumptions, and open questions.
  • Partner with engineering and architecture teams to clarify technical scope and implementation approach.
  • Track dependencies across features, integrations, implementations, and shared platform capabilities.
  • Identify common capabilities that can support multiple clients, workflows, or future implementations rather than creating one-off solutions.
  • 8+ years of experience as a Business Analyst, Technical Product Manager, Product Owner, or equivalent role in a software-, data-, or technology-driven environment.
  • Experience working within healthcare technology, healthcare operations, payer/provider systems, pharmacy, claims, revenue cycle, eligibility, or related healthcare domains.
  • Ability to understand and reason about SQL, data structures, system logic, APIs, configuration, and technical workflows well enough to validate platform behavior and collaborate effectively with engineering teams.
  • Demonstrated ability to write clear requirements, user stories, acceptance criteria, and development tickets that engineering teams can implement with minimal rework.
  • Strong analytical rigor with the ability to distinguish confirmed facts from assumptions, challenge unclear reasoning, and validate conclusions.
  • Experience facilitating requirements and solution-review sessions involving business, clinical, operational, and technical stakeholders.
  • Strong written and verbal communication skills, with the ability to adapt business and technical information for different audiences.

Preferred Qualifications

  • Familiarity with healthcare claims, eligibility, reimbursement, clinical workflows, pharmacy operations, or healthcare financial processes.
  • Experience working with configurable or rules-driven healthcare platforms.
  • Experience supporting client, provider, health system, or partner implementations.
  • Understanding of data pipelines, ETL processes, APIs, healthcare integrations, and data exchange concepts.
  • Experience managing a shared product backlog across multiple customers, implementations, or business units.
  • Familiarity with healthcare data standards, regulatory requirements, or privacy considerations such as HIPAA.

Key Competencies

  • Requirements elicitation and translation
  • Healthcare workflow analysis
  • Technical and data analysis
  • System behavior reconciliation
  • Product and backlog management
  • Stakeholder facilitation and decision-driving
  • Cross-functional collaboration
  • Analytical rigor and structured problem-solving
  • Dependency and impact analysis
  • Documentation discipline and traceability

#8196. The Best Cross-Country Skis of 2027

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

What to know: Testers in the Midwest and Maine put more than 56 demo cross-country skis to the test. They named the Salomon Escape Outpath 65 Grip Cross-Country Skis with Prolink Bindings as the most versatile for skiing in and out of tracks. For skiers who like to go fast, they named the Fischer Speedpro 50 Skate as the best budget race ski.

Cross-country skiing is surging in popularity in the U.S. That expansion is due, in part, to the broad range of ski styles that suit every fitness level.

We tested all three styles of cross-country skis, including skate, classic, and backcountry. From a pool of 56 demo models, we evaluated skis that are optimized for beginners as well as models capable of helping accomplished skiers push their limits. From the most versatile in tracks to the best pairs for racing, these six cross-country skis impressed our testers most.

Sidecut: 60-55-65 Weight: 4 lbs 12 oz (per pair) Length: 180, 195 cm

Pros and Cons + Confidence-inspiring control + Energetic glide – Lacks flotation in snow depths greater than 4 inches

With a tip that’s barely narrower than the machine-set, 68-millimeter cross-country ski tracks grooved into Nordic trails, the versatile Escape Outpath impressed testers in all situations shy of deep snow. “It feels snappy and efficient,” reports our Maine tester after logging 20 miles on groomed and ungroomed terrain. “Very energy conserving.”

This narrow-waisted ski is a true jack-of-all-trades: It climbs, descends, easily breaks trail, and reliably floats atop several inches of fresh snow (though it became overwhelmed in more than 4 inches of powder). “It doesn’t feel squirrely on the downhills like most other skis I’ve used,” reports one novice skier.

Several design factors explain this ski’s multi-faceted performance. The three-quarter-length metal edge has a softer flex, particularly in the tip—which is built around a core made of lighter, bendier recycled ABS material that facilitates flotation on ungroomed snow. Those soft tips also adapted to other terrain features (such as the curves on classic tracks) and made this ski feel unusually easy to control in tracks and out.

A wood core and ample camber in the rest of the ski achieves a winning balance of energy and stability. “I loved the edge grip I felt on icy descents,” said one tester (who used this ski with the backcountry-oriented Salomon Escape Outrack boot). Novices appreciated its low-effort responsiveness; advanced skiers praised its playful personality and long, speed-preserving glide. In deeper snow, the Fischer S-Bound 98 Crown bested its performance, but for enjoying groomed conditions and light-duty trail-breaking, the Escape Outpath 65 was our definitive winner.

Sidecut: 85-61-75 Weight: 5 lbs 8 oz (per pair) Length: 165-195 cm

Pros and Cons + Handles mixed conditions, from firm snow to powder + Easy to turn – Heavy for a midfat

On tours that include the full range of snow conditions across mountain terrain, this ski shines. It’s narrow and stiff enough for efficient glide on flats (something that pack-laden testers appreciated as they logged miles-long commutes over frozen lakes). Its stiffness smooths the ride over chunky surfaces and provides reassuring grip on firm, wind-scoured descents. And its almost-fat width (85 millimeters at the tip) provided capable flotation in snow depths up to 10 inches.

Some of its success in mixed conditions comes from the tried-and-true pairing of a wood core with full metal edges, which bite into firm snow and provide a stable platform on chunky, cut-up slopes. Yes, that layup emphasizes stability over weight savings: It’s heavier than the Fischer S-Bound 98 Crown, for example, but more reassuring when sidehilling or descending through chop. The scaled bases delivered a likeable balance of grip and glide, and for steep climbs, attaching kicker skins ($150, sold separately) delivers skimo capability.

If cruising through touring centers is all you’ll do, the BC85 might be overkill. But if you need a versatile, all-conditions ski that performs reliably on off-piste mountain routes, here’s your winner.

Sidecut: 98-69-88 Weight: 4 lbs 9 oz (per pair) Length: 159-189 cm

Pros and Cons + Light enough for longer tours + Best-in-test grip – Lacks stability on firm conditions

If fresh pow is what lures you onto the hills, here’s your joystick. This perennial favorite still earns high scores for being floaty yet light—and its bases dazzled testers with their best-in-test performance. “The scales gripped great in all conditions, even refrozen granular, and they never clumped up when I hit mixed-temperature snow that caused icing problems for other skis,” reported one tester.

Though it’s not the floatiest of them all, the S-Bound 98 Crown proved easier to turn in deep snow. Its lightweight paulownia wood and fiberglass core has hollow air channels throughout. Not only does the fiberglass reinforcement make the ski stronger than one with a solid wood core, but the air chambers distribute pressure better, too. A rockered tip preserves the ski’s underfoot camber while also floating to the surface and facilitating turns in deep, untracked snow. On our testing trip near Maine’s Medawisla Hut, narrow steel edges helped one novice skier feel confident on smooth, groomed descents, while the wide tips provided good flotation in 18 inches of freshies.

For touring on steeps, Fischer’s two compatible mohair and nylon skins—the short “EZ Skin” or the full-length “Super Skin”—create a lightweight skimo setup.

Sidecut: 41-44-44 Weight: 2 lbs 6 oz (per ski) Length: 168-204 cm

Pros and Cons + Light, stable, and affordable + Edgehold remains on uphills – Best for beginners

Learning to skate ski requires coordination, making stability especially important in a beginner ski. But a stable beginner ski is often heavy, which can lead to fatigue. That’s why our testers gravitated toward Fischer’s entry-level race ski, the Speedpro Skate 50, as their beginner pick. It’s light and stable, but still affordable—all helpful ingredients for a first-timer.

To shave grams, Fischer built the Speedpro Skate 50 with the same “air core” construction used in its elite-level skis. Think of the ski’s core as a rectangular box made of ultralight wood. Inside, thin, wave-shaped walls of basalt-reinforced resin run the length of the ski, with air pockets in between. A lightweight fiberglass laminate reinforced with basalt fibers wraps the core, adding strength and torsional stiffness without much weight.

To improve stability, Fischer widened its contact areas and used a World Cup-level base that provides easy glide in a wide variety of snow temperatures. To add a hair more speed, they shaped it with a narrow, 41 millimeter tip that gave it an edge, especially on uphills.

Two testers used the Speedpro Skate 50 in varying snow conditions—sometimes all in the same day. During one 10-kilometer ski at Duluth’s Spirit Mountain Nordic Center after a late-spring storm, they started out in slushy, mashed potato snow at the bottom then climbed a few hundred feet to where the skate track was still frozen and riddled with chunks of ice that had fallen from trees. But the skis made it possible to steadily glide through the crud without a twist of the knee or ankle.

Sidecut: 44-43-44 Weight: 2 lbs 2 oz (per pair) Length: 177-192 cm

Pros and Cons + Super stable + Binding is adjustable on the fly – Not as playful as other skis in its class

Salomon’s new Equipe Pro replaces the S/Max. The improved ski is 20 percent lighter, a feat accomplished by replacing the foam core with the brand’s in-house “Innowave” technology. Salomon’s air core, previously reserved for elite-level race skis, is engineered from paper and glue and encased by ultralight wood sidewalls—visualize a sidecut from the corrugated wall of a cardboard box, but exponentially stronger.

Even with the ski’s dramatic weight savings, it still feels grounded and stable underfoot, a hallmark of Salomon. The almost-always-in-control feeling is largely a result of the ski’s stiff flex profile (or the stiffness of the ski’s camber), which influences speed and turning. The Equipe Pro’s outer laminate is fiberglass from tip to tail, which is heavier than the thin-ply carbon used on elite-level skis, but it also provides stability while edging.

Our testers had fun using the Equipe Pro during a leisurely ski at Wisconsin’s Superior Municipal Forest, a mostly flat course interspersed with beautifully-groomed, fun, steep, and fast rollers. On their next time out, they took it up a notch on the 25-kilometer “Picnic Loop,” a series of seemingly endless and unforgiving hills deep in the Superior National Forest. Thanks to soft new snow and the comfort and stability of the Equipe Pro, they returned with limbs intact, which isn’t always the outcome on this remote and tiring loop.

Sidecut: 44-44-43 Weight: 665 g (per ski, 196cm, with the binding installed) Length: 178-205 cm

Pros and Cons + Works well in almost every condition + Comes with a durable, 100-percent mohair skin – Quick studies may quickly outgrow this beginner-to-intermediate ski

The Atomic Pro C2 Skintec has been a top seller in Atomic’s lineup for ten years. But in late 2025, Atomic gave it a substantial makeover, shaving its weight by about eight percent, improving the camber to make it easier to kick, and simplifying the lengths and flexes.

The core is lightweight polyurethane foam (Densolite 300). Above and below that foam layer are fiberglass laminates. Carbon laminates are the go-to on higher-end skis, but fiberglass offers its own rewards—skiers can flatten the ski’s camber with less effort, which makes the kick easier. Fiberglass is also less springy than carbon, so the skis feel more stable and grounded, an attribute that stood out to both of our testers.

Of the six pairs of classic skis our tester sampled, the Pro C2 Skintec was best in all kinds of crazy backward conditions, from springtime slush in February to sub-arctic single digits in March.

As a bonus, the Pro C2 Skintec includes a set of 100 percent mohair skins, which offer the best combination of durability and water resistance and is simple to replace when it wears out (generally after 1,000 kilometers of skiing.)

Olympic racers compete in two dominant forms: Skate, in which skiers use a V-shaped stride that maximizes speed, and classic, using a parallel ski stance that looks like walking but with more glide. Both ski styles are intended for groomed cross-country ski trails, and both are accessible to newbies as well as elites.

A third type of cross-country ski is dedicated to off-trail adventure. Backcountry skis are generally wider for better flotation in uncompacted snow, with fish-scale texture on their bases that provide enough grip to stride uphill and glide down. While some classic skis have scaled bases, most—and all skate skis—rely on wax to deliver the desired balance of grip and glide.

When buying cross-country skis, it’s easy to get intimidated by Nordork speak, a tech-heavy vocabulary including terms like flex pattern, torsional stiffness, camber, grind, sidecut, and adjectives like soft, medium, stiff, extra stiff, cold, warm, and universal—all of which can apply to a different version of the same ski. Even Nordic ski manufactures admit it’s a little much, and the reason the industry is making a concerted effort to simplify the jargon for the sake of confused consumers.

Before you invest in new skis, take a ski lesson. If none are available in your area, there are some good tutorials online, including REI’s “Classic Cross-Country Skiing for Beginners” and “How To Skate Ski.” A good ski coach can break down technique in a way that makes it fun and easy to learn right off the bat so you can spend your remaining ski career feeling joy rather than frustration.

And before you buy a ski, it’s ideal to test it first—either at a race, festival, or shop that offers demo skis. It’s also a good idea to pick the brain of the Nordic manager in the ski shop who can direct you to the best ski for your weight and ability level (usually categorized as beginner, endurance/intermediate, and race).

For the backcountry test, Kelly Bastone organized two large-group testing sessions in February and March in Maine. One took place on trails around Carrabasset Valley. Some testers skied to the Poplar Stream Hut, part of Maine Huts and Trails network, for a mid-afternoon warmup with the hut’s complimentary tea and cocoa by the fire. Conditions were beautifully cold snow: five inches of fresh, compacted in places, with no ice or crust. The other session took place on a tester’s family property in central Maine in conditions that presented sun-warming snow on top of cold, fresh snow—a perfect recipe for clumping, which were also good conditions for testing. Bastone then tested skis closer to home in Yarmouth in variable conditions, involving crust layers and refrozen slush. It wasn’t ideal snow, but it was telling.

Stephanie Pearson and fellow tester Brian Hayden took the long approach to testing classic and skate skis, skiing over the course of four months in every condition. On weekdays, they rotated between five trail systems in Duluth and nearby Superior, Wisconsin. On weekends, they ventured farther north and east. It turned out to be a banner snow year in the upper Midwest with some of the best, most consistent snow in the country, from cold Styrofoam snow in December and January to perfect corduroy decks in February to corn snow in March. Even in early April, Pearson and Hayden were still skiing.

Category Manager Kelly Bastone moved to the Colorado Rockies in 1998 and has pursued outdoor sports ever since. A freelancer who writes about gear and other outdoor topics for publications such as Backpacker, AFAR, and The Red Bulletin, Bastone has contributed many gear reviews to Outside over the years. An avid skier (resort, Nordic, and backcountry), fly-fisher, mountain biker, and mushroom forager, she gets the news she needs from the weather report.

Category manager Stephanie Pearson grew up in Duluth, cross-country skiing out her backyard. Realizing her skate skiing needed a tune-up, this season she took skate-skiing lessons with Kara Salmela, a former Olympic biathlete who coaches through Duluth XC Ski Club. Pearson started at Outside as an intern in 1995 and has worked on staff and as a contributing editor for three decades. She is also a National Geographic Explorer.

Flowerbuds should be forming by late fall but you'll need to get November Christmas cactus care right to enjoy a first-rate festive flower show.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By November, your Christmas cactus should be busy preparing to flower, and what you do with your plant now is the difference between a disappointing bud-drop or a dazzling display of festive flowers. We think of cacti as being easy plants to grow but the Christmas cactus is a rather sensitive soul. Native to the coastal rainforests of Brazil, Shlumbergera x buckleyi can struggle to flower well in the very different environment of our homes, and even jettison all its buds.

Get November Christmas cactus care right, however, and you’ll have a happy plant in full, fabulous bloom for the holidays. What's more, stick to these guidelines and those flowers will last for longer, even brightening the first few weeks of the new year.

The four principles of caring for a Christmas cactus in late fall are super-simple to achieve, and knowing exactly what your plant needs to stay focused on swelling those precious buds changes everything. Here's what to do to stop a Christmas cactus dropping its buds so you can enjoy weeks of fabulous flowers right through the holidays.

In November, your Christmas cactus should be setting buds so check regularly for tiny pinpricks of color on the leaf tips. These nubs will be bright red, pink or purple or, if you have a white-flowering variety, a very pale green, so they’re easy to spot.

If you’ve been using light and dark to trick your Christmas cactus into flowering right on time for the holidays, you’ll very likely spot plenty of these baby flowerbuds in mid-November. If you haven’t, don’t panic, because you may still get Christmas cactus flowers this winter. Your Shlumbergera may well have set flowerbuds without any extra encouragement from you, especially if its natural seasonal cues haven't been interrupted by artificial evening light or too much warmth or water.

If you're trying the light and dark trick, carry on until you spot buds. If not, and there’s no sign of buds yet, move your cactus to a cool room that’s not often used so lights aren’t routinely switched on – a spare bedroom is ideal. Turn the radiator down and leave the blind or curtains open so the air naturally cools at night to 50-55°F – a cheap indoor thermometer such as this from Amazon makes it easy to check. Only water the cactus sparsely once the top 2-3 inches of soil feel dry, as drought conditions can trigger flowering, and keep your fingers crossed!

As soon as you spot buds, move your Christmas cactus to a spot that gets bright, indirect sunlight and the temperature stays around 65-70°F. You can give your plant a little more water now, too, irrigating when the top inch of soil feels dry or take out the guesswork with a moisture meter such as this long-probe soil meter from Amazon. Aim to keep the soil consistently just-damp.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

The dry air of a heated home is a far cry from a Christmas cactus’ natural environment of a moist rainforest , and this is a real threat to the holiday flowers. When the heat is first turned on, the shock is a common reason why Christmas cacti drop a leaf segment. And if the too-dry conditions continue, a cactus can lose so much moisture from its stems that it goes into survival mode and, because those developing flowers are using a heap of energy, jettisons its buds.

Setting your plant on a humidity tray is a quick and easy answer. A bonsai pebble tray such as this from Lowe’s is perfect, or make your own with a plant saucer and pea gravel pebbles like this Landscape Rock from The Home Depot. Add water to the tray but sit the plant pot on the pebbles so its base is above the water level: the water will then naturally evaporate, increasing air humidity for your houseplant, rather than being drawn up into the potting soil. Keeping the tray topped up with water will also help flowers last for longer once they open.

As well as being very sensitive to the level of moisture in the air, your Christmas cactus will respond negatively to any other changes in its environment. So, if you want those flowerbeds to swell right on schedule, you must leave your plant in the same spot.

In the rainforest beneath a dense tree canopy, the buds of Shlumbergera lock onto whichever direction precious sunlight comes from. So, if you move the cactus, those buds will likely twist towards the changed light source and drop off. Any change in temperature can also trigger bud drop – and your cactus is so reactive, it’ll notice being moved to another table, not just a different room.

You have until the flowerbuds start to form a teardrop shape or reach around ¼ inch long to decide where you want your cactus to sit until after it’s finished flowering, but then leave it be. Don’t even rotate it a half inch! It's even worth making a pencil mark on the pot and on the surface it sits on so you can line them back up if the pot gets knocked. If there’s not enough natural light in the spot you’d like it, then a basic dimmable LED grow light such as this from Walmart is the answer.

Now you know exactly what to do with a Christmas cactus in November to keep it happy and healthy. It takes around 4-6 weeks for buds to grow from those tiny pinpricks you first spotted into flamboyant flowers with flared petals, so there's still plenty of time to get festive blooms in time for the holidays. Just give your Shlumbergera the correct soil moisture, the humidity it craves and the stability it needs, and your plant will reward you with a phenomenal show. With each flower lasting up to 9 days and buds continuing to open over a few weeks, your plant's blooming period will last for at least a month, so you'll have plenty of time to enjoy the festive flowers.

As a keen natural crafter, her cutting patch and veg bed are increasingly being taken over by plants that can be dried or woven into a crafty project.

Is it legal for a neighbor to film your backyard? Sadly, the answer to this question is a bit wishy-washy: it depends. Like many of the issues I tackle in my Gardening Lawyer series, the legality of this kind of neighborhood surveillance depends on state and local laws, what the camera captures, and how it’s being used. Read on to find out what to do.

Sign up for the Gardening Know How newsletter today and receive a free copy of our e-book "How to Grow Delicious Tomatoes".

All cameras “see,” but some also “hear.” Does the fact that a surveillance camera also records sound impact its legality? It definitely can.

If the neighbor’s camera has a microphone, you may have another layer of legal protection. Rules about recording are separate and apart from rules about filming. Have you heard of wiretapping laws? Well, they can apply to surveillance camera audio. Just because the filming may be legal doesn’t mean capturing conversations is.

This is a federal issue that is determined under the terms of the federal Wiretap Act. It provides that unless a recording is taken as part of a criminal or civil investigation, at least one of the people whose private conversation is being recorded must give consent to the recording. The neighbor with the camera is not considered part of the conversation, and therefore cannot give that consent.

And that’s just a base level of protection. I live in California, and it is among the states that impose even stricter requirements for consent to recording conversations. The state Penal Code requires that all parties to a confidential conversation consent, although the statute includes a few exceptions.

The law rarely offers a clear litmus test for when a crime is committed. Think about it. Even killing someone is not a crime in some situations. So it’s no surprise that the question of when surveillance becomes harassment involves a weighing of relevant factors.

You need to know your local laws in order to move forward if your neighbor decides not to accommodate your concerns. Check your city laws and state laws. If you are part of an HOA, check the CC&Rs (Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions). Speak with an attorney if necessary to figure out your rights.

If you decide you want to take the matter to law enforcement or the courts, start documenting the surveillance and all written communications between you. This material will be helpful if you decide to file a police report or a civil claim against them.

Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler currently splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

#8192. How to Make a Handprint Calendar

Hanging around the house for the holidays? Spend an afternoon or two working on a handprint calendar for 2027. It’s an easy project anyone can complete, and little helpers will love to lend a hand or two. After all, you’ve got a long winter break to fill with activities and printables, and by New Year’s Eve, you’ll have reached the point where painting your kids’ hands sounds like a rational idea!

We love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Related: How to Make a Vision Board for Kids in 2027

Paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome.

Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. While you may have a perfect vision in mind for how to execute a gorgeous Christmas tree using their sweet little hands, they might have another idea, and that’s okay.

Now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Related: New Year’s Eve Confetti Poppers You Can Make with the Kids

Print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

Then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.
